GPR26 ↔ L-glutamic acid LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET VALIDATE medium confidence ipTM 0.94 · pTM 0.82
Rationale
The fold is confident (ipTM 0.94, iface pLDDT 94.5), but that is the expected result for a small molecule in a GPCR pocket and is not evidence of specificity. ChEMBL records no activity of glutamate at GPR26, while glutamate is measured at ≥76 distinct unrelated targets — a classic promiscuous metabolite that will dock confidently into one more pocket. Note also that all known glutamate GPCRs are class C receptors with an extracellular Venus-flytrap domain, whereas GPR26 is a class A 7TM orphan, so the modeled pocket is not the established glutamate-recognition architecture.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists only 1 disulfide bond and no glycosylation/lipidation features; the single PubMed "PTM" hit is an unrelated behavioural paper. No PTM artifact concern.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
Resolved to CHEMBL575060 (glutamate, SMILES C(CC(=O)O)[C@@H](C(=O)O)N, InChIKey WHUUTDBJXJRKMK-VKHMYHEASA-N). chembl_known_activity at Q8NDV2 (GPR26): 0 activities — no measured affinity at this receptor. chembl_ligand_promiscuity: 462 affinity measurements across ≥76 distinct targets (EAAT1/2, beta-2 adrenergic, D1 dopamine, CYPs, estrogen receptor, bacterial enzymes) — a highly promiscuous small metabolite.
Follow-up (not yet executed): Counter-screen: fold glutamate against 2-3 unrelated class-A GPCRs with the identical protocol — if it scores comparably everywhere, the GPR26 pose carries no information. If pursued, check whether contacts lie in the TM bundle (buried_fraction, pocket topology) and test functionally with a cAMP assay in GPR26-transfected cells, since GPR26 is constitutively Gs-active.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Counter-screen format: GPR26 vs. mock/parental cells and vs. a pocket-mutant GPR26, with a mGluR positive control and structurally related amino acids (D-glutamate, L-aspartate, GABA, L-glutamine) as specificity comparators)
Why this method
L-glutamate is a small-molecule soluble ligand and GPR26 is an orphan class A GPCR, so a functional signalling readout is the direct test of whether glutamate activates it. PLA and co-IP are unsuitable for a metabolite. GPR26 is reported to be constitutively active (Gs-coupled), so the assay must be designed to detect modulation of a high basal signal.
Target tissue(s)
Brain (cerebral cortex), Retina, Ovary (oocytes)
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA shows GPR26 RNA is tissue-enriched only in brain (4.2 nTPM). At the single-cell level it is highest in retinal amacrine cells (7.9 nCPM) and brain excitatory neurons (6.8 nCPM), with oocytes at 4.7. These are glutamatergic environments, so glutamate exposure is physiologically plausible. The assay itself is run in a heterologous cell line, not in tissue. Glutamate has no HPA entry, as it is a metabolite.
Cell type(s)
Brain excitatory neurons, Retinal amacrine cells, Retinal horizontal cells, Oocytes
Protocol notes
1) Express human GPR26 in HEK293 cells (and in a null-GPCR background) with an N-terminal epitope tag. Confirm surface or total expression by flow or ELISA. Compare to empty-vector cells. 2) Read out the Gs/cAMP axis (GloSensor or HTRF cAMP) and also run a CRE-luciferase reporter. Add Gq (calcium flux/IP1) and β-arrestin (PathHunter/BRET) readouts to cover alternative coupling. Run a glutamate dose-response from 1 nM to 10 mM in a buffer free of contaminating glutamate, using a glutamate-free medium and dialysed serum. 3) Run a glutamate-pocket mutant. Mutate the 2–3 AF3-contacting residues to alanine and check that any response is lost while surface expression is retained. 4) Where possible, run orthogonal binding evidence, such as a thermal shift or radioligand/MST binding on purified membranes. 5) Consider validating in primary neurons or retinal cultures with GPR26 knockdown.
Controls
Positive: a known glutamate GPCR (mGluR2 or mGluR5, or a class C receptor with Gi/Gq readout) with glutamate. Forskolin for cAMP assay dynamic range. Negative: mock-transfected/parental HEK293 cells, which also reveal endogenous glutamate responses. A non-related class A orphan GPCR expressed to the same level. Specificity: D-glutamate, L-aspartate, GABA and L-glutamine. Pocket mutant GPR26. Inverse-agonist or basal-activity comparison versus a known GPR26 constitutive-activity baseline.
Caveats
The verdict is LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET. The high ipTM/pLDDT is expected for a small molecule in a GPCR pocket and is not evidence of specificity. ChEMBL has no record of glutamate activity at GPR26, and glutamate is active at 76 or more other targets. The established glutamate GPCRs are class C receptors with a Venus-flytrap domain, while GPR26 is class A, so a negative result is the most likely outcome. GPR26 is constitutively active and an orphan, which can mask agonism. Glutamate at high millimolar concentrations can cause nonspecific effects through osmolarity, pH, or endogenous glutamate receptors and transporters in HEK cells. Glutamate also has no HPA data, so tissue choice is based on GPR26 alone. Brain tissue expression is low (4.2 nTPM), and extracellular glutamate in vivo is tightly regulated.

GPR26 ↔ acetylcholine LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET VALIDATE medium confidence ipTM 0.91 · pTM 0.81
Rationale
The fold is confident (ipTM 0.91, ligand pLDDT 80.5) but nothing ties that confidence to GPR26 specifically: acetylcholine has measured affinity at 105+ distinct targets in ChEMBL (a floor), and GPR26 is a UniProt-annotated orphan, constitutively active Gs-coupled receptor with no known ligand. Brain co-expression of GPR26 and the producer marker SLC10A4 makes an encounter possible but does not show binding. The ChEMBL lookup for activity at GPR26 failed twice with a server error, so novelty is unverified rather than confirmed.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists no glycosylation or lipidation features for GPR26, only 1 disulfide bond. The single pubmed_ptm_glycosylation hit is a knockout-mouse behaviour paper (pCREB), unrelated to receptor modification. There is no PTM concern for the pocket.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
UniProt describes GPR26 as an orphan receptor with constitutive Gs activity and no assigned endogenous ligand. The ChEMBL activity lookup at Q8NDV2 errored, so it is unverified. STRING, CellPhoneDB and pubmed_cooccurrence were not called because they do not index a metabolite partner.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule matched acetylcholine via the PubChem fallback only (SMILES CC(=O)OCC[N+](C)(C)C, InChIKey OIPILFWXSMYKGL-UHFFFAOYSA-N, identical to the supplied structure) and returned no ChEMBL id. I supplied CHEMBL667 from my own recall, not from a tool; the promiscuity result's serotonin, adenosine, adrenergic and cholinergic target list is consistent with it being acetylcholine, but the id was not tool-verified. chembl_ligand_promiscuity(CHEMBL667): 301 affinity measurements across 105 distinct targets sampled (a floor), spanning 5-HT, adenosine and adrenergic receptors, PDE4, AChE and nicotinic subunits, so the molecule is highly promiscuous. chembl_known_activity(Q8NDV2, CHEMBL667) returned HTTP 500 on both attempts, so there is no data either way on measured activity at GPR26; this is not a confirmed zero. The supplied min_sep of 2.23 Å is on the short side and the supplied BSA of 450 Å2 is unremarkable for a molecule this small; no buried_fraction or pocket topology was available and no fold was run.
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Retry chembl_known_activity for Q8NDV2 / CHEMBL667 once the ChEMBL API recovers. 2) Counter-screen: fold acetylcholine against two or three unrelated class A GPCRs, plus a muscarinic receptor (e.g. CHRM1 or CHRM2) as a positive control, and compare ligand pLDDT, buried_fraction and pocket topology; confidence that is equal everywhere would confirm non-specificity. 3) Inspect the GPR26 pose for whether contacts sit in the transmembrane bundle and whether there is an acidic or aromatic cage for the quaternary ammonium. 4) If it survives, run a cAMP assay in GPR26-expressing cells with and without acetylcholine, noting that high constitutive activity will complicate agonist readout.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Counter-screen format: GPR26-transfected vs. mock/parental cells, plus a binding-pocket mutant arm and a muscarinic/nicotinic receptor-positive control arm)
Why this method
Acetylcholine is a small-molecule neurotransmitter, not a protein that can be probed by PLA or co-IP. GPR26 is an orphan, constitutively active Gs-coupled GPCR, so the testable question is whether acetylcholine changes receptor signalling (cAMP) above the constitutive baseline, compared with a receptor-null background. Because ACh binds 105+ other targets, the counter-screen (parental cells, a pocket mutant, and a structurally unrelated cholinergic ligand) matters more than the positive readout.
Target tissue(s)
Brain (cerebral cortex), Retina, Ovary (oocytes)
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA shows GPR26 RNA is tissue-enriched in brain (4.2 nTPM). At the single-cell level it is highest in retinal amacrine cells (7.9 nCPM) and brain excitatory neurons (6.8), with lower levels in other brain neurons (5.0), oocytes (4.7), retinal horizontal cells (4.1) and inhibitory neurons (2.7). HPA has no acetylcholine entry because it is a metabolite. The ligand side comes from the SLC10A4 cholinergic-marker co-expression noted in the triage, so brain and retina, where cholinergic neurons (e.g. starburst amacrine cells in retina) sit near GPR26-expressing neurons, are the relevant contexts.
Cell type(s)
Brain excitatory neurons, Retinal amacrine cells, Brain inhibitory neurons, Retinal horizontal cells
Protocol notes
1) Express human GPR26 (epitope-tagged, with surface expression confirmed by anti-tag flow cytometry or ELISA) in HEK293 cells. Include a mock/parental arm and a GPR26 pocket-mutant arm (alanine substitutions of the residues contacting ACh in the AF3 pose). Use a cAMP readout (GloSensor or HTRF) with an acetylcholine dose-response from 1 nM to 1 mM. Add an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (e.g. physostigmine or neostigmine) so ACh is not degraded, and add atropine and mecamylamine to block endogenous muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. Because the receptor is constitutively active, also test an inverse-agonist or basal-signalling readout, and a β-arrestin recruitment assay (e.g. PathHunter or Tango) as an orthogonal, Gs-independent readout. 2) Run a binding orthogonal check on GPR26 membranes: a competition or thermal-shift assay (e.g. cellular thermal shift or nanoDSF on purified receptor) with ACh versus choline and carbachol. 3) Test specificity by comparing with other orphan or aminergic GPCRs expressed to similar levels. 4) Optionally, follow up in primary retinal or cortical neuron cultures with GPR26 knockdown or knockout, measuring cAMP or PKA-substrate phosphorylation (pCREB) after ACh in the presence of cholinergic receptor antagonists.
Controls
Positive: M-receptor Gs-compatible or Gq control, e.g. M1/M3 with ACh (calcium flux), and forskolin for maximal cAMP. Negative: mock/parental cells, untagged-vector cells, a GPR26 pocket mutant, choline and an unrelated neurotransmitter (e.g. dopamine, serotonin) on GPR26, and heat-inactivated or vehicle-only treatment. Another orphan GPCR expressed at the same level serves as a specificity control.
Caveats
The verdict is LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET: the high ipTM (0.91) and ligand pLDDT (80.5) do not show GPR26-specific binding, because AF3 will likely dock ACh into many pockets and ACh has measured affinity at 105+ targets. The ChEMBL lookup for GPR26 activity failed, so novelty is unverified and should be rechecked by hand. GPR26 is constitutively active, so a small ligand effect may be hard to see over the high basal cAMP; inverse agonism or a modest shift could be the real phenotype. HPA gives no subcellular or protein-level data for GPR26 (RNA only, low expression of about 4–8 nCPM), and acetylcholine has no HPA record. Endogenous muscarinic receptors in HEK293 (M3) can create false positives unless blocked or the parental control is used. ACh is unstable (esterase hydrolysis), so fresh stocks and esterase inhibitors are needed.

GPR101 ↔ L-glutamic acid LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET VALIDATE medium confidence ipTM 0.89 · pTM 0.63
Rationale
L-glutamic acid resolved only via PubChem (no ChEMBL id returned; ChEMBL API returned 500 on both retries, so no measured activity or promiscuity count could be retrieved), but glutamate is a ubiquitous endogenous metabolite active at dozens of targets (iGluRs, class C mGluRs, transporters) and its well-characterized receptors bind it in a large extracellular Venus-flytrap domain, not the class A transmembrane pocket of GPR101 (UniProt Q96P66, "Orphan receptor", 7 TM, Glycoprotein). The AF3 numbers (ipTM 0.89, iface pLDDT 88, BSA 451 Å2) are exactly the expected result for a tiny zwitterionic metabolite dropped into any GPCR pocket and are not on the same scale as protein-pair confidence, so they add nothing about specificity. Coexpression context is at least coherent (GPR101 is brain/neuron-enriched in HPA; producer gene SLC1A2 is the astrocytic glutamate transporter), which keeps this from being IMPLAUSIBLE.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists 2 Glycosylation sites and 1 disulfide on GPR101 (typical GPCR N-terminal/ECL glycans); pubmed_ptm_glycosylation returned 1 unrelated hit (GnRH-(1-5)/EGFR transactivation). Not a specific concern for a TM-bundle small-molecule pocket.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule: PubChem fallback, SMILES C(CC(=O)O)[C@@H](C(=O)O)N, InChIKey WHUUTDBJXJRKMK-VKHMYHEASA-N, no ChEMBL id. chembl_known_activity and chembl_ligand_promiscuity both failed with ChEMBL 500 errors on two attempts — no measured affinity at Q96P66 could be confirmed or excluded; glutamate is nonetheless a canonically promiscuous endogenous ligand.
Follow-up (not yet executed): Retry ChEMBL once the API is up to confirm zero measured activity at Q96P66 and glutamate's target count. The decisive experiment is a counter-screen: fold glutamate against 2-3 unrelated class A GPCRs — if the pose is equally confident everywhere, the signal is pocket-generic. Also inspect whether contacts lie within the TM bundle (orthosteric) rather than on extracellular loops, and validate with a cell-based cAMP/BRET assay for glutamate at GPR101.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Counter-screen format: dose-response of L-glutamate on GPR101-expressing vs. mock/parental cells, with GPR101 pocket-mutant arm and iGluR/mGluR blockers present)
Why this method
Glutamate is a small diffusible metabolite, not a protein, so PLA/co-IP cannot test binding; GPR101 is an orphan class A GPCR that couples constitutively to Gs, so a functional readout (cAMP) is the appropriate test of whether glutamate acts as an agonist or modulator. The 'promiscuous pocket' verdict requires a counter-screen showing specificity versus empty-vector cells and other GPCRs.
Target tissue(s)
brain
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA shows GPR101 RNA is tissue-specific to brain (11.5 nTPM), with no other tissue enriched. Glutamate has no HPA entry, but it is abundant in brain, so a brain-derived neuronal context is the only one where both could meet. Assays should still be run in recombinant HEK293 cells because endogenous GPR101 is low.
Cell type(s)
Other brain neurons, Brain inhibitory neurons
Protocol notes
1) Transfect HEK293 (or CHO) cells with GPR101 or empty vector. Add a tagged-receptor surface-expression check (e.g. FLAG ELISA or flow cytometry). Measure cAMP (HTRF or GloSensor) after a glutamate dose-response from 1 nM to 10 mM, including a pre-incubation with an iGluR/mGluR antagonist cocktail (e.g. MK-801, NBQX, LY341495) to rule out endogenous glutamate receptor effects. 2) Because GPR101 is constitutively active, compare the basal signal GPR101 vs mock and test for inverse agonism or agonism relative to forskolin. Add a second readout (CRE-luciferase or β-arrestin recruitment, e.g. PathHunter/NanoBiT) to confirm. 3) Mutate the AF3-predicted contact residues in the TM pocket (e.g. alanine scan of the 3-5 residues that contact the carboxylates and amine) and test for loss of response. 4) Optionally confirm binding with a label-free or radioligand method (e.g. [3H]-glutamate binding on membranes, or thermal shift/NanoBRET competition), and test neuronal cultures or iPSC-derived neurons for endogenous responses.
Controls
Positive: forskolin (cAMP ceiling) and a glutamate-responsive GPCR such as mGluR2 or mGluR5 cells as an assay-validity control. Negative: empty-vector/parental cells; unrelated orphan class A GPCR (e.g. GPR3 or GPR161) as a promiscuity counter-screen; related amino acids (D-glutamate, L-aspartate, L-glutamine, GABA) for selectivity; GPR101 pocket-mutant.
Caveats
The verdict is LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET: AF3 ipTM 0.89 and BSA 451 Å2 for a small zwitterion in a GPCR pocket are not specificity evidence, so a negative result is the expected outcome. GPR101 is constitutively active, so the dynamic range for agonism is small and an effect may only be seen as inverse agonism or modulation. Millimolar glutamate may cause nonspecific effects (osmolarity, pH, transporter uptake, endogenous glutamate receptors in HEK cells), so potency should be physiologically plausible (low µM to sub-mM). HPA has no data for glutamate (a metabolite) and no subcellular location for GPR101, so tissue co-occurrence is inferred only from brain enrichment and from the producer gene SLC1A2 mentioned in the triage. ChEMBL data were unavailable, so literature promiscuity has not been checked. GPR101 is annotated as a glycoprotein, but glycosylation is not expected to matter for a TM-pocket ligand.

Rationale
ChEMBL records no measured activity of T3 (CHEMBL1544) at MRGPRF (Q96AM1), so the pair is not already known, but nothing beyond the confident fold (ipTM 0.89, ligand pLDDT 70.3) supports specificity. The promiscuity lookup failed twice with a server error, so the number of distinct T3 targets is unmeasured here, which is why confidence is low. MRGPRF is an orphan GPCR that UniProt suggests may bind a neuropeptide (a different chemical class), and the listed producer gene DIO3 is, to my knowledge, the deiodinase that inactivates T3 rather than making it, so the production-site link is weak.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: Glycoprotein keyword with 1 annotated glycosylation site (location not checked; on a GPCR this is typically the extracellular N-terminus). pubmed_ptm_glycosylation: 0 hits. There is no evidence that the glycan affects a transmembrane-bundle pocket, so this is not treated as a PTM artifact.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
ChEMBL: no measured activity for T3 at MRGPRF. STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence were not queried because they do not index a metabolite against a receptor. UniProt lists MRGPRF as an orphan receptor ("may bind to a neuropeptide").
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule: CHEMBL1544 (resolved via PubChem), SMILES and InChIKey AUYYCJSJGJYCDS-LBPRGKRZSA-N match the supplied structure. chembl_known_activity at Q96AM1 (target CHEMBL4523903): 0 activities, 0 affinity measurements. chembl_ligand_promiscuity: HTTP 500 on both attempts, so no target count was obtained. From background knowledge, not tool output: T3 is a hormone with established high-affinity targets (thyroid hormone receptors, serum binding proteins, transporters), so it would be expected to dock confidently into other pockets too. Supplied fold metrics: ligand pLDDT 70.3, interface pLDDT 86.6, min separation 3.01 A (no clash), BSA 841 A2. No fold was run here, so there is no ligands block: buried fraction and pocket topology (transmembrane bundle vs loops) are unverified.
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Counter-screen: fold T3 against two or three unrelated GPCRs (including other MRGPR family members) and check whether ipTM and ligand pLDDT are equally high; that is the experiment that would establish specificity. 2) Read the ligand pose for MRGPRF-T3: buried fraction and whether contacts are on the transmembrane bundle rather than loops or the cytoplasmic face. 3) Re-run chembl_ligand_promiscuity when ChEMBL is back up. 4) Re-check the producer-gene assignment: DIO1/DIO2 (T4 to T3) are the more appropriate producers than DIO3. 5) If the pose survives the counter-screen, test T3 in an MRGPRF functional assay (beta-arrestin recruitment or Ca2+/cAMP) with reverse T3 and T4 as controls.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Counter-screen format: dose-response of T3 vs. structural analogs (T4, rT3, Tiratricol, GC-1) on MRGPRF-expressing vs. parental/mock cells, plus a pocket-mutant arm)
Why this method
T3 is a small-molecule hormone and MRGPRF is a plasma-membrane orphan GPCR, so PLA/co-IP are poorly suited (no protein partner, and a small-molecule ligand can't be detected by antibody pairs). A functional readout in receptor-expressing cells directly tests agonism and also lets us counter-screen for non-specific pocket binding, which is the verdict's concern.
Target tissue(s)
Fallopian tube, Smooth muscle (smooth muscle cells / vascular smooth muscle), Placenta/decidua (decidual stromal cells), Kidney (podocytes, pericytes)
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA gives no RNA tissue-specific nTPM for MRGPRF; the only protein-level signal is in fallopian tube, and single-cell RNA is highest in smooth muscle cells (161.7 nCPM), decidual stromal cells (139.8), vascular smooth muscle cells (132.8), peritubular myoid cells (104.4) and pericytes (89.0). T3 has no HPA entry (it is a circulating hormone, not a gene product), so the ligand is systemically available to all of these; the receptor-bearing cells define the tissues.
Cell type(s)
Smooth muscle cells, Vascular smooth muscle cells, Decidual stromal cells, Pericytes, Peritubular myoid cells
Protocol notes
1) Express human MRGPRF (N-terminal tag, e.g. HA/FLAG, to confirm surface expression by flow or ELISA) in HEK293 or CHO cells. Use parental cells and a related MRGPR (e.g. MRGPRX1 or MRGPRE) as negative-receptor controls. Read out Gi/Gq/Gs signalling in parallel: cAMP (GloSensor/HTRF), Ca2+ flux (Fluo-4/FLIPR), and β-arrestin recruitment (PathHunter/BRET). MRGPRF is reported to couple to Gi, so include forskolin-stimulated cAMP inhibition. 2) Run 10-point T3 dose-response (1 nM-100 µM) in serum-free or charcoal-stripped medium, with BSA carrier to limit nonspecific lipophilic binding. Compare T3 with T4, reverse T3, Tiratricol, and an unrelated iodinated/lipophilic compound to measure the promiscuity that the failed lookup could not. 3) Mutate 2-3 predicted pocket contact residues from the AF3 pose to Ala and check loss of response. Confirm any hit in a native cell: primary or cultured vascular smooth muscle cells or decidual stromal cells, with MRGPRF siRNA/CRISPR knockdown. Optionally run a thyroid hormone receptor (TR) antagonist or nuclear receptor control to exclude genomic effects. Include a short time-course, since genomic TR effects are slow and GPCR signalling is rapid. controls="Positive: a known MRGPRF agonist (the peptide RFRP/γ2-MSH, or angiotensin-(1-7)/β-alanine reported for MRGPR family members) and forskolin/ATP/ionomycin for assay readiness. Negative: parental cells, empty vector, vehicle/BSA, MRGPRF pocket-mutants, and an unrelated GPCR transfected cell line. Specificity: T4/rT3/Tiratricol and a TR antagonist; compare EC50 with physiological free T3 (~pM-low nM) to judge relevance.
Controls
Positive: a known MRGPRF agonist (e.g. angiotensin-(1-7) or γ2-MSH/RFRP-type peptide as reported for MRGPRF/MRGPR family) plus assay-readiness controls (forskolin, ATP, ionomycin). Negative: parental/empty-vector cells, a different MRGPR family member, vehicle/BSA, and the MRGPRF pocket-mutant. Specificity: T4, reverse T3, Tiratricol and an unrelated lipophilic iodinated compound; compare EC50 to physiological free T3 (pM to low nM) to judge relevance.
Caveats
Verdict is LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET with low confidence: the T3 promiscuity lookup failed, so the number of T3 targets is unknown. A confident fold (ipTM 0.89) with ligand pLDDT 70.3 does not show specificity; T3 is a lipophilic, amphipathic ligand that could fit many hydrophobic pockets. MRGPRF's suggested natural ligand is a neuropeptide (different chemical class). DIO3 as a producer is doubtful, since it inactivates T3 (converting T3 to 3,3'-T2) rather than making it. HPA RNA tissue data are absent, protein data are limited to fallopian tube, and the intensity value looks like a raw/unnormalized number, so expression evidence is weak and cell-type specific. Effects at supraphysiological T3 doses may be nonspecific; T3 also acts through nuclear TRs and via integrin αvβ3, which can confound native-cell readouts. MRGPRF is also annotated in HPA as vesicular as well as plasma membrane, so surface expression must be verified.

Nothing beyond the confident fold (ipTM 0.88) supports glutamate binding GPR12 specifically, and a confident pose is the expected result for a small molecule in a GPCR pocket. UniProt describes GPR12 as constitutively active with putative lipid ligands (sphingosylphosphorylcholine, sphingosine-1-phosphate), a different chemical class from a small polar amino acid, and the supplied p_twoway of 0.055 is not significant. Both ChEMBL checks failed with server errors on two attempts, so novelty and promiscuity are unverified; that is why confidence is low.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists GPR12 as a glycoprotein and palmitoylated lipoprotein (2 glycosylation sites, 1 lipidation site, 2 modified residues, 1 disulfide). The glycosylation sites are probably on the extracellular N-terminus or loops and could affect pocket access, but their position relative to the pose was not checked. The pubmed_ptm_glycosylation hits (7) were not informative about GPR12 glycosylation. This is not the main concern for this candidate.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
ChEMBL activity lookup was unavailable (server error), so prior pharmacology for this pair could not be checked. UniProt's function text does not mention glutamate; it names only the lipids SPC and S1P as possible endogenous ligands. STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence do not apply to a metabolite partner and were not run.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule returned CHEMBL575060 (via the PubChem fallback), SMILES C(CC(=O)O)[C@@H](C(=O)O)N, InChIKey WHUUTDBJXJRKMK-VKHMYHEASA-N, matching the folded structure. chembl_known_activity (P47775) and chembl_ligand_promiscuity both returned HTTP 500 on two attempts each, so there is NO ChEMBL data: neither absence of measured affinity at GPR12 nor a promiscuity count was established. No fold was re-run, so pocket topology (transmembrane bundle vs loops) is unchecked; supplied metrics are BSA 438 Å2, min separation 3.14 Å, ligand pLDDT 83.8.
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Re-run chembl_known_activity (P47775 / CHEMBL575060) and chembl_ligand_promiscuity when ChEMBL is back; a measured affinity would change the verdict to ALREADY_KNOWN. 2) Counter-screen: fold glutamate against two or three unrelated class A GPCRs, with a real metabotropic glutamate receptor as positive control; similar ipTM everywhere would confirm the pocket is non-specific. 3) Inspect the pose for contacts on the transmembrane bundle and compare it with the lipid-binding site in the available GPR12 structure. 4) If the candidate is still pursued, test glutamate in a cAMP assay on GPR12-expressing cells, bearing in mind the receptor's high constitutive Gs activity.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Counter-screen format: dose-response of L-glutamate on GPR12-expressing vs. mock cells, benchmarked against S1P/SPC, plus pocket-mutant and other-amino-acid specificity arms)
Why this method
Glutamate is a small diffusible metabolite, not a protein, so PLA and co-IP can't be used. GPR12 is a constitutively active Gi/o-coupled orphan GPCR, so a functional readout (cAMP change) tests whether glutamate modulates it specifically. The verdict also calls for a counter-screen before believing the pose.
Target tissue(s)
brain, retina
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA shows GPR12 RNA is tissue-enriched in brain (11.6 nTPM) and retina (7.8 nTPM), with lower levels in skin (5.1). Both brain and retina are glutamatergic tissues, so glutamate is physiologically present there. The assay itself should run in a heterologous cell line, because no HPA data exists for glutamate and native GPR12 levels are low.
Cell type(s)
HEK293 (heterologous GPR12 expression), CHO-K1 (heterologous GPR12 expression), cortical/hippocampal neurons (secondary, native context)
Protocol notes
1) Express GPR12 (with an epitope tag to confirm surface expression by flow or ELISA) in HEK293 or CHO cells. Use mock cells and an unrelated constitutively active Gi/o GPCR as negative controls. Measure cAMP with a GloSensor or HTRF assay, with forskolin to reveal Gi-mediated suppression. Alternatively use a BRET Gi/β-arrestin assay. The basal constitutive-activity baseline matters, so compare against an inverse agonist or a GPR12 knockdown if one is available. 2) Run an L-glutamate dose-response (1 nM–10 mM). Include D-glutamate, L-aspartate, L-glutamine and GABA as chemical-neighbour specificity controls. Run mGluR/iGluR-null cells, or add mGluR antagonists, to rule out endogenous glutamate receptors. 3) Test the AF3 pose by mutating 2–3 predicted pocket contact residues (for example to Ala) while keeping surface expression equal. Loss of any glutamate effect supports pocket specificity. Optionally add a binding-level orthogonal check such as thermal shift/DSF on purified GPR12 or a radioligand/competition assay. 4) Counter-screen: test glutamate on 2–3 unrelated GPCRs, using the same pocket-type receptors where AF3 also predicts glutamate binding. This directly tests the promiscuous-pocket hypothesis.
Controls
Positive: SPC and S1P on GPR12 (disputed but the best available), plus forskolin to set the cAMP window. Negative: mock/empty-vector cells, a pocket-mutant GPR12, an unrelated GPCR, and D-Glu, Asp, Gln and GABA as chemical neighbours. Use pH- and osmolarity-matched vehicle (for example NaCl), since glutamate is acidic.
Caveats
Verdict is LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET with low confidence. A confident AF3 pose for a small molecule is expected in any GPCR pocket, and the p_twoway of 0.055 is not significant. The putative GPR12 ligands are lipids (SPC, S1P), and even those are disputed. The ChEMBL novelty and promiscuity checks failed, so prior activity data are unverified and should be re-run. Constitutive GPR12 activity can mask small agonist effects. High-millimolar glutamate may cause nonspecific effects (osmolarity, pH, endogenous glutamate transporters or receptors), so a physiologically relevant response should appear at or below roughly 100 µM. HPA has no subcellular location or protein-level data for GPR12, and there is no entry for glutamate, so tissue choice rests on RNA only.

GPR12 ↔ 4-aminobutanoic acid LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET VALIDATE medium confidence ipTM 0.87 · pTM 0.78
Rationale
ChEMBL records no measured activity of GABA (CHEMBL96) at GPR12 (P47775), but GABA has 277 affinity measurements across at least 75 distinct, largely unrelated targets, so a confident fold (ipTM 0.87) into one more pocket is not specific evidence. UniProt gives GPR12's proposed endogenous ligands as the lipids S1P and SPC, a different chemical class from a small zwitterionic amino acid, and the supplied BSA of 386 A2 only shows the molecule is contacted, not that it sits in the orthosteric site. Brain co-expression with the GABA producer GAD2 makes an encounter possible but does not show binding.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists 2 glycosylation sites, 1 lipidation (palmitate) and 2 modified residues on GPR12. For a GPCR these are most likely N-terminal/extracellular glycans and a C-terminal palmitate, which would not obviously occlude a transmembrane-bundle pocket, but site positions were not checked. The PubMed PTM hits were about GPR3, SPC and unrelated proteins, with nothing specific to GPR12 glycosylation. Not treated as the main concern.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
No ChEMBL activity for GABA at GPR12. UniProt describes GPR12 as a constitutively active Gs-coupled orphan receptor with S1P and SPC as possible endogenous lipid ligands; GABA is not mentioned. STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence were not queried because they index protein pairs, not a metabolite against a receptor.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule: 4-aminobutanoic acid = CHEMBL96, SMILES C(CC(=O)O)CN, InChIKey BTCSSZJGUNDROE-UHFFFAOYSA-N (matches the supplied structure). chembl_known_activity at P47775 (CHEMBL5006): 0 activities (first call returned a server error; the retry succeeded). chembl_ligand_promiscuity: 277 affinity measurements at >=75 distinct targets (a floor), including GABA-A receptors, 5-HT3A, dopamine D1, FFAR3, several CYPs, arylsulfatase A and ferritin light chain. Many of these are probably inactive screening records, but the molecule is broadly profiled and not selective.
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run here. (1) Counter-screen: fold GABA against two or three unrelated class A GPCRs, plus GPR3 and GPR6 as close paralogs, and compare ligand pLDDT and buried fraction; similar confidence everywhere would confirm non-specificity. (2) Re-fold GPR12 with GABA and read the ligands block: buried_fraction and whether the contacts are on transmembrane segments (the orthosteric lipid pocket) or on loops or the cytoplasmic face. (3) Fold S1P or SPC as a positive-control comparison. (4) If the pose still looks specific, test GABA in a GPR12 cAMP assay; the receptor's high constitutive Gs activity means an inverse-agonist or modulator readout is needed.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Counter-screen format: GPR12 vs. parental/mock cells and vs. GABA-A/B receptor-expressing cells, with S1P/SPC as reference agonists and a pocket-mutant arm)
Why this method
GABA is a small-molecule ligand, not a protein. PLA and co-IP can't detect it, so a functional readout in a receptor-expressing cell is the only practical test. GPR12 is a constitutively active Gs/Gi-coupled orphan GPCR, so cAMP (Gs/Gi) and β-arrestin assays in GPR12-transfected cells versus mock cells can show whether GABA modulates it specifically.
Target tissue(s)
brain, retina, skin 1
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA RNA data show GPR12 enriched in brain (11.6 nTPM), retina (7.8) and skin 1 (5.1). Brain is where GABAergic signalling is physiologically relevant, so it is the key tissue for follow-up. There is no HPA data for GABA itself, so the assay is run in recombinant cells first and tissue relevance is inferred from GPR12 expression alone.
Cell type(s)
neurons (cortical/striatal), retinal neurons, HEK293 or CHO cells overexpressing GPR12 (primary assay system)
Protocol notes
1) Express GPR12 in HEK293 cells with a cAMP biosensor (GloSensor or HTRF cAMP). Run GABA dose-response (1 nM–1 mM) against mock-transfected cells and a vector control. Compare with S1P and SPC as reference ligands. Use an inverse agonist or Gi/Gs readout to account for the high basal activity. 2) Run a PathHunter or BRET β-arrestin recruitment assay in parallel. Test GABA, the GABA-A agonist muscimol, and the GABA-B agonist baclofen to check that any effect is not mediated by endogenous GABA receptors. 3) Mutate the predicted contact residues from the AF3 pose, plus a known S1P-site residue as a comparison. If the response is specific, it should be lost with the pocket mutants. 4) If a signal appears, confirm binding orthogonally, for example with a radioligand/[3H]-GABA competition or SPR/thermal shift on purified receptor in nanodiscs.
Controls
Positive: S1P or SPC on GPR12 (reference lipid agonists, although reported activity is debated), forskolin for cAMP assay dynamic range. Negative: mock/parental cells, an unrelated Gs/Gi-coupled GPCR (e.g. another orphan receptor) challenged with GABA, a structurally similar inert amino acid (glycine or β-alanine), vehicle. Use GABA-A/B antagonists (bicuculline, CGP-55845) to exclude endogenous GABA receptor effects.
Caveats
The verdict is LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET. ChEMBL has no measured GABA activity at GPR12, and GABA has activity at at least 75 targets. So the ipTM of 0.87 is weak evidence of specificity. The 386 A2 buried surface area does not show that GABA sits in the orthosteric site. The expected outcome is a negative result, and a negative result should be reported as such. GPR12 is constitutively active, so ligand-induced changes may be small. Overexpression can create artifacts, and HEK293 cells express endogenous GABA-related and other GPCRs. GABA is zwitterionic with likely low affinity, so any effect may only appear at millimolar concentrations, which is not physiologically meaningful. Orphan GPCR ligand assignments are often not reproducible. HPA has no protein-level or single-cell data for GPR12, and no data for GABA as a non-protein.

Acetylcholine is a small-molecule ligand, not a protein, so PLA and co-IP don't apply. GPR139 is an orphan Gq/11-coupled GPCR, so a functional readout (Ca2+ flux or IP1) in receptor-expressing cells against a mock control directly tests whether acetylcholine activates it. The same assay can separate specific activation from a promiscuous-pocket artifact.

brain, pituitary gland

HPA shows GPR139 RNA is tissue-specific to brain (2.2 nTPM). Its single-cell signal is highest in lactotrophs (68.2 nCPM), which are pituitary cells. Acetylcholine has no HPA entry because it is a metabolite. Cholinergic innervation of the brain gives the ligand side, so recombinant GPR139 cells are the practical test system, with habenula or pituitary-derived cells as follow-up.

Lactotrophs, Habenular/striatal neurons (brain)
Protocol notes
1) Stably or transiently express human GPR139 in HEK293 or CHO-K1 cells, with Gα15 or Gqi5 co-expression if coupling is weak. Use mock-transfected parental cells in parallel. Controls
Positive: L-Trp, L-Phe and JNJ-63533054 on GPR139 cells; carbachol on M1/M3-expressing cells as an assay-validity control. Negative: mock/parental cells, vehicle, atropine pre-treatment, and an unrelated Gq GPCR. Specificity: an unrelated quaternary ammonium compound such as choline, which tests whether any positive effect is specific to acetylcholine.
Caveats
The verdict is LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET. Acetylcholine binds many unrelated targets, so a high ipTM (0.87) is weak evidence of specificity. The known GPR139 activators are aromatic amino acids, a different chemical class, and the ChEMBL lookup for GPR139 activity failed, so novelty is unverified. HEK/CHO cells express endogenous muscarinic receptors that can give false-positive Ca2+ signals. Acetylcholine is rapidly hydrolysed in serum and by cellular esterases. HPA has no subcellular location or protein-level data for GPR139, and RNA expression is low (2.2 nTPM in brain). A negative result in a heterologous system doesn't rule out a native-context effect.

GPR50 ↔ leukotriene D4 LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET VALIDATE medium confidence ipTM 0.87 · pTM 0.54
Rationale
The confident fold (ipTM 0.87) is the expected result for a flexible lipid in a GPCR pocket and nothing independent supports specificity for GPR50. GPR50 is an orphan melatonin-related receptor, enriched in pituitary lactotrophs and at the plasma membrane, with no lipid ligand in its UniProt function text. Leukotriene D4 resolved only via PubChem with no ChEMBL id, so neither ChEMBL check could be run; novelty and promiscuity are therefore unmeasured, not shown.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt for GPR50 lists no glycosylation or lipidation features, only one disulfide bond. The 4 pubmed_ptm_glycosylation hits are functional papers, not PTM reports. There is no receptor-side PTM artifact concern.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
No measured LTD4–GPR50 pharmacology was retrievable (no ChEMBL id). UniProt describes GPR50 as an orphan melatonin-related receptor with scaffold and signalling-modulator roles (TGFBR1, KAT5) and names no small-molecule ligand. STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence were not run, as they index protein pairs rather than a metabolite against a receptor.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule returned a PubChem-only record (no ChEMBL id); SMILES and InChIKey (YEESKJGWJFYOOK-IJHYULJSSA-N) match the supplied structure. Because there is no ChEMBL id, chembl_known_activity at GPR50 (Q13585) and chembl_ligand_promiscuity were not run. From background knowledge, not tool output: LTD4 is the high-affinity agonist of CYSLTR1 and also acts at CYSLTR2, so it already has dedicated cognate GPCRs. Supplied fold metrics: ligand pLDDT 63.1 (only moderate, well below the interface pLDDT of 85.7), min separation 2.59 Å, 224 contacts, BSA 865 Å². No buried fraction or pocket topology was available, so whether the pose sits in the transmembrane bundle is unknown.
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Counter-screen: fold LTD4 against two or three unrelated class A GPCRs, plus CYSLTR1 as a positive control. If ipTM is similar everywhere, the GPR50 pose is non-specific. 2) Check the pose's buried fraction and pocket topology to see whether contacts are in the transmembrane bundle or on loops or the long C-terminal tail. 3) Look up LTD4 in ChEMBL by InChIKey to recover the activity and promiscuity records. 4) If the pose survives the counter-screen, test GPR50 in a functional assay (β-arrestin or Ca2+) with LTD4 against CYSLTR1 as control.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Counter-screen design: GPR50 vs. empty-vector vs. CysLT1R/CysLT2R (positive control receptors), plus a lipid-specificity panel (LTC4, LTE4, LTB4, other lipids))
Why this method
LTD4 is a small lipid ligand, so a direct functional readout in receptor-expressing cells is more informative than PLA or co-IP, which don't suit a small molecule. The verdict calls for a counter-screen, so specificity must be tested against mock cells, known LTD4 receptors and related lipids.
Target tissue(s)
pituitary gland
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA shows GPR50 RNA is tissue-enriched only in the pituitary gland (15.6 nTPM), and in lactotrophs (4.4 nCPM) at the single-cell level. LTD4 has no HPA entry because it is a metabolite, not a gene product. The primary assay should use a recombinant heterologous system (HEK293) and be followed up in pituitary lactotroph-like cells (e.g. GH3 or primary pituitary cultures).
Cell type(s)
Lactotrophs
Protocol notes
1) Transfect HEK293 (or CHO) cells with epitope-tagged GPR50, empty vector, or CysLT1R as a positive control. Confirm surface expression by anti-tag flow cytometry or ELISA. Use a promiscuous Gα16 or Gqi5 chimera, or run parallel Gs/Gi/Gq readouts, because GPR50 coupling is unknown. 2) Run LTD4 dose-response curves (1 pM–10 µM) with Ca2+ flux (Fluo-4), cAMP (GloSensor or HTRF) and β-arrestin recruitment (PathHunter or BRET). Compare GPR50 against mock cells, and test LTC4, LTE4, LTB4 and a non-related lipid in the same panel. 3) Use the CysLT1 antagonist montelukast to test whether any response is receptor-specific. If a response appears, confirm binding with a radioligand ([3H]-LTD4) or a competition-binding assay on membranes. Then repeat in pituitary lactotroph-like cells with GPR50 knockdown or knockout. 4) Use fresh LTD4 stocks with a stability check, because LTD4 is labile and is converted to LTE4. Include a serum-free buffer and a bestatin/serine-borate peptidase inhibitor control, if appropriate.
Controls
Positive: CysLT1R + LTD4 (Ca2+ flux, EC50 in the low nM range) and a non-GPR50 receptor-specific agonist for assay validity. Negative: empty-vector or parental cells, an unrelated orphan GPCR given the same lipid (to estimate promiscuity), vehicle-only, and montelukast pre-treatment. GPR50 can show constitutive activity or heteromerize with MT1/MT2, so also include melatonin on MT1-expressing cells as a pathway comparator.
Caveats
The AF3 ipTM of 0.87 for a flexible lipid in a GPCR pocket is expected and does not show specificity. Neither ChEMBL check could be run, so novelty and promiscuity are unmeasured. GPR50 is an orphan receptor with unknown G-protein coupling, and it is reported to heterodimerize with MT1/MT2 and to be constitutively active, which could produce false negatives or confound the readouts. GPR50 RNA expression is low (4.4 nCPM in lactotrophs), and HEK293 cells may endogenously express CysLT receptors, so a CysLT1/2 antagonist or knockout background is needed. LTD4 is unstable, and its metabolites could be responsible for any effect. A negative result in heterologous cells would not exclude a context-dependent interaction.

GPR15 ↔ prostaglandin D2 LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET VALIDATE low confidence ipTM 0.86 · pTM 0.78
Rationale
The confident fold (ipTM 0.86) is the expected result for a small lipid in a GPCR pocket and nothing retrieved supports specificity: UniProt gives GPR15's natural ligand as the chemokine-like polypeptide GPR15LG, a different chemical class from a prostanoid, and HPA shows no particular overlap between the producer PTGDS and GPR15's intestine/lymphocyte expression. Both ChEMBL queries (known activity at P49685 and promiscuity) returned HTTP 500 on two attempts each, so neither prior measured affinity nor the molecule's target count could be checked; confidence is low for that reason.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists no glycosylation or lipidation features for GPR15 (one modified residue; Phosphoprotein keyword). PubMed (PMID 33758080) reports tyrosine sulfation and O-glycosylation of GPR15 regulating its interaction with GPR15L; this presumably concerns the extracellular N-terminus and the peptide ligand rather than a small molecule in the transmembrane bundle, so it is not the main concern here.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
ChEMBL activity lookup at GPR15 failed (500 errors), so prior pharmacology for this pair is unchecked. UniProt names GPR15LG (a polypeptide) as the natural ligand and makes no mention of prostanoids; the PTM literature search also surfaced thrombomodulin EGF5 and TRAP-6 as reported GPR15 ligands, all peptides/proteins. STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence were not run, as they do not index a metabolite against a receptor.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule resolved prostaglandin D2 via PubChem to CHEMBL1235252, with SMILES and InChIKey (BHMBVRSPMRCCGG-OUTUXVNYSA-N) matching the supplied structure. chembl_known_activity (P49685) and chembl_ligand_promiscuity both failed with server 500 errors on two attempts each, so there is NO ChEMBL data for this candidate: ALREADY_KNOWN is not excluded and no promiscuity count is available. From the supplied fold metrics only: the ligand's own pLDDT is 62 (modest, above the ~50 unreliability line), interface pLDDT 85.8, min separation 2.52 Å (no obvious clash), buried surface 900 Å2. No pocket topology or buried-fraction readout was available, so whether the pose sits in the transmembrane orthosteric site is unverified.
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Re-run chembl_known_activity (P49685 / CHEMBL1235252) and chembl_ligand_promiscuity once ChEMBL is back; a measured affinity would change the verdict to ALREADY_KNOWN. 2) Counter-screen: fold PGD2 against two or three unrelated GPCRs, and against its established receptors as positive controls, to see whether the confidence is specific to GPR15. 3) Inspect the pose for buried fraction and whether contacts fall on transmembrane residues rather than the extracellular N-terminus/loops where GPR15LG binds. 4) If it survives, test PGD2 in a GPR15 Gi/cAMP or beta-arrestin assay with GPR15LG as the positive control.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Counter-screen format: PGD2 dose-response vs. GPR15LG (positive ligand) and vs. known PGD2 receptors (DP1/PTGDR, DP2/CRTH2/GPR44) in parallel, with GPR15-null parental cells)
Why this method
PGD2 is a small diffusible lipid and GPR15 is a Gi-coupled GPCR, so a functional readout (Gi signalling, β-arrestin recruitment) tests real receptor activation. PLA and co-IP are poorly suited to a small-molecule lipid, and the main risk is a promiscuous pocket fit, which a counter-screen can address.
Target tissue(s)
intestine (colon/small intestine), peripheral blood lymphocytes (T-cells), NK-cells and plasma cells (lymphoid/gut-associated)
Why these tissues (HPA)
GPR15 RNA is tissue-specific to intestine (29.4 nTPM). Single-cell data show it in plasma cells (26.2 nCPM), T-cells (19.2) and NK-cells (11.6). HPA has no entry for PGD2, a lipid made by enzymes such as PTGDS and HPGDS. No real overlap is supported, so the primary test uses recombinant GPR15 in a heterologous system and the native cell types serve as a secondary check.
Cell type(s)
T-cells (gut-homing CD4+ / regulatory T cells), Plasma cells, NK-cells, HEK293 or CHO cells expressing GPR15 (heterologous system)
Protocol notes
1) Make HEK293 or CHO stable lines expressing GPR15 (with a Gαqi5 chimera or a cAMP biosensor such as GloSensor). Include a parental line and a DP2/CRTH2-expressing line as a PGD2-responsive control. Read out Gi-mediated forskolin-induced cAMP inhibition and β-arrestin recruitment (PathHunter or NanoBiT) over a PGD2 range of 1 nM to 30 µM. Use fresh PGD2 stocks, since it degrades quickly to 15d-PGJ2 and other metabolites, and test those metabolites as well. 2) Run the same assay with recombinant GPR15LG as the specific-agonist benchmark. Compare potency and efficacy, and note whether PGD2 only acts at supraphysiological concentrations. 3) Run a structure-guided pocket-mutant test (mutate the residues predicted to contact PGD2) and a competition test against GPR15LG. 4) As a secondary check, treat primary human gut-homing T cells or GPR15+ cell lines with PGD2 and measure chemotaxis or cAMP, with and without GPR15 knockdown or knockout.
Controls
Positive: GPR15LG, which should give a robust GPR15-dependent response. PGD2 on DP1 or DP2 cells, which should respond. Negative: parental cells without GPR15. Vehicle (ethanol or DMSO) controls. An unrelated lipid such as PGE2 or LTB4 for specificity. An unrelated Gi-coupled GPCR as a transfection control.
Caveats
The verdict is LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET with low confidence. The ChEMBL queries failed, so prior activity data and the molecule's target count are unknown and should be re-queried first. A high ipTM for a small lipid in a GPCR pocket is expected regardless of specificity. UniProt lists GPR15LG, a polypeptide, as the natural ligand. PGD2 is unstable in aqueous media and in serum and gives non-specific effects through endogenous DP1/DP2 or PPARγ (via its metabolite 15d-PGJ2). Any response must therefore be shown to be GPR15-dependent. HPA has no data for PGD2, so tissue co-presence cannot be judged. Intestinal GPR15 expression may reflect lymphocytes, not epithelium.

GPR174 ↔ prostaglandin D2 LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET VALIDATE medium confidence ipTM 0.86 · pTM 0.8
Rationale
GPR174 (UniProt Q9BXC1) is a class-A GPCR whose documented endogenous agonist is lysophosphatidylserine (also CCL21 under testosterone), i.e. a lipid pocket that readily accommodates an amphipathic fatty-acid-like ligand; PGD2 is a prostanoid with its own established receptors (DP1/CRTH2), so a confident AF3 pose (ipTM 0.86, iface pLDDT 82.5) in this lipid-binding TM bundle is the expected result, not evidence of specificity. ChEMBL was unavailable (repeated 500 errors), so neither measured activity at Q9BXC1 nor the molecule's promiscuity count could be retrieved — prostaglandins are nonetheless broadly active lipid mediators. Receptor localization (HPA: plasma membrane, approved) and expression (lymphoid tissue, T/NK/B cells) are compatible with exposure to PGD2, which is abundantly made by mast cells/PTGDS, so the pairing is not implausible — just unproven by this fold.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists 2 glycosylation sites and 1 disulfide; these are extracellular/ECL2 features typical of GPCRs and unlikely to occlude an intra-bundle orthosteric pocket. PubMed PTM search returned only 2 unrelated functional papers.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule: PGD2 = CHEMBL1235252, InChIKey BHMBVRSPMRCCGG-OUTUXVNYSA-N, SMILES matches supplied. chembl_known_activity and chembl_ligand_promiscuity both failed with ChEMBL API 500 errors on two attempts — no measured-affinity or promiscuity data obtained.
Follow-up (not yet executed): Retry ChEMBL for measured PGD2 activity at Q9BXC1 and its target count once the API is back. Experimentally, the decisive test is a counter-screen: fold/assay PGD2 against GPR174 alongside 2-3 unrelated GPCRs, and run a cAMP/TGFalpha-shedding assay comparing PGD2 with lysoPS at GPR174 (with PTGDR/PTGDR2 as controls).
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Counter-screen format: GPR174-expressing vs. empty-vector/parental cells, with LysoPS as positive-control agonist, PGD2 and related prostanoids (PGE2, 15d-PGJ2, PGD2 metabolites) as specificity panel, and a pocket-mutant arm)
Why this method
PGD2 is a small diffusible lipid and GPR174 is a plasma-membrane GPCR, so PLA and co-IP are unsuitable (no protein partner, and low-affinity lipid binding would not survive IP). A functional readout in receptor-expressing cells directly tests whether PGD2 is an agonist or only a promiscuous-pocket artifact, and the panel and mutant arm address the verdict.
Target tissue(s)
lymphoid tissue
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA shows GPR174 RNA tissue-specific expression only in lymphoid tissue (15.7 nTPM). Single-cell data show highest expression in T-cells (105.1 nCPM), NK-cells (76.4), basophils (59.7) and thymocytes (37.7). PGD2 has no HPA entry (it is a lipid made by PTGDS/HPGDS), so the assay is built around receptor-bearing cells. Basophils are also a PGD2-responsive cell type and make a physiologically relevant context.
Cell type(s)
T-cells, NK-cells, Basophils, Thymocytes, B-cells
Protocol notes
1) Heterologous system: HEK293 or CHO cells stably expressing human GPR174, with empty-vector parental cells as the control. Use a Gs-coupled readout (cAMP, e.g. GloSensor or HTRF), since GPR174 couples mainly to Gs. Add a β-arrestin recruitment assay (e.g. PathHunter/NanoBiT) as an orthogonal readout. Run full 8-10 point dose-response curves for PGD2 from 1 nM to 30 µM, and compare EC50 and Emax with LysoPS (18:1). Include DP1 and CRTH2 expressing cells as PGD2 positive controls, and use freshly prepared PGD2 because it is unstable and degrades to J-series prostaglandins. 2) Specificity panel: PGE2, PGF2α, 15d-PGJ2, 9α,11β-PGF2 and a fatty-acid or lysophospholipid such as LPA/LPS-lyso. Show whether the response is specific or a general lipid effect. 3) Pocket test: mutate known LysoPS-contacting residues in GPR174 (e.g. the polar/basic residues that coordinate the phosphoserine headgroup, per published cryo-EM structures) and check whether PGD2 activity is lost along with LysoPS activity. Also test whether DP1/CRTH2 antagonists change the response. 4) Physiological follow-up: primary human T or NK cells, or Jurkat, with GPR174 knockdown/CRISPR knockout. Measure cAMP/pCREB (and IL-2 suppression as a downstream readout) after PGD2 stimulation, with DP1/CRTH2 inhibitors present to separate off-target receptor effects.
Controls
Positive: LysoPS (known GPR174 agonist) in GPR174 cells; PGD2 in DP1/CRTH2-expressing cells; forskolin for total cAMP capacity. Negative: parental/empty-vector cells; GPR174 pocket-dead mutant; vehicle (ethanol/DMSO, matched); structurally unrelated prostanoids (PGE2/PGF2α); DP1/CRTH2 antagonists in primary cells so their effect is not mistaken for GPR174 signalling.
Caveats
The verdict is LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET: a high ipTM (0.86) for a lipid in a lipid-binding GPCR pocket is expected and does not show specificity, so a null result in the assay is the likely outcome. ChEMBL activity data were unavailable, so prior evidence of PGD2 activity at GPR174 is unchecked. The HPA contains no entry for PGD2, so tissue choice rests only on the receptor. Lymphocytes also express DP1/CRTH2 (CRTH2 on Th2/ILC2), which confound primary-cell experiments, so use knockout or antagonist controls. PGD2 is chemically unstable, and some effects may come from its metabolites. Expression of GPR174 is low in absolute terms (15.7 nTPM), so endogenous signals may be small. Overexpression in HEK/CHO cells can produce artifactual low-potency lipid responses, so only an EC50 in a physiologically plausible range (and lost in the pocket mutant) would support a real interaction.

GPR6 ↔ 4-aminobutanoic acid LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET VALIDATE low confidence ipTM 0.86 · pTM 0.71
Rationale
The fold is confident (ipTM 0.86, ligand pLDDT 76.3), but that is the expected result for a small zwitterionic metabolite in a GPCR pocket and nothing receptor-specific supports it. UniProt describes GPR6 as a constitutively active Gs receptor possibly activated by lipid-derived agonists (oleic acid, sphingosine 1-phosphate), a different chemical class from GABA. The two ChEMBL checks (known activity at GPR6, promiscuity) could NOT be run because the resolver returned no ChEMBL id, so neither novelty nor promiscuity is established; confidence is low for that reason.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: Glycoprotein with 3 glycosylation sites, 1 lipidation (palmitate) and 3 modified residues. Whether any glycosylation site lies near the modeled pocket was not checked. The pubmed_ptm_glycosylation hits (8) are generic GPR3/GPR6 expression and signalling papers, not PTM studies. No evidence of a PTM artifact at the pocket.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
No curated pharmacology check was possible (no ChEMBL id). STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence were not called because they do not index a metabolite against a receptor. The UniProt function text names only lipid-derived candidate agonists for GPR6 and does not mention GABA.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule was tried under three names (4-aminobutanoic acid, GABA, gamma-aminobutyric acid). Each resolved via PubChem only, to SMILES C(CC(=O)O)CN and InChIKey BTCSSZJGUNDROE-UHFFFAOYSA-N, which match the folded structure, but with molecule_chembl_id = null. chembl_known_activity and chembl_ligand_promiscuity were therefore NOT called: I did not substitute a ChEMBL id from memory, since an unverified id could attach another molecule's data to this candidate. Measured affinity at GPR6 (P46095) and the distinct-target count are both unknown, not zero. Not tool-derived: GABA is a major neurotransmitter with well-established receptors and transporters of its own, so a high target count would be expected.
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Obtain GABA's ChEMBL id by InChIKey (BTCSSZJGUNDROE-UHFFFAOYSA-N) from ChEMBL directly, then run chembl_known_activity at P46095 and chembl_ligand_promiscuity; a measured affinity would change this to ALREADY_KNOWN. 2) Counter-screen: fold GABA against 2-3 unrelated class A GPCRs, plus GPR3/GPR12 as paralogs, and compare ipTM and ligand pLDDT; similar confidence everywhere confirms non-specificity. 3) Inspect the pose: confirm contacts are on the transmembrane bundle and check buried_fraction; the supplied BSA of 370 Å2 and min separation of 3.49 Å do not by themselves show an orthosteric pose, and the pocket is reported to bind lipids. 4) If still of interest, a cAMP assay of GABA on GPR6-expressing cells, noting that high constitutive activity will complicate the agonist readout.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Counter-screen format: GPR6 vs. mock/parental and vs. a closely related receptor (GPR3/GPR12) and a GABA-B positive control, with lipid agonist (S1P) comparator arm)
Why this method
GABA is a small soluble metabolite and GPR6 is a constitutively active Gs-coupled GPCR, so PLA/co-IP don't fit (no protein partner, and a low-affinity ligand wouldn't survive IP). A cAMP functional readout directly tests whether GABA modulates GPR6 above its high basal signalling, and the counter-screens address the 'promiscuous pocket' concern.
Target tissue(s)
brain (striatum/caudate), brain (cerebral cortex), pituitary gland
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA shows GPR6 RNA is brain-specific (34.4 nTPM), with single-cell expression in brain inhibitory neurons (13.6 nCPM), other brain neurons (4.5) and lactotrophs (4.2). GABA has no HPA entry as a metabolite, but GABAergic inhibitory neurons are the physiologically relevant context. The primary assay is done in recombinant HEK293 cells, with follow-up in neuronal cultures.
Cell type(s)
Brain inhibitory neurons, Lactotrophs, Other brain neurons
Protocol notes
1) Transfect HEK293 cells with GPR6 or empty vector. Use a cAMP readout (GloSensor or HTRF) in a GABA dose-response (1 nM-10 mM) with an osmolarity/pH-matched vehicle. Because GPR6 is constitutively active, use an inverse agonist or titrate GPR6 expression to widen the window, and measure changes in basal cAMP. 2) Run an orthogonal β-arrestin recruitment (e.g., PathHunter) or CRE-luciferase assay. Confirm surface expression of GPR6 (tagged construct, flow/ELISA). 3) If any activity appears, test pocket-residue mutants predicted by AF3 to contact GABA, and structural analogues (glycine, β-alanine, taurine, muscimol) to check specificity. Follow up in primary striatal neurons or an inhibitory neuron line with GPR6 knockdown.
Controls
Positive: forskolin (cAMP max), S1P or a reported GPR6 modulator as the lipid agonist comparator, and GABA on GABA-B (GABBR1/2, Gi) as a ligand-activity control. Negative: mock-transfected cells with GABA, an unrelated Gs GPCR (e.g., one not GABA-responsive), other small zwitterions (glycine, β-alanine), and a vehicle with matched pH/osmolarity. Also include a GPR3/GPR12 paralog comparison for selectivity.
Caveats
The ChEMBL novelty and promiscuity checks were not run, so prior activity at GPR6 is unknown. The ipTM of 0.86 is expected for small zwitterions in a GPCR pocket and is weak evidence. Constitutive Gs activity may mask weak agonism, and high-mM GABA may cause osmotic or pH artifacts. HEK293 cells endogenously express some GABA-related and other GPCR machinery. GPR6 has no HPA subcellular location or protein-level data, and GABA has no HPA data, so tissue-level overlap cannot be assessed. GABA is also a physiological brain metabolite, so any response may be indirect.

GPR82 ↔ prostaglandin D2 LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET VALIDATE medium confidence ipTM 0.86 · pTM 0.83
Rationale
ChEMBL records no measured activity of PGD2 (CHEMBL1235252) at GPR82 (Q96P67), so the pair is not already known, but nothing beyond the fold supports it. GPR82 is an orphan GPCR (UniProt: "Orphan receptor") enriched in lymphoid tissue and Kupffer cells, while the listed producer PTGDS is enriched in testis, epididymis, decidua and retinal pigment epithelium, with no overlap. A confident ipTM (0.86) is the expected result for a lipid metabolite in a GPCR pocket, and the ligand's own pLDDT is only moderate (68.7).
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists GPR82 as a glycoprotein with 2 glycosylation sites; pubmed_ptm_glycosylation returned 0 hits. The sites were not mapped to the pose, but in a GPCR they are typically on the extracellular N-terminus or loops and unlikely to block a pocket inside the transmembrane bundle. Not treated as the main concern.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
No ChEMBL activity for PGD2 at GPR82, and UniProt lists GPR82 as an orphan receptor with no ligand. STRING, CellPhoneDB and pubmed_cooccurrence were not run because they do not index a metabolite against a receptor.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule returned CHEMBL1235252 via the PubChem fallback, with SMILES and InChIKey (BHMBVRSPMRCCGG-OUTUXVNYSA-N) matching the supplied structure. chembl_known_activity at Q96P67 returned 0 activities. chembl_ligand_promiscuity (500 error on the first call, succeeded on retry) returned 4 affinity measurements at 4 distinct targets, including ALDH1A1 and SLCO2A1. That count is a floor and probably an undercount for this record: it does not show PGD2's cognate receptors PTGDR and PTGDR2, which I know from general pharmacology rather than from a tool result. The low count is therefore not evidence of selectivity.

No fold was run here. 3) Check HPGDS expression in Kupffer and lymphoid cells as an alternative PGD2 source. 4) If specificity holds, test in a functional assay (β-arrestin recruitment or cAMP/Gi) for PGD2 at GPR82, with PTGDR and PTGDR2 as positive controls.

Why this method
GPR82 is an orphan GPCR and PGD2 is a diffusible lipid, so the question is whether PGD2 functionally activates the receptor. That is best tested with a signalling readout in a receptor-expressing system, not by co-localization. A counter-screen against other lipids and parental cells is needed because a high ipTM for a lipid in a GPCR pocket is the expected result and not evidence of specificity.
Target tissue(s)
lymphoid tissue, intestine
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA shows GPR82 RNA only in lymphoid tissue (6.5 nTPM) and intestine (2.5 nTPM), and the single-cell data show Kupffer cells at 65.1 nCPM. PGD2 has no HPA entry. Its producer PTGDS is enriched in testis, epididymis, decidua and RPE, so there is no real tissue overlap. This is a paracrine/exogenous-ligand test: use GPR82-bearing immune cells as the receptor side. PGD2 is also made by other cells, such as mast cells and Th2 cells, in lymphoid and gut tissue.
Cell type(s)
Kupffer cells, lymphoid cells (T/B lymphocytes), recombinant HEK293 or CHO cells expressing GPR82
Protocol notes
1) Make HEK293 or CHO cells stably expressing epitope-tagged GPR82. Confirm surface expression by flow cytometry or ELISA. Controls
Positive: DP1 (PTGDR) cells or DP2 (CRTH2/GPR44) cells with PGD2, which should respond. A generic GPCR agonist, such as ATP via endogenous P2Y receptors or forskolin, shows the assay is working. Negative: parental or empty-vector cells, a GPR82 pocket-mutant, and vehicle (ethanol or DMSO). Specificity: other prostanoids and an unrelated lipid.
Caveats
The verdict is LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET. The high ipTM (0.86) is the expected result for any lipid in a GPCR pocket, and the PGD2 pLDDT is only moderate (68.7), so the pose is not evidence of specific binding. GPR82 is an orphan receptor with low and sparse HPA expression, and its G-protein coupling is unclear, so a negative result in one readout may be a false negative. Use several readouts. PGD2 is unstable and converts to J-series prostaglandins. HPA has no data for PGD2, and the producer PTGDS has no tissue overlap with GPR82, so physiological relevance is uncertain. Mouse and human GPR82 may differ.

GPR75 ↔ 2-arachidonoylglycerol INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE low confidence ipTM 0.85 · pTM 0.63
Rationale
The two checks that discriminate for a small molecule could not be run: chembl_known_activity (O95800 x CHEMBL122972) and chembl_ligand_promiscuity both returned HTTP 500 on two attempts each, so neither ALREADY_KNOWN nor novelty nor promiscuity is established from tool evidence. What remains is a confident fold (ipTM 0.85), which is the expected result for a metabolite in a GPCR pocket and not evidence of specificity; the supplied p_twoway of 0.056 and ligand pLDDT of 61.7 are unremarkable. Receptor-side evidence is compatible (plasma-membrane GPCR, brain/retina enhanced; UniProt lists CCL5 as activator), so this is not IMPLAUSIBLE, and my lean, if ChEMBL shows no activity at GPR75, is LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET rather than CONFIRMED_NOVEL.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: GPR75 is a glycoprotein with 3 annotated glycosylation sites. Their position relative to the modeled pocket is unknown without a fold; on a GPCR these are typically on the extracellular N-terminus/loops and would be unlikely to block a transmembrane-bundle lipid site, so this is a minor caveat. pubmed_ptm_glycosylation returned 11 hits, but the titles shown concern 20-HETE/GPR75 signalling, not GPR75 modification.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
ChEMBL lookup for this pair failed (server error), so known pharmacology is unchecked. UniProt's function text names the chemokine CCL5/RANTES as the activator of GPR75. The PubMed hits returned by the PTM search are all about 20-HETE signalling through GPR75 (e.g. PMID 39541047, 35081581, 33011364), i.e. an arachidonate-derived lipid is already the literature's proposed ligand. That makes an eicosanoid-like lipid pocket chemically plausible, but it also means a pocket that accepts 20-HETE would be expected to accept 2-AG in a fold whether or not it binds. STRING, CellPhoneDB and pubmed_cooccurrence are protein-pair tools and were not applicable to a metabolite partner.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule: 2-arachidonoylglycerol = CHEMBL122972, SMILES CCCCC/C=C\C/C=C\C/C=C\C/C=C\CCCC(=O)OC(CO)CO, InChIKey RCRCTBLIHCHWDZ-DOFZRALJSA-N (matches the supplied structure). chembl_known_activity at O95800: NOT OBTAINED (ChEMBL API 500 error, tried twice). chembl_ligand_promiscuity: NOT OBTAINED (500 error, tried twice). No measured-affinity count or distinct-target count is available from this run. From general background, not verified here: 2-AG is an endocannabinoid with established activity at CB1/CB2 and several other targets, which would argue for promiscuity, but that is not a tool result. Supplied pose metrics: BSA 875 A2, 293 contacts, min separation 1.97 A (on the tight side), ligand pLDDT 61.7 (modest), interface pLDDT 79.2. No ligands block or pocket topology was available, so whether the pose sits in the transmembrane bundle is unknown.
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Re-run chembl_known_activity (O95800, CHEMBL122972) and chembl_ligand_promiscuity (CHEMBL122972) when the ChEMBL API recovers; a measured affinity at GPR75 makes this ALREADY_KNOWN, and a large distinct-target count makes it LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET. 2) Inspect the pose: buried fraction, whether contacts are on transmembrane segments versus loops or cytoplasmic side, and the 1.97 A minimum separation for clashes. 3) Counter-screen: fold 2-AG against two or three unrelated GPCRs, and fold 20-HETE and a decoy lipid against GPR75, to see whether the confidence is specific. 4) Only if those hold up, a wet-lab test (e.g. Gq calcium/IP1 assay in GPR75-expressing cells with 2-AG, with 20-HETE as comparator).

GPR171 ↔ prostaglandin D2 LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET VALIDATE low confidence ipTM 0.84 · pTM 0.84
Rationale
The confident fold (ipTM 0.84) is the expected result for a small molecule in a GPCR pocket, and nothing retrieved supports specificity for GPR171. UniProt annotates GPR171 as the receptor for the neuropeptide Big LEN, a different chemical class from a prostanoid lipid, and HPA shows no overlap between GPR171 expression (T cells, NK cells, lymphoid tissue) and the PTGDS producer cell types. Both ChEMBL checks failed with HTTP 500 on two attempts each, so neither known activity at this receptor nor the molecule's promiscuity was measured; confidence is low for that reason.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists the Glycoprotein keyword and 1 glycosylation site on GPR171; pubmed_ptm_glycosylation returned 0 hits. A single N-glycan on a GPCR is typically on the extracellular N-terminus or a loop and is unlikely to occlude a transmembrane-bundle pocket, but its position relative to the modeled pose was not checked. Not treated as the main concern.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
Not established either way. The ChEMBL lookup for PGD2 at GPR171 (O14626) errored twice, so the pair could not be confirmed as novel or already known. UniProt's function text for GPR171 names only Big LEN (a proSAAS-derived peptide) as its ligand and does not mention prostaglandins. STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence were not called because they do not index a metabolite against a receptor.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule returned CHEMBL1235252 (PROSTAGLANDIN D2), InChIKey BHMBVRSPMRCCGG-OUTUXVNYSA-N, matching the supplied InChIKey, so the folded structure is the right molecule. chembl_known_activity (O14626) and chembl_ligand_promiscuity both returned 500 Internal Server Error on two attempts each: NO ChEMBL data was obtained. Whether a measured affinity at GPR171 exists and how many distinct targets PGD2 is active at are therefore unknown from this run; no promiscuity count is reported. Supplied fold metrics: ligand pLDDT 64.6 (moderate, above the ~50 unreliability line), interface pLDDT 85.1, min separation 2.14 A (tight for an un-relaxed pose), BSA 815 A2, p_twoway 0.037. No fold was run here, so pocket topology (transmembrane bundle vs. loops) and buried fraction were not checked.
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Re-run chembl_known_activity (O14626 / CHEMBL1235252) and chembl_ligand_promiscuity once ChEMBL is back. A measured affinity would change the verdict to ALREADY_KNOWN, and the target count is needed to make the promiscuity call properly. 2) Counter-screen: fold PGD2 against two or three unrelated GPCRs, plus its cognate receptors PTGDR and PTGDR2 as positive controls, and compare ligand pLDDT, buried fraction and pocket topology. 3) Inspect the existing pose: confirm the contacts lie in the transmembrane bundle and that the 2.14 A minimum separation is not a clash. 4) If it still stands, test PGD2 in a Gi-coupled functional assay (cAMP inhibition or beta-arrestin) on GPR171-expressing cells, with Big LEN as the reference agonist.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Counter-screen format: side-by-side dose-response of PGD2 vs. Big LEN (positive ligand) on GPR171-expressing vs. parental/GPR171-KO cells, plus a pocket-mutant arm and comparison with PGD2's known receptors (DP1/PTGDR, DP2/CRTH2) and unrelated lipids (PGE2, PGJ2).)
Why this method
PGD2 is a small-molecule lipid and GPR171 is a Gi/o-coupled GPCR, so the question is whether PGD2 actually activates it. A functional readout answers this better than PLA, which can't be used for a non-protein ligand, or co-IP. The counter-screen design tests the verdict's 'promiscuous pocket' concern directly.
Target tissue(s)
Lymphoid tissue, Spleen, Lymph node, Tonsil
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA shows GPR171 RNA tissue-specific only in lymphoid tissue (20.1 nTPM). At the single-cell level it is in T-cells (143.7 nCPM), NK-cells (43.7) and innate lymphoid cells (33.6). PGD2 has no HPA entry, so no tissue overlap can be judged. The PGD2 source (PTGDS/HPGDS-expressing cells such as mast cells and Th2 cells) is not in the GPR171 data, so use exogenous PGD2 on receptor-bearing cells.
Cell type(s)
T-cells, NK-cells, Innate lymphoid cells
Protocol notes
1) Cell systems: HEK293 or CHO cells stably expressing human GPR171 (plus a Gαi/Gαqi5 chimera or Gβγ-sensitive reporter if needed), with parental cells and GPR171-KO cells as controls. Confirm with primary human T cells or NK cells, or a T-cell line (e.g. Jurkat), with and without GPR171 knockdown. 2) Readouts: forskolin-stimulated cAMP inhibition (Gi), [35S]GTPγS or BRET G-protein activation, β-arrestin recruitment (PathHunter/Tango) and pERK. Run 10-point dose-response curves from 1 nM to 100 µM PGD2, and run Big LEN (proLEN/BigLEN peptide) in parallel. 3) Specificity checks: PGD2 stability (it degrades quickly to PGJ2 species, so use fresh stock, LC-MS to confirm identity and concentration, and a stabilised analogue); the DP1/DP2 antagonists (laropiprant, fevipiprant) to rule out signal from endogenous receptors; and AF3-pose-guided point mutants in the predicted contact residues to see whether activity is lost. 4) If a binding signal appears, confirm it with a radioligand [3H]-PGD2 displacement or thermal-shift/NanoBRET binding assay.
Controls
Positive: Big LEN (proSAAS-derived peptide) in GPR171 cells, giving Gi-mediated cAMP drop. Negative: parental/GPR171-KO cells, vehicle, and an unrelated lipid (e.g. PGE2/arachidonic acid) at matched concentrations. Assay-validity controls: PGD2 on DP1 (Gs, cAMP rise) and DP2/CRTH2 (Gi, calcium/cAMP) to show the PGD2 batch is active. Promiscuity control: PGD2 on a few unrelated orphan/class A GPCRs with similar AF3 pocket scores.
Caveats
The verdict is low confidence because both ChEMBL checks failed (HTTP 500), so known activity of PGD2 at GPR171 and PGD2's promiscuity were not measured. Do those lookups manually (ChEMBL, GtoPdb, and the GPR171 deorphanisation literature) before running the wet-lab work. A confident ipTM (0.84) for a small molecule in a GPCR pocket is expected and weak evidence of specificity. PGD2 has no HPA entry, and its producer cells (PTGDS/HPGDS) do not overlap with GPR171-expressing cells in the data, so any physiological relevance would have to be paracrine. PGD2 is chemically unstable and also acts on DP1/DP2 receptors that T/NK cells may express, which could confound responses in primary cells. A null result in recombinant cells would support the 'promiscuous pocket' reading. Surface expression of GPR171 is partly vesicular in HPA, so confirm plasma-membrane localisation of the construct.
