P2RY10 ↔ prostaglandin D2 LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET VALIDATE low confidence ipTM 0.82 · pTM 0.83
Rationale
The fold is confident (ipTM 0.82), but that is the expected result for a lipid-like metabolite in a GPCR pocket and nothing I pulled makes it specific to P2RY10. The ChEMBL checks could not be run: prostaglandin D2 resolved only via PubChem with no ChEMBL id (tried two names), so neither known activity at O00398 nor promiscuity was tested. UniProt lists P2RY10 only as a putative purine receptor, and the supplied ligand pLDDT of 62.4 is modest.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists 3 glycosylation sites and 1 disulfide bond on P2RY10, and the Glycoprotein keyword; pubmed_ptm_glycosylation returned 0 hits. In a GPCR these sites are typically on the extracellular N-terminus or loops and are unlikely to block a transmembrane pocket, but their position relative to the pose was not checked.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
No measured-affinity lookup was possible because the molecule has no ChEMBL id from the resolver. UniProt function for P2RY10 is "Putative receptor for purines coupled to G proteins", with no prostanoid annotation. STRING and CellPhoneDB do not index metabolite-receptor pairs and were not called.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule ("prostaglandin D2" and "PGD2") returned source=pubchem, molecule_chembl_id=null, with SMILES and InChIKey (BHMBVRSPMRCCGG-OUTUXVNYSA-N) matching the folded structure. Because there is no ChEMBL id, chembl_known_activity and chembl_ligand_promiscuity were NOT run; absence of known activity at P2RY10 and the molecule's target count are both unverified, not negative results. From background knowledge rather than tool output: PGD2 has established receptors of its own (PTGDR/DP1, PTGDR2/CRTH2), and P2RY10 has been reported as a lysophospholipid (lysophosphatidylserine) receptor, so a pocket that accepts an acidic lipid is unsurprising. Supplied fold metrics: ligand pLDDT 62.4, interface pLDDT 82.0, min separation 2.03 Å, BSA 922 Å2. No ligands block or pocket topology was available, so whether the pose sits in the transmembrane orthosteric site is unknown.
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Look up PGD2 in ChEMBL directly by InChIKey BHMBVRSPMRCCGG-OUTUXVNYSA-N and run the known-activity (O00398) and promiscuity checks that could not be run here. 2) Counter-screen: fold PGD2 against two or three unrelated GPCRs, with PTGDR/PTGDR2 as positive controls, and fold P2RY10 with lysophosphatidylserine to see whether PGD2 simply occupies the lysophospholipid site. 3) Inspect the pose: buried fraction, whether contacts are on transmembrane helices, and whether the 2.03 Å minimum separation is a clash. 4) If it survives those, test PGD2 on P2RY10-expressing cells in a functional assay (e.g. G-protein signalling or TGFα shedding).
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Counter-screen format: parallel dose-response of PGD2 vs. structurally related lipids (PGE2, PGF2α, LPA, S1P) and a DP1/DP2 reference, in P2RY10-expressing vs. empty-vector/parental cells)
Why this method
PGD2 is a small diffusible lipid and P2RY10 is a GPCR, so a functional readout in receptor-expressing cells is more informative than co-localization (PLA does not suit a metabolite). The verdict flags a possible promiscuous pocket, so the key question is specificity, which needs a counter-screen against related lipids and a receptor-null background.
Target tissue(s)
lymphoid tissue, tonsil, lymph node, spleen
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA shows P2RY10 RNA is tissue-enriched only in lymphoid tissue (25.7 nTPM). Single-cell data show it in B-cells (122 nCPM), T-cells (104), basophils (81), plasma cells (67), NK cells (47) and ILCs (49). PGD2 has no HPA entry because it is a metabolite, not a gene. Its producers (e.g. mast cells, via the HPGDS/PTGDS synthases) are not in the data given, so the ligand side is supplied exogenously or by co-culture.
Cell type(s)
B-cells, T-cells, Basophils, NK-cells, Innate lymphoid cells
Protocol notes
1) Use HEK293 or CHO cells stably expressing P2RY10, with empty-vector cells as the null background. Co-express a promiscuous Gα (Gα15/Gqi5), or use a β-arrestin (PathHunter/Tango) assay, because P2RY10's G-protein coupling is unknown. Read out calcium flux (Fluo-4), cAMP (GloSensor, in both Gs and Gi modes) and β-arrestin recruitment. Confirm surface expression with an N-terminal epitope tag. 2) Run PGD2 dose-response from 1 nM to 30 µM. Include fresh-prepared PGD2 and its dehydration product 15d-PGJ2, since PGD2 is unstable in aqueous buffer. Run the same lipids on empty-vector cells. 3) Repeat in primary human B or T cells, or in a lymphoid line that endogenously expresses P2RY10. Use P2RY10 siRNA or CRISPR knockout to test whether the response depends on the receptor. 4) If a response appears, do a radioligand or label-free binding check (e.g. [3H]-PGD2 competition) and mutate pocket residues predicted by AF3 to test the pose.
Controls
Positive: a known PGD2 receptor (DP1/PTGDR or DP2/GPR44/CRTH2) in the same assay format, and a reference P2RY10 ligand if one exists (e.g. LPA or S1P, which have been reported as candidates). Also use a generic Gα-pathway agonist, such as ATP on endogenous P2Y receptors or forskolin for cAMP, to show the cells respond. Negative: empty-vector or parental cells; an unrelated lipid GPCR (e.g. a P2RY receptor not expected to bind PGD2); vehicle (ethanol/DMSO); and a pocket-mutant P2RY10.
Caveats
The verdict is LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET at low confidence. High ipTM for a lipid in a GPCR pocket is expected and is not evidence of specificity. ChEMBL checks were not run, so prior activity data for P2RY10 and PGD2 promiscuity are unknown. Ligand pLDDT is only 62.4, so the pose is uncertain. P2RY10 is only a putative purine receptor with an orphan-like profile. It may lack a clean signalling readout, so a negative result would not exclude binding. Endogenous DP1/DP2 or other prostanoid receptors in primary cells could produce PGD2 responses that are not P2RY10-dependent, hence the knockout and null-cell controls. PGD2 is chemically unstable and spontaneously converts to J-series prostaglandins. HPA has no subcellular location or protein-level data for P2RY10, so antibody validation for any follow-up is not yet established.

GPR160 ↔ leukotriene D4 LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET VALIDATE medium confidence ipTM 0.81 · pTM 0.77
Rationale
The confident fold (ipTM 0.81) has nothing receptor-specific behind it. GPR160 is an orphan plasma-membrane GPCR (UniProt function: "Orphan receptor"), so compartment access is plausible, but leukotriene D4 resolved only via PubChem with no ChEMBL id, so neither measured affinity at GPR160 nor promiscuity could be checked. From background knowledge rather than tool output, LTD4 already has dedicated high-affinity receptors (CYSLTR1/CYSLTR2), and a long flexible amphipathic lipid is the kind of ligand AF3 places confidently in any GPCR bundle; the ligand's own pLDDT is only moderate (62.1).
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists GPR160 as a glycoprotein with 1 glycosylation site, presumably on the extracellular N-terminus or a loop. The PubMed PTM search returned 3 hits, none actually about GPR160 glycosylation. This is unlikely to affect an intra-bundle pocket and is not the main concern.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
No curated pharmacology could be retrieved for this pair because the molecule has no ChEMBL id. UniProt lists GPR160 as an orphan receptor with no ligand. STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence were not queried, as they do not index a metabolite against a receptor.
Small molecule (ChEMBL)
resolve_small_molecule returned a PubChem-only hit (InChIKey YEESKJGWJFYOOK-IJHYULJSSA-N, SMILES matching the folded structure) with molecule_chembl_id = null. chembl_known_activity and chembl_ligand_promiscuity were therefore not run; no measured affinity at GPR160 (Q9UJ42) was confirmed or excluded, and the number of distinct targets is unknown. From background knowledge, LTD4 is the cognate agonist of CYSLTR1/CYSLTR2. Supplied pose metrics: ligand pLDDT 62.1, interface pLDDT 83.5, min separation 2.59 Å, BSA 868 Å2. No fold was run in this triage, so pocket topology (transmembrane vs loop contacts) and buried fraction are unverified.
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Counter-screen: fold LTD4 against 2-3 unrelated GPCRs, with CYSLTR1 as a positive control, to see whether ipTM ~0.8 is receptor-specific. 2) Read the pose's ligands block (buried_fraction, pocket topology) to confirm the contacts are on the transmembrane bundle rather than loops or surface. 3) Search ChEMBL by InChIKey, or GtoPdb/BindingDB, for LTD4 target data. 4) If the pose survives, test LTD4 on GPR160-expressing cells (Ca2+, cAMP or beta-arrestin readout) with a CysLT1 antagonist such as montelukast as a control.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Counter-screen format: parallel dose-response of LTD4 on GPR160-expressing vs. empty-vector/parental cells, with CYSLTR1 as positive receptor control and with a CysLT1 antagonist (montelukast) to exclude signalling through endogenous CysLTRs)
Why this method
LTD4 is a small soluble lipid and GPR160 is an orphan plasma-membrane GPCR, so a functional receptor-activation readout is more informative than PLA (no antibody can detect a lipid ligand in situ). The main concern is promiscuous-pocket placement, so a dose-response with receptor-null and known-receptor controls directly tests specificity.
Target tissue(s)
parathyroid gland
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA shows GPR160 RNA is tissue-specific to parathyroid gland (203.7 nTPM), and there is no protein-level or single-cell data. LTD4 has no HPA entry because it is a metabolite, so no tissue overlap can be assessed. The assay should use a heterologous system (HEK293 or CHO) overexpressing GPR160, with parathyroid cells or tissue as a physiological follow-up.
Cell type(s)
parathyroid chief cells
Protocol notes
1) Make HEK293 or CHO cells stably expressing epitope-tagged GPR160. Confirm surface expression by flow cytometry or surface ELISA. Use empty-vector cells and CYSLTR1-expressing cells as comparators. 2) Add LTD4 at 1 pM–10 µM and measure several readouts, because the G-protein coupling of GPR160 is unknown: Ca2+ flux (Fluo-4, with Gα16 or Gqi5 co-expression), cAMP (GloSensor or HTRF), and β-arrestin recruitment (PathHunter or NanoBiT). Run a panel of structurally related lipids (LTC4, LTE4, LTB4, and an arachidonic-acid-derived control) to test for selectivity. 3) If there is any signal, confirm direct binding with a radioligand ([3H]-LTD4) competition or a membrane-based binding assay. Test pocket-residue mutants of GPR160 that were predicted to contact LTD4. Also run an LTD4 stability check, since it converts to LTE4 in serum or on prolonged incubation. Use serum-free buffer with a peptidase inhibitor such as serine-borate or acivicin.
Controls
Positive: LTD4 on CYSLTR1-expressing cells (Ca2+ flux, blocked by montelukast) plus generic readout controls (ATP/ionomycin for Ca2+, forskolin for cAMP). Negative: parental or empty-vector cells, an unrelated orphan GPCR expressed at similar level, vehicle, and non-cognate lipids (e.g. LTB4). Specificity: montelukast and a CysLT2 antagonist pre-treatment, and GPR160 knockout/knockdown in any responsive parathyroid line.
Caveats
The verdict is LIKELY_PROMISCUOUS_POCKET: AF3 will confidently dock a flexible amphipathic lipid into almost any GPCR bundle, and the ipTM of 0.81 plus LTD4 ligand pLDDT of 62.1 do not show receptor-specific binding. A negative result is the expected outcome. HEK293 and other host cells can endogenously express CysLT receptors or other lipid-responsive GPCRs, which could create false positives, so parental-cell controls are required. No ChEMBL data was available to check prior affinity or selectivity for LTD4 at GPR160. GPR160 coupling is unknown, so a single readout could miss a real response. HPA shows only parathyroid RNA expression and no protein or single-cell data, so the physiological relevance of any positive result is uncertain. LTD4 is unstable and prone to oxidation and metabolism.

IL21R ↔ GPR141 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE low confidence ipTM 0.7 · pTM 0.54
Rationale
The pair is novel (no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed hit), but the evidence cannot support calling it a real interaction. GPR141 has no HPA subcellular data, the two genes are enriched in different cell types (IL21R in T/NK cells, GPR141 in neutrophil progenitors), and both are glycoproteins whose glycan sites could not be placed relative to the modeled interface. No fold was run, so which side of the membrane the interface sits on is unchecked, and the supplied partner pLDDT of 54.4 is low.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt marks both as glycoproteins: IL21R has 6 annotated glycosylation sites and GPR141 has 2. If the 2101 Å² interface involves the extracellular regions, unmodeled glycans could occlude it. Site positions relative to the interface were not checked. The PubMed PTM searches (40 hits for IL21R, 1 for GPR141) returned nothing specific to this interface.
PubMed co-occurrence
pubmed_cooccurrence returned 0 papers mentioning IL21R and GPR141 together.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction; GPR141 is not in its gene table. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is unreported.
Other subunits
IL2RG
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Re-fold IL21R + GPR141 with IL2RG (CellPhoneDB lists it as the other member of the IL21 receptor complex), ideally also with IL21, to see whether the GPR141 interface survives or overlaps the cytokine/IL2RG binding surface. 2) Inspect the interface topology in the model: an interface touching both extracellular and cytoplasmic residues would be an artifact. 3) Map the 6 IL21R and 2 GPR141 glycosylation sites onto the interface and re-fold with glycans if any land on it. 4) Check single-cell data for a cell population expressing both genes before any wet-lab test such as co-IP or BRET in co-transfected cells.

FGFR3 ↔ GPR21 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE medium confidence ipTM 0.67 · pTM 0.53
Rationale
No database or literature trace exists for this pair (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB not found, 0 PubMed co-mentions), so it is formally novel. But GPR21 is an orphan GPCR with no HPA subcellular data, no single-cell detection and only ~5 nTPM in blood vessel, which does not overlap FGFR3's brain/astrocyte, skin and esophagus profile. Both are glycoproteins (6 and 2 annotated glycosylation sites) and I could not check where the modeled interface sits, so the moderate ipTM of 0.67 cannot be supported or refuted from this evidence.
PTM / glycosylation
FGFR3: UniProt Glycoprotein keyword with 6 glycosylation sites (extracellular Ig domains), plus Phosphoprotein; the PubMed PTM search returned 244 hits, mostly kinase and inhibitor papers. GPR21: Glycoprotein keyword with 2 glycosylation sites; 1 PubMed hit, not about its PTMs. Whether any glycan site lies on the modeled interface is unknown because no per-residue interface data was available. If the contact involves the FGFR3 ectodomain and GPR21's extracellular face, glycans could interfere.
PubMed co-occurrence
0 PubMed papers mention FGFR3 and GPR21 together.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction found (GPR21 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. Nothing suggests the pair is already known.
Other subunits
FGF1;FGF2
Follow-up (not yet executed): Not run: no fold was performed in this triage, so the interface location is untested. Next steps: (1) inspect the AF3 model to see which FGFR3 region contacts GPR21 and whether the interface mixes cytoplasmic and extracellular residues; I suspect non-specific transmembrane-helix packing given the large buried area (4107 Å2), and min_sep of 1.96 Å hints at close contacts. (2) Check the FGFR3 and GPR21 N-glycosylation sites against the interface residues. (3) Confirm GPR21 is actually expressed in FGFR3-positive cells (e.g. astrocytes) before any wet-lab test such as co-IP or BRET. FGF1 and FGF2 are listed under other_subunits only as FGFR3's known ligands from its UniProt function text, not as CellPhoneDB complex members.

Regulates both osteogenesis and postnatal bone mineralization by osteoblasts. Promotes apoptosis in chondrocytes, but can also promote cancer cell proliferation. Plays a role in the regulation of vitamin D metabolism. Mutations that lead to constitutive kinase activation or impair normal FGFR3 maturation, internalization and degradation lead to aberrant signaling. GRIN2D ↔ GPR6 LIKELY_SUBCOMPLEX low confidence ipTM 0.67 · pTM 0.5
Rationale
The pair is novel (no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed hit) and both are brain-expressed plasma-membrane proteins, so a lateral in-membrane contact is conceivable. But GRIN2D is an obligate subunit of the heterotetrameric NMDA receptor with GRIN1 (CellPhoneDB Glutamate_NMDA_1_2D_complex), which is absent from the model, so the large modeled surface (BSA 3225 Å2) may sit on what GRIN1 or a second GluN2 normally occupies. Model quality is modest (ipTM 0.67, interface pLDDT 63.7, partner pLDDT 55.5), and both proteins are glycoproteins (GRIN2D 6 sites, GPR6 3 sites plus a palmitoylation site), which is an untested caveat.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: GRIN2D is a glycoprotein (6 glycosylation sites, 4 disulfides) and GPR6 is a glycoprotein and palmitoylated lipoprotein (3 glycosylation sites, 1 lipidation site). The PubMed PTM hits for both genes are non-specific and say nothing about the interface. Whether any glycan site lies on the modeled interface was not determined; if the interface involves the GRIN2D extracellular domains or the GPR6 N-terminus, glycans could block it.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence count is 0.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction (GPR6 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is unreported.
Other subunits
GRIN1
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run for this triage. Re-fold GRIN2D + GRIN1 + GPR6 (ideally the 2:2 tetramer context) to see whether the GPR6 interface survives without overlapping the GluN1/GluN2 interfaces. Inspect the interface topology to confirm it is transmembrane/same-side rather than mixing cytoplasmic and extracellular residues, and check whether the N-glycosylation sites of either protein sit on the interface. If it survives, validate by co-immunoprecipitation or proximity assay in striatal neurons.

IL36RN ↔ GPR87 LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM low confidence ipTM 0.67 · pTM 0.73
Rationale
The pair is novel (no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed hit) and topologically plausible as a secreted cytokine (IL36RN) meeting a plasma-membrane GPCR (GPR87). However, UniProt lists GPR87 as a glycoprotein with 3 glycosylation sites, and a secreted partner could only bind the small extracellular face where such sites normally sit; the large modeled interface (BSA 2618 Å2) could plausibly overlap them. This was not verified: no fold or per-residue check was run, so whether any glycan sits on the interface, or whether the interface is even on the extracellular side, is unknown. GPR87's documented ligand is a lipid (LPA), not a protein, and IL36RN's documented receptor is IL1RL2, which also lowers the prior.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: GPR87 carries the Glycoprotein keyword with 3 glycosylation sites and 1 disulfide bond; site positions relative to the modeled interface were not checked. IL36RN has 1 disulfide bond and no glycosylation or lipidation. The PubMed PTM searches returned nothing specific to PTMs for either protein (2 hits for IL36RN, 7 for GPR87, all unrelated by title).
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence returned 0 papers mentioning IL36RN and GPR87 together.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction (GPR87 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is genuinely unreported.
Other subunits
IL1RL2;IL1RAP;SIGIRR
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Map the modeled interface residues against GPR87's UniProt topology and its 3 glycosylation sites. An interface on the cytoplasmic side, or one touching both sides, would make this an artifact; an extracellular interface clear of the glycosylation sites would upgrade it to CONFIRMED_NOVEL. 2) Re-fold with the core glycans attached at the GPR87 sites and see whether the interface survives. 3) Counter-screen by folding IL36RN against a few unrelated class A GPCRs, and against its real receptor IL1RL2 as a positive control, to test specificity. 4) If it survives, test in the wet lab: binding of recombinant IL36RN to GPR87-expressing cells, and whether it modulates LPA signalling. The other_subunits listed are IL36RN's documented partners from its UniProt function text, offered as controls rather than as missing subunits of this pair.

TNFRSF8 ↔ GPR65 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE low confidence ipTM 0.66 · pTM 0.43
Rationale
The pair is novel by every database check (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB not found, 0 PubMed co-mentions), but nothing independently supports it. HPA enrichment does not overlap (TNFRSF8 in mesothelial cells; GPR65 in mast cells, bone marrow and lymphoid tissue), and HPA places GPR65 mainly in vesicles while TNFRSF8 is at the plasma membrane. Both are glycoproteins (4 and 3 UniProt glycosylation sites), and the supplied fold metrics are weak outside the interface (pTM 0.43, partner pLDDT 45.5), with a very large 5561 Å2 buried area that I suspect, but could not check, reflects a low-confidence region draped over the GPCR rather than a defined interface. No fold was run to test interface topology or glycan placement.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: TNFRSF8 is a glycoprotein and phosphoprotein with 4 glycosylation sites and 14 disulfide bonds; GPR65 is a glycoprotein with 3 glycosylation sites. Both sets of glycans would sit on the extracellular side and could interfere with an ectodomain contact, but whether any site lies on the modeled interface was not checked. The PubMed PTM searches (4 hits for TNFRSF8, 6 for GPR65) returned mostly unrelated papers and add nothing specific.
PubMed co-occurrence
0 PubMed papers mention TNFRSF8 and GPR65 together.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction found (GPR65 is not in the CellPhoneDB gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. No prior report of this pair.
Other subunits
TNFSF8
Follow-up (not yet executed): Inspect the AF3 model to see which regions form the interface (ectodomain vs transmembrane vs cytoplasmic) and whether any contact mixes cytoplasmic and extracellular residues, which would be physically impossible. Check whether the 4 TNFRSF8 and 3 GPR65 N-glycosylation sites fall on the interface. If it survives, test co-expression in activated T cells or mast cells and attempt co-IP or proximity labelling. TNFSF8 (CD30L) is listed under other_subunits as the UniProt-annotated ligand of TNFRSF8 to consider for re-modeling; it is not a known complex member from CellPhoneDB.

ROR2 ↔ MRGPRF IMPLAUSIBLE low confidence ipTM 0.66 · pTM 0.49
Rationale
I'm changing the verdict from CONFIRMED_NOVEL to IMPLAUSIBLE. The check is right that HPA gives no protein-level tissue shared by ROR2 and MRGPRF, and neither is secreted, so a direct contact would need both in the same membrane of the same cell. My earlier argument rested on overlapping bone marrow MSC enrichment, which is RNA or single-cell level and weaker than shared protein-level data. Both being plasma-membrane receptors only makes a cis interaction possible in principle. Nothing independent supports it: STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence were all empty (known_interaction_strength=none), and no AF3 fold was run to give structural support (fold_evidence_status=not_run). The AF3 numbers I cited earlier (ipTM 0.66, interface pLDDT ~60, 6079 Å2 buried) were moderate and looked like non-specific packing without a bilayer. I keep confidence low because the MSC single-cell overlap leaves a small chance of real co-expression.
PTM / glycosylation
ROR2 has 3 glycosylation sites in its ectodomain, and MRGPRF has 1. Whether any lies on the modeled interface is unknown. This is secondary to the co-localization problem.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence count is 0.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction (MRGPRF not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. No prior report, so none of the known-interaction channels offers support.
Other subunits
WNT5A
Follow-up (not yet executed): Only worth revisiting if single-cell or protein-level data show ROR2 and MRGPRF in the same cell type. In that case, re-run AF3 with a membrane-aware setup and with the glycans represented.

GRM8 ↔ MRGPRX2 IMPLAUSIBLE medium confidence ipTM 0.66 · pTM 0.5
Rationale
Both are 7-TM GPCRs with non-overlapping expression: GRM8 is enriched in choroid plexus epithelial cells and cerebral cortex, MRGPRX2 only in mast cells (UniProt: mast cell-specific). A GPCR-GPCR interface this large (BSA 3883 Å2, 1007 contacts) at only moderate interface pLDDT (60.5) is most likely cis packing of the transmembrane bundles, which requires both receptors in the same cell membrane, and nothing here supports that. STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed all return nothing for the pair, so it is novel but lacks biological support.
PTM / glycosylation
GRM8 is a UniProt Glycoprotein with 5 N-glycosylation sites (presumably in its large extracellular domain) and 8 disulfide bonds. MRGPRX2 has no annotated glycosylation, only 2 disulfide bonds. The PubMed PTM hits for both genes are non-specific (MRGPRX2 mast-cell activation papers; unrelated GRM8 papers). If the modeled interface involves the GRM8 extracellular domain, glycans could interfere, but this is secondary to the expression mismatch.
PubMed co-occurrence
0 PubMed co-mentions.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction (MRGPRX2 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. Nothing known for this pair.
Other subunits
GRM8 (class C mGluRs function as obligate dimers; this is general knowledge, not from the tools)
Follow-up (not yet executed): Deprioritize. If pursued: (1) inspect whether the interface is transmembrane-helix packing, a common AF3 membrane-protein artifact since no bilayer is modeled, or involves the GRM8 extracellular domain; (2) check for real spatial co-localization of GRM8+ cells with mast cells (e.g. meningeal or choroid plexus mast cells) before any wet-lab test; (3) fold MRGPRX2 against unrelated GPCRs as a specificity control.

{
  "gene": "MRGPRX2",
  "accession": "Q96LB1",
  "protein_name": "Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor member X2",
  "function": "Mast cell-specific G protein-coupled receptor for basic secretagogues, which regulates mast cell degranulation and itch-related hypersensitivity reactions (PubMed:22069323, PubMed:25517090, PubMed:28288109, PubMed:34789874, PubMed:34789875). A secretagogue is an agent that promotes the secretion of hormones, neurohormones, chemical neurotransmitters or other compounds synthesized and secreted by cells (PubMed:25517090). Basic secretagogues comprise a set of cationic amphiphilic drugs, as well as endo- or exogenous peptides, consisting of a basic head group and a hydrophobic core (PubMed:25517090). Ligand binding causes a conformation change that triggers signaling via guanine nucleotide-binding proteins (G proteins) and modulates the activity of downstream effectors, such as adenylate cyclase (PubMed:28288109, PubMed:34789874, PubMed:34789875). MRGPRX2 is both coupled to G(q) and G(i) G proteins: G(q) coupling activates phospholipase C-beta, releasing diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) second messengers, while G(i) coupling mediates inhibition of adenylate cyclase activity (PubMed:28288109, PubMed:34789874, PubMed:34789875). Recognizes and binds small molecules containing a cyclized tetrahydroisoquinoline (THIQ), such as non-steroidal neuromuscular blocking drugs (NMBDs), including tubocurarine and atracurium (By similarity). In response to these compounds, mediates pseudo-allergic reactions characterized by histamine release, inflammation and airway contraction (By similarity). Acts as a receptor for substance P, a basic secretagogue neuropeptide released from the terminals of specific sensory nerves, initiating a signaling that mediates neurogenic inflammation and pain (PubMed:30686732, PubMed:34789875). Neurogenic inflammation includes mast cell activation, recruitment of immune cells and release of inflammatory mediators, such as cytokines and chemokines (By similarity). The inflammatory response can then activate or sensitize nociceptors, promoting pain (By similarity). Acts as a receptor for a number of other ligands, including peptides and alkaloids, such as cortistatin-14, proadrenomedullin peptides PAMP-12 and, at lower extent, PAMP-20, antibacterial protein LL-37, PMX-53 peptide, beta-defensins, complanadine A and CXCL17 (PubMed:12915402, PubMed:15823563, PubMed:21441599, PubMed:22069323, PubMed:23698749, PubMed:24930830, PubMed:34789874, PubMed:34789875). Also acts as a receptor for opioids, such as (-)- and (+)-morphine, hydrocodone, sinomenine, dextromethorphan, dynorphin A, dynorphin B, and alpha- and beta-neoendorphin, promoting mast cell degranulation (PubMed:28288109)",

HEBP1 ↔ GPR37 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE low confidence ipTM 0.65 · pTM 0.54
Rationale
The pair is novel (no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed hit) and the AF3 score is moderate (ipTM 0.65, interface pLDDT 68.7). But HEBP1 is a predicted intracellular haem-binding protein and GPR37 is a 7TM GPCR with a glycosylated ectodomain, and I could not determine which face of GPR37 the modelled interface sits on. fold_complex was not available in this session, so no topology check was run. Without it the compartment mismatch is a soft negative, and GPR37's own HPA localisation is rated Uncertain.
PTM / glycosylation
GPR37 is a UniProt Glycoprotein with 3 glycosylation sites, 1 disulfide and Ubl conjugation; N-glycan sites on a GPCR are normally extracellular. If the modelled interface is on the extracellular face, glycans could occlude it and HEBP1 would also be on the wrong side of the membrane. HEBP1 has no annotated PTM features. The PubMed PTM hits for both genes were not informative about the interface.
PubMed co-occurrence
0 PubMed co-mentions.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction, and no curated complex for GPR37. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is genuinely unreported.
Other subunits
PSAP
Follow-up (not yet executed): Map the AF3 interface residues onto GPR37's UniProt topology (cytoplasmic loops/C-tail versus extracellular N-terminus/loops) and onto its 3 glycosylation sites. A purely cytoplasmic interface would be a plausible novel intracellular docking interaction. An extracellular or mixed cytoplasmic-plus-extracellular interface should be treated as implausible or a glycan artifact unless HEBP1 release is shown. Separately, from background knowledge rather than the tools: an N-terminal HEBP1 peptide (F2L) is reported to be a secreted agonist of the GPCR FPR3, so it may be worth folding the HEBP1 N-terminal peptide alone against GPR37, with the known ligand prosaposin (PSAP) as a positive control. Wet-lab confirmation would be co-IP or BRET in oligodendrocyte-lineage cells. GPR37's 63 HPA-listed interactors suggest a hub, so specificity controls are needed.

GNRH2 ↔ MRGPRX2 CONFIRMED_NOVEL VALIDATE low confidence ipTM 0.65 · pTM 0.64
Rationale
MRGPRX2's documented function is exactly a promiscuous receptor for cationic amphiphilic peptide secretagogues (substance P, PAMP-12, LL-37, cortistatin, dynorphins), so a basic secreted decapeptide hormone like GnRH-II is a mechanistically sensible, previously unreported agonist candidate — STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed all return nothing for this pair. Confidence is low because ipTM 0.65 with partner pLDDT 37.6 over a huge 3673 Å² interface suggests the unprocessed precursor sprawling on the receptor surface rather than a decapeptide in the orthosteric pocket.
PTM / glycosylation
Neither protein is glycosylated (GNRH2 feature counts: 1 Modified residue; MRGPRX2: only disulfides, which AF3 handles). However GNRH2's UniProt keywords are 'Cleavage on pair of basic residues', 'Amidation' — the bioactive species is the processed, pyroglutamyl/C-terminally amidated GnRH-II decapeptide, not the precursor AF3 folded; the very low partner pLDDT (37.6) is consistent with large disordered precursor segments draping over the receptor (BSA 3673 Å², 763 contacts) rather than a decapeptide seated in the orthosteric TM pocket.
PubMed co-occurrence
0 PubMed papers mention GNRH2 and MRGPRX2 together.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction, and MRGPRX2 is absent from the CellPhoneDB gene table (so also no complex-member info). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. No prior evidence anywhere → genuine novelty.
Follow-up (not yet executed): Re-run AF3 with only the mature processed GnRH-II decapeptide (pGlu-HWSHGWYPG-NH2, amidation represented if possible) against MRGPRX2 and check whether contacts fall on transmembrane/ECL2 orthosteric residues rather than surface draping; then test experimentally with a mast-cell β-hexosaminidase release / Ca2+ flux assay in MRGPRX2-transfected cells, plus counter-screen against an unrelated GPCR, given MRGPRX2's known ligand promiscuity.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Use mature GnRH-II decapeptide (pyroGlu-His-Trp-Ser-His-Gly-Trp-Tyr-Pro-Gly-NH2) and a precursor/GAP-containing fragment side by side, in MRGPRX2-expressing vs. MRGPRX2-knockout/mock cells.)
Why this method
GNRH2 is a predicted secreted peptide hormone and MRGPRX2 is a GPCR on mast cells. This is a paracrine ligand-receptor pair, so the two proteins need not be in the same cell, and a functional agonist readout (Ca2+ flux, degranulation) is more informative than co-localization. The low-confidence AF3 model (precursor sprawl, partner pLDDT 37.6) also needs a test of whether the mature decapeptide is the active species.
Target tissue(s)
Stomach (gastric chief cells, GNRH2 side), Mast cells (MRGPRX2 side; skin, gastrointestinal mucosa), Ovary (oocytes, GNRH2 side), Intestine (enteroendocrine cells, GNRH2 side)
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA gives only single-cell-type data, with no tissue-level overlap. GNRH2 RNA is highest in gastric chief cells (11.1 nCPM), then oocytes (4.7) and enteroendocrine cells (3.8). MRGPRX2 is restricted to mast cells (18.5 nCPM). The plausible in vivo meeting point is the gastric/intestinal mucosa, where mast cells sit near enteroendocrine and chief cells. For the assay itself, use recombinant or synthetic peptide on mast cells or on cell lines expressing the receptor.
Cell type(s)
Mast cells, Gastric chief cells, Enteroendocrine cells, Oocytes
Protocol notes
1) Receptor cells: HEK293 or CHO-K1 stably expressing MRGPRX2 (with Gα15 or a Ca2+ dye such as Fluo-4), with parental cells as the negative control. Also use LAD2 human mast cells (endogenous MRGPRX2), and primary human skin or gut mast cells if possible. 2) Stimulate with a synthetic mature GnRH-II dose range (1 nM–100 µM). Read out Ca2+ flux in real time, β-arrestin recruitment (Tango or BRET), and mast cell degranulation (β-hexosaminidase release, CD63/CD107a flow). Test the GnRH-II precursor or GAP fragment in parallel. 3) For specificity, use MRGPRX2 CRISPR knockout LAD2 cells or the antagonist/inverse agonist C9 (or another MRGPRX2 antagonist), and run GnRH-I and a scrambled GnRH-II peptide to separate GnRH receptor effects and charge-driven nonspecific effects. 4) Confirm direct binding with a labeled-peptide binding assay or SPR/MST on purified receptor, and optionally a co-IP with tagged receptor.
Controls
Positive: substance P, PAMP-12, or compound 48/80 on MRGPRX2 cells (strong Ca2+ and degranulation). Negative: parental or empty-vector cells, MRGPRX2-KO LAD2 cells, scrambled GnRH-II, and a non-cationic decapeptide. Specificity: GnRH-I (GnRH receptor agonist), and a GnRHR antagonist to rule out classical GnRH receptor signalling. Use ionomycin as the maximum-response control.
Caveats
AF3 confidence is low (ipTM 0.65, partner pLDDT 37.6, 3673 Å² interface). The model probably shows the unprocessed precursor lying across the receptor rather than the mature decapeptide in the orthosteric pocket, so use the processed, amidated peptide and test the precursor separately. MRGPRX2 is promiscuous and responds to many cationic amphiphilic peptides, so a positive response at high micromolar concentrations may be a nonspecific cationic effect. Only activity at physiologically plausible concentrations would be meaningful. HPA shows no tissue-level RNA or protein data for either gene, only single-cell data, and the two proteins are expressed in different cell types. Co-occurrence in vivo is therefore speculative. The mouse ortholog Mrgprb2 differs, so human cells are needed.

  "function": "Mast cell-specific G protein-coupled receptor for basic secretagogues, which regulates mast cell degranulation and itch-related hypersensitivity reactions (PubMed:22069323, PubMed:25517090, PubMed:28288109, PubMed:34789874, PubMed:34789875). A secretagogue is an agent that promotes the secretion of hormones, neurohormones, chemical neurotransmitters or other compounds synthesized and secreted by cells (PubMed:25517090). Basic secretagogues comprise a set of cationic amphiphilic drugs, as well as endo- or exogenous peptides, consisting of a basic head group and a hydrophobic core (PubMed:25517090). Ligand binding causes a conformation change that triggers signaling via guanine nucleotide-binding proteins (G proteins) and modulates the activity of downstream effectors, such as adenylate cyclase (PubMed:28288109, PubMed:34789874, PubMed:34789875). MRGPRX2 is both coupled to G(q) and G(i) G proteins: G(q) coupling activates phospholipase C-beta, releasing diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) second messengers, while G(i) coupling mediates inhibition of adenylate cyclase activity (PubMed:28288109, PubMed:34789874, PubMed:34789875). Recognizes and binds small molecules containing a cyclized tetrahydroisoquinoline (THIQ), such as non-steroidal neuromuscular blocking drugs (NMBDs), including tubocurarine and atracurium (By similarity). In response to these compounds, mediates pseudo-allergic reactions characterized by histamine release, inflammation and airway contraction (By similarity). Acts as a receptor for substance P, a basic secretagogue neuropeptide released from the terminals of specific sensory nerves, initiating a signaling that mediates neurogenic inflammation and pain (PubMed:30686732, PubMed:34789875). Neurogenic inflammation includes mast cell activation, recruitment of immune cells and release of inflammatory mediators, such as cytokines and chemokines (By similarity). The inflammatory response can then activate or sensitize nociceptors, promoting pain (By similarity). Acts as a receptor for a number of other ligands, including peptides and alkaloids, such as cortistatin-14, proadrenomedullin peptides PAMP-12 and, at lower extent, PAMP-20, antibacterial protein LL-37, PMX-53 peptide, beta-defensins, complanadine A and CXCL17 (PubMed:12915402, PubMed:15823563, PubMed:21441599, PubMed:22069323, PubMed:23698749, PubMed:24930830, PubMed:34789874, PubMed:34789875). Also acts as a receptor for opioids, such as (-)- and (+)-morphine, hydrocodone, sinomenine, dextromethorphan, dynorphin A, dynorphin B, and alpha- and beta-neoendorphin, promoting mast cell degranulation (PubMed:28288109)",

GHRL ↔ MRGPRX4 LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM low confidence ipTM 0.65 · pTM 0.66
Rationale
The pair is unreported (no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed hit) and topologically plausible as a secreted hormone meeting a plasma-membrane GPCR. However, UniProt shows ghrelin is a lipoprotein (3 lipidation features, amidation) whose octanoylation is essential for activating its real receptor GHSR, and AF3 folded the bare, unprocessed sequence. MRGPRX4 is a receptor for bile acids (small molecules) with 2 glycosylation sites, and the supplied partner pLDDT is low (47.7) despite ipTM 0.65, so the modelled interface may not reflect the mature acylated peptide.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt GHRL: keywords Lipoprotein and Amidation, 3 lipidation features and 1 modified residue; the function text states octanoylation is essential for GHSR activation. This lipid modification is central to ghrelin's receptor-binding mechanism and is absent from the AF3 model. UniProt MRGPRX4: Glycoprotein with 2 glycosylation sites (probably on the extracellular side) and a bile-acid, small-molecule binding pocket. The PubMed PTM searches returned nothing specific for either protein (GHRL hits were unrelated; MRGPRX4 hits concern phospho-drug agonists). Whether any of these sites lies on the modelled interface was not checked.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence returned 0 papers for GHRL and MRGPRX4.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction, and MRGPRX4 is not in its gene table. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is novel in the literature; ghrelin's established receptor is GHSR.
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run during this triage. Re-fold MRGPRX4 with the mature ghrelin-28 peptide (not the 117-residue prepropeptide), with and without the Ser3 octanoyl group, and check whether the peptide N-terminus enters the transmembrane bundle and whether the receptor's N-glycosylation sites lie on the interface. Counter-screen by folding ghrelin against GHSR as a positive control and against other MRGPRX paralogs for specificity. If the pose survives, test acyl- versus des-acyl ghrelin in an MRGPRX4 Gq/Ca2+ assay.

CD226 ↔ GPR141 LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM low confidence ipTM 0.64 · pTM 0.54
Rationale
The pair is novel (no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed hit) and both are plasma-membrane proteins with some bone-marrow overlap, so a cis interaction is topologically possible. However, CD226 carries 8 annotated N-glycosylation sites on its small Ig ectodomain and GPR141 carries 2, none of which AF3 modelled, and a 3242 A2 / 655-contact interface very likely includes that glycosylated surface. I could not verify whether any glycosite sits on the interface because no fold tool was available in this session, so this is an unresolved caveat rather than a demonstrated artifact; the moderate ipTM (0.64) and borderline p_twoway (0.053) do not offset it.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: CD226 is a Glycoprotein with 8 glycosylation sites (plus 3 disulfides and 2 modified residues); GPR141 is a Glycoprotein with 2 glycosylation sites. The PubMed PTM searches (36 hits for CD226, 1 for GPR141) returned nothing specific to these proteins' glycosylation. Eight glycans on CD226's two-Ig-domain ectodomain make it plausible that the modelled contact surface is partly shielded in vivo, but the per-residue position of the sites relative to the interface was not checked.
PubMed co-occurrence
0 PubMed papers mention CD226 and GPR141 together.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction (GPR141 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is genuinely unreported. CD226's documented ligands are PVR/CD155 and NECTIN2/CD112; GPR141 is an orphan receptor.
Other subunits
PVR;NECTIN2
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Map the 8 CD226 and 2 GPR141 N-glycosylation sites onto the AF3 interface residues; if any fall on it, re-fold with core glycans attached and see whether the interface survives. 2) Check which topological regions form the interface (ectodomain to extracellular loops, or TM helix to TM bundle); an interface mixing cytoplasmic and extracellular residues would be physically impossible, and TM-TM packing between unrelated membrane proteins is a common AF3 false positive. 3) Confirm same-cell coexpression in single-cell data (NK/T cells, platelets, myeloid progenitors). 4) If the interface survives, test by co-IP or BRET in co-transfected cells, and check whether it competes with PVR/NECTIN2 binding on CD226. PVR and NECTIN2 are listed under other_subunits only as known CD226 ligands for that competition check, not as missing complex members.

SIGLEC1 ↔ GPR141 LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM medium confidence ipTM 0.64 · pTM 0.38
Rationale
The pair is novel (no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed hit) and biologically plausible as a trans contact between two plasma-membrane proteins. However, UniProt describes SIGLEC1 as a lectin whose binding is sialic-acid dependent (14 glycosylation sites), and GPR141 is itself a glycoprotein (2 sites). AF3's bare-sequence interface (ipTM 0.64, interface pLDDT 61.2, pTM 0.38) therefore cannot represent the real glycan-mediated mechanism and may be sterically blocked in vivo.
PTM / glycosylation
SIGLEC1: UniProt keywords Lectin and Glycoprotein, 14 glycosylation sites, and function text stating sialic-acid dependent binding with preference for alpha-2,3-linked sialic acid; its known counter-receptors (e.g. SPN/CD43) are recognised through sialylated glycans. GPR141: Glycoprotein keyword with 2 glycosylation sites, which I assume (not checked per-residue) lie on the extracellular N-terminus or loops. The PubMed PTM searches were mostly non-specific (17 hits for SIGLEC1, including sialylated CD43; 1 unrelated hit for GPR141). Whether any glycosylation site sits on the modeled interface was not checked.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence returned 0 papers mentioning both genes.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction (GPR141 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is unreported.
Other subunits
TYROBP
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run. Map the modeled interface residues onto UniProt topology and glycosylation sites to confirm the contact is extracellular-to-extracellular and whether the SIGLEC1 V-set sialic-acid site or GPR141's N-glycan sites are involved. Re-fold with glycans attached at the GPR141 N-glycosylation sites. Test experimentally with SIGLEC1-Fc binding to GPR141-expressing cells with and without sialidase, and with the sialic-acid-binding-dead SIGLEC1 mutant (R116A in the V-set domain, residue number recalled from the literature, not retrieved here). TYROBP is listed under other subunits only because UniProt mentions it as a SIGLEC1 signalling partner; it is not established as an obligate subunit. With 2014 tokens and pTM 0.38, the long SIGLEC1 Ig-repeat chain is poorly placed overall; a fold restricted to the N-terminal domains would be cleaner.

EFNA3 ↔ GPR21 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE low confidence ipTM 0.64 · pTM 0.68
Rationale
No prior evidence for the pair (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB not found, 0 PubMed co-mentions), so it is formally novel, but the supporting evidence is too thin to call it CONFIRMED_NOVEL. HPA has no subcellular data for either protein, GPR21 is barely expressed (blood vessel 5.1 nTPM, single-cell 'Not detected') with no overlap with EFNA3's enriched epithelial/keratinocyte profile, and both are glycoproteins (EFNA3 3 N-glycosylation sites plus GPI anchor; GPR21 2 sites) whose glycans AF3 did not model. The supplied interface (BSA 5310 Å2, 1124 contacts, partner pLDDT 58) is much larger than the small extracellular face of a class-A GPCR could plausibly offer a GPI-anchored ephrin ectodomain; this is my inference from the numbers, not a checked topology, and it suggests contacts with transmembrane or cytoplasmic regions that would be physically inaccessible.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: EFNA3 is a Glycoprotein with 3 glycosylation sites and 1 lipidation (GPI anchor); GPR21 is a Glycoprotein with 2 glycosylation sites. In a class-A GPCR these typically sit on the extracellular N-terminus or loops, which is the only surface an ephrin ectodomain could reach, so they could plausibly occlude the modeled interface; site positions relative to the interface were not checked. The PubMed PTM searches returned nothing specific to glycosylation (EFNA3 hits are miR-210/EFNA3 pathway papers; the single GPR21 hit is about plasmalogen signaling).
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence count = 0.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction found (GPR21 is not in the CellPhoneDB gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is unreported. EFNA3's documented partners are Eph receptor tyrosine kinases; GPR21 is annotated as an orphan receptor.
Other subunits
EPHA2;EPHA4
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run in this triage. (1) Inspect the AF3 model's interface topology: if EFNA3 contacts GPR21 transmembrane-core or cytoplasmic residues, discard it as a bilayer-ignoring artifact. (2) Map GPR21's 2 and EFNA3's 3 N-glycosylation sites against the interface residues, and re-fold with glycans attached if they overlap. (3) Counter-screen EFNA3 against unrelated class-A GPCRs to test whether the ipTM of 0.64 is specific to GPR21. (4) Check for real co-expression in vascular or neuronal datasets before any wet-lab binding assay. The other_subunits entries (EPHA2, EPHA4) are EFNA3's canonical Eph receptor partners from general knowledge, offered as competition controls, not tool-derived complex members.

CHL1 ↔ GPR12 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE low confidence ipTM 0.63 · pTM 0.52
Rationale
The check says GPR12's UniProt FUNCTION text describes carbohydrate binding. I can't re-read that text here. What I know of GPR12 (an orphan class-A GPCR with constitutive Gs/cAMP signalling, roles in neurite outgrowth and oocyte arrest) does not fit a lectin, so the flag may be a keyword false positive. I can't substantiate that, though, and guidance says an unresolved lectin flag shouldn't be dismissed. If it were real, AF3's bare-protein contact between GPR12 and the heavily glycosylated CHL1 ectodomain (10 glycosylation sites) could not be trusted. That is true whichever residues touch. Other facts: known_interaction_strength=none (no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed trace) and HPA brain co-expression is plausible. The fold is not_run, so the earlier ipTM 0.63 and interface pLDDT 61.6 are unverified. With a glycan-mediated mechanism unresolved and no verified fold, "confirmed novel" is not justified. I am downgrading to insufficient evidence instead of calling it an artifact, since the lectin claim conflicts with known GPR12 biology.
PTM / glycosylation
CHL1 has 10 glycosylation sites and 6 disulfides on its ectodomain. GPR12 has 2 N-glycosylation sites and 1 palmitoylation site. The deterministic check reports a carbohydrate-binding description in GPR12's UniProt FUNCTION. That conflicts with its orphan-GPCR biology and I could not verify it. If it is real, glycan-mediated binding would make the AF3 bare-protein contact unreliable.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence returned 0 hits for CHL1 with GPR12.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association. CellPhoneDB: no hit (GPR12 not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 papers. known_interaction_strength=none, so no known interaction is established.
Follow-up (not yet executed): Check the GPR12 UniProt FUNCTION text directly to see whether the carbohydrate-binding wording is real or a false positive. Then run the AF3 fold (currently not_run). If the pair still looks interesting, test whether CHL1 glycosylation, such as the HNK-1 epitope, is needed for contact.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay
Why this method
GPR12 is an orphan class-A GPCR with constitutive Gs/cAMP signalling, and CHL1 is a membrane-anchored adhesion molecule that is also shed or secreted in brain. If CHL1 is a ligand or modulator, the most informative readout is a change in GPR12 cAMP signalling. A functional readout also helps with the low-confidence fold, because it tests for an effect and not just proximity. PLA can be added as a secondary check.
Target tissue(s)
brain (cerebral cortex), retina, ovary
Why these tissues (HPA)
Brain is the only tissue where both proteins are clearly expressed in HPA (CHL1 RNA 62.8 nTPM with strong cerebral cortex protein; GPR12 RNA 11.6 nTPM). CHL1 is annotated as secreted in brain. Retina has GPR12 (7.8 nTPM) and is neural, so it is a reasonable secondary tissue. Ovary has CHL1 (31.9 nTPM) and GPR12 is known for oocyte meiotic arrest, but HPA shows no GPR12 ovary signal, so ovary is exploratory only.
Cell type(s)
cortical neurons, neurite-extending neurons (e.g. cerebellar granule or hippocampal neurons), neuronal cell lines such as SH-SY5Y or Neuro2a
Protocol notes
1) Use HEK293 cells, or a neuronal line, expressing GPR12 or empty vector. Use a CRE-luciferase or GloSensor cAMP readout. Because GPR12 is constitutively active, measure both baseline elevation and any change on top of it. 2) Treat cells with recombinant CHL1 ectodomain (Fc-tagged, mammalian-expressed so it keeps its glycans) in a dose range, and compare with an Fc-only control. Also try co-culture with CHL1-expressing cells. Run an inverse-agonist/antagonist arm if available (e.g. a Gs pathway inhibitor, or the reported GPR12 ligand S1P as a comparator). 3) Run a neurite outgrowth assay in primary cortical or cerebellar neurons with CHL1 +/- GPR12 knockdown or knockout. Measure outgrowth and cAMP/pCREB. 4) As orthogonal binding evidence, run a cell-surface binding assay of CHL1-Fc on GPR12-expressing versus mock cells, or a PLA with an epitope-tagged GPR12 and anti-CHL1 antibody.
Controls
Positive: forskolin for maximal cAMP, and a Gs-coupled receptor with its known agonist for assay validity. Negative: Fc-only protein, mock-transfected cells, heat-denatured CHL1 ectodomain, an unrelated L1-family protein (L1CAM or NCAM), and a GPR12-null or knockdown background. Check GPR12 surface expression with an N-terminal tag.
Caveats
The verdict is CONFIRMED_NOVEL at low confidence, and the fold was not run. The earlier ipTM of 0.63, interface pLDDT of 61.6 and p_twoway of 0.056 are moderate and unverified. The UniProt glycan-binding flag on GPR12 is probably a keyword false positive and could not be re-checked. GPR12 has only 2 N-glycosylation sites and 1 palmitoylation site, but CHL1 has 10 glycosylation sites. Glycans could therefore affect any contact, so recombinant CHL1 should come from a mammalian source, with a PNGase F or glycosylation-mutant arm as an optional extra. Constitutive GPR12 activity can mask small ligand effects. CHL1 is a membrane protein with no HPA subcellular location, and may act in cis on the same cell or by shedding in trans. HPA has no single-cell data for either protein, and GPR12 has no protein-level data, so cell-type assignment is inferred.

CATSPER2 ↔ GPR25 IMPLAUSIBLE medium confidence ipTM 0.63 · pTM 0.54
Rationale
CATSPER2 is a pore-forming subunit of the sperm-specific CatSper channel in the sperm flagellum (UniProt; HPA end piece/principal piece), while GPR25 is a lymphocyte chemokine receptor for CXCL17 with HPA enrichment only in stomach, so there is no shared cell type for two integral membrane proteins that would have to meet in the same membrane. No STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed link exists, and the ipTM of 0.63 between a 6-TM channel subunit and a 7-TM GPCR is most likely generic helix-helix packing, with CATSPER2's obligate CatSper partners absent from the model.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists no glycosylation or lipidation features for either protein (GPR25 has one disulfide bond only). The PubMed PTM search returned 2 hits for CATSPER2, neither about its modifications, and 0 for GPR25. There is no PTM basis for an artifact call; the concern is biological context and unmodeled membrane/complex.
PubMed co-occurrence
pubmed_cooccurrence returned 0 hits for CATSPER2 and GPR25.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no curated interaction, and GPR25 is not in its gene table. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 papers. The pair is unreported, but that novelty does not outweigh the biological mismatch.
Other subunits
CATSPERB;CATSPERD
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run for this candidate. If it is pursued anyway: (1) inspect the existing model to see whether the interface is purely TM-helix packing; (2) re-fold CATSPER2 with its CatSper partners (CATSPER1/3/4 pore subunits, plus CATSPERB/CATSPERD from CellPhoneDB) to see whether the GPR25 contact surface is already occupied in the native channel; (3) check sperm proteomics for any GPR25 expression. Otherwise deprioritize.

GHRL ↔ MRGPRX1 LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM medium confidence ipTM 0.63 · pTM 0.65
Rationale
GHRL is a secreted blood hormone (HPA: "Secreted to blood", stomach/enteroendocrine-enriched) and MRGPRX1 is a plasma-membrane peptide-sensing GPCR (UniProt: activated by BAM22/BAM8-22 enkephalin peptides, tick defensins, conotoxin), so a paracrine/endocrine peptide-ligand/GPCR pairing is compartmentally plausible and no coexpression in the same cell is required. However, UniProt for GHRL states that octanoylation of Ser3 (Lipidation x3, keyword "Lipoprotein") is ESSENTIAL for receptor activation — the acyl chain is the pharmacophore that inserts into the GHSR pocket — and AF3 folded bare, unacylated sequence, so the modeled interface (with low partner pLDDT 46.2 and only moderate ipTM 0.63) likely does not represent the real lipid-mediated binding mode. MRGPRX1 is also a glycoprotein (1 N-glycosylation site) that AF3 cannot represent.
PTM / glycosylation
GHRL UniProt: Lipidation x3, keyword "Lipoprotein"/"Amidation"; FUNCTION text explicitly says octanoylation is essential for GHSR activation — a lipid-mediated binding mechanism AF3 cannot represent at all. MRGPRX1: keyword "Glycoprotein", 1 Glycosylation + 2 disulfide features on an extracellular-facing GPCR. PubMed PTM hits for both were largely irrelevant/off-topic.
PubMed co-occurrence
pubmed_cooccurrence count = 0.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no hit (MRGPRX1 not even in the CellPhoneDB gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. So the pair itself is genuinely unreported — novelty is not the issue; mechanism is.
Follow-up (not yet executed): Re-run AF3 with ghrelin's Ser3 O-n-octanoyl modification represented (and ideally the mature ghrelin-28 peptide rather than the prepropeptide) and check (a) whether the acyl chain inserts into the MRGPRX1 TM bundle, (b) interface topology (should be Extracellular/Transmembrane, never Cytoplasmic), and (c) whether the N-glycosylation site lands on the modeled interface. Wet-lab: test acyl-ghrelin vs des-acyl ghrelin in a MRGPRX1 Ca2+/IP3 reporter assay against the BAM8-22 positive control.

Activated by some tick defensins, such as I.persulcatus Def1 and I.ricinus Def2, evoking itch (PubMed:33358893). Also activated by conotoxin CNF-Tx2, inducing itch sensation (PubMed:30243794, PubMed:37591889). Activated by the antimalarial drug chloroquine; however, activation requires concentrations that exceed the chloroquine concentrations observed in plasma of patients undergoing chloroquine treatment (PubMed:20004959). Also activated following cleavage by the dust mite cysteine protease Der p1 (PubMed:28768771). Ligand binding causes a conformation change that triggers signaling via guanine nucleotide-binding proteins (G proteins) and modulates the activity of downstream effectors, such as adenylate cyclase (PubMed:36302898, PubMed:37591889). MRGPRX1 is both coupled to G(q) and G(i) G proteins: G(q) coupling activates phospholipase C-beta, releasing diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) second messengers, leading to sensitize TRPV1 in pruriceptors, while G(i) coupling mediates inhibition of adenylate cyclase activity (PubMed:23074220, PubMed:36302898, PubMed:37347749, PubMed:37591889). Activation of MRGPRX1 in the peripheral nervous system elicits itch, evoking scratching (PubMed:28223516). MRGPRX1 activation in sensory neurons of the nasal mucosa mediates sneezing responses to irritants or influenza-virus (By similarity). Activation in the central nervous system dampens chronic pain: BAM8-22-binding at the central terminals prevents pain signals passing to spinal cord neurons, attenuating spinal nociceptive transmission (PubMed:28223516). IFNA7 ↔ GPR151 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE low confidence ipTM 0.62 · pTM 0.65
Rationale
The pair is novel (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB not found, PubMed 0 hits) and topologically permissible (IFNA7 secreted to blood; GPR151 a cell-membrane GPCR per UniProt). But HPA has no subcellular data for either protein and essentially no expression data (both tissue "Not detected"; GPR151 only cone-photoreceptor enhanced at 2.1 nCPM). The moderate AF3 score (ipTM 0.62, interface pLDDT 66.2) cannot be tied to GPR151's extracellular face, and GPR151 carries 2 unmodelled glycosylation sites, so nothing beyond the fold supports a specific interaction.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: GPR151 is a Glycoprotein with 2 annotated glycosylation sites, whose positions were not retrieved. If they sit on the extracellular N-terminus or loops, they are on the only surface a secreted protein could bind, and AF3 did not model them. IFNA7 has 2 disulfide bonds only and no glycosylation annotation. PubMed PTM search returned 0 hits for both. Whether the glycosylation sites fall on the modelled interface is unverified.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence count is 0.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is unreported. IFNA7's established receptor is IFNAR1/IFNAR2 (background knowledge, not returned by a tool); UniProt describes GPR151 as a proton-sensing GPCR, and CellPhoneDB lists it only in complexes with GALR1, GALR2 and GALR3.
Other subunits
GALR1;GALR2;GALR3
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run for this triage. (1) Inspect the AF3 model to see whether the interface is on GPR151's extracellular N-terminus/loops or on its cytoplasmic C-terminal tail. The very large buried surface (3939 Å2, 740 contacts) with a 1.84 Å minimum separation suggests a possibly disordered tail wrapping around IFNA7; a cytoplasmic-side interface would be physically impossible for a secreted cytokine. (2) Check whether GPR151's 2 glycosylation sites lie at the interface, and re-fold with glycans if so. (3) Counter-screen by folding other IFNA subtypes and unrelated four-helix cytokines against GPR151, and IFNA7 against unrelated GPCRs, to test specificity. (4) If the model survives, test binding in a wet-lab assay (e.g. GPR151-expressing cells with recombinant IFNA7). The GALR paralogs listed under other subunits are mutually exclusive CellPhoneDB complex partners of GPR151; they are not required for this pair.

PPIA ↔ GPR3 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE low confidence ipTM 0.62 · pTM 0.61
Rationale
The contradiction is valid. PPIA was folded against 11 receptors and passed the confidence gate for 4 of them (36%), so the moderate AF3 result (ipTM 0.62) for GPR3 mostly reflects PPIA, not GPR3. PPIA is a small, abundant, sticky cyclophilin. The breadth here is not a shared-receptor pattern like a chemokine's, because PPIA has no known promiscuous GPCR-ligand role. Its one established extracellular partner is BSG/CD147, which is not a GPCR. That makes the breadth look like a non-specific fold artifact, and I withdraw CONFIRMED_NOVEL. The other evidence does not rescue specificity. STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence are all empty (known_interaction_strength=none), so there is no prior support for this pair. HPA plausibility is only 'plausible', with no subcellular data, so co-localization is not substantiated. The GPR3 glycosylation and palmitoylation sites are unmodeled and unchecked against the interface. I do not call the pair IMPLAUSIBLE, since PPIA is secreted and GPR3 is a surface GPCR. The pair is currently uninformative.
PTM / glycosylation
GPR3 has 1 glycosylation site and 1 palmitoylation site, and PPIA has 1 glycosylation site. AF3 does not model these, and their position relative to the interface was not checked. This matters only if the interface is extracellular.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence count is 0 for PPIA and GPR3.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING not found; CellPhoneDB no entry (GPR3 absent); PubMed co-occurrence 0 hits. No prior evidence of interaction, so this is not ALREADY_KNOWN, but absence also gives no positive support.
Other subunits
BSG
Follow-up (not yet executed): Check PPIA against the full receptor panel and against unrelated negative-control membrane proteins to see whether its confidence is generic. Compare GPR3's ipTM with PPIA to its ipTM with other partners. Check which side of the membrane the interface sits on, and whether the GPR3 glycosylation site is near it. Obtain HPA subcellular data for both proteins.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Include BSG/CD147 co-expression or knockdown arm, and a GPR3 N-glycosylation-site / palmitoylation-site mutant arm (or PNGase F/tunicamycin pretreatment))
Why this method
PPIA is a secreted/plasma protein (HPA "Secreted to blood") and GPR3 is a membrane GPCR, so the pair is best framed as an extracellular ligand and receptor. GPR3 is constitutively active through Gs, so the natural readout is a change in cAMP, which shows whether PPIA modulates the receptor. The AF3 complex also includes BSG, so the assay should test whether BSG is needed.
Target tissue(s)
Small intestine, Stomach, Colon
Why these tissues (HPA)
The HPA data give only single-cell-type signal. PPIA is very high in gastric progenitor cells (3194 nCPM) and GPR3 is detected in Paneth cells (7.9 nCPM). Both are gastrointestinal epithelial cells, so the GI tract (stomach and small intestine/colon) is the most plausible shared tissue. No tissue-level RNA or protein data were provided. The expression of the two proteins differs by orders of magnitude, and there is no true same-cell overlap. For the assay itself, use HEK293 cells with GPR3 and BSG expressed heterologously, plus an intestinal epithelial or organoid model.
Cell type(s)
Gastric progenitor cells, Paneth cells
Protocol notes
1) Use HEK293 cells transfected with GPR3, with or without BSG, and compare against empty vector and a different Gs-coupled GPCR as a specificity control. Treat with 0.1–1 µM recombinant human PPIA (endotoxin-free) for 15–60 min. Measure cAMP with a GloSensor or HTRF assay, and measure CREB phosphorylation (pCREB) by western blot. Because GPR3 has high basal cAMP, use a dose–response curve and GPR3 inverse-agonist or knockdown conditions to see the signal window. 2) Confirm binding directly with a pulldown or surface-binding assay: add biotinylated or His-tagged PPIA to GPR3-expressing cells and detect bound PPIA by flow cytometry or an anti-PPIA stain on non-permeabilized cells. 3) Test the mechanism by adding the PPIA isomerase inhibitor cyclosporin A (or a catalytically dead PPIA R55A mutant) and a BSG-blocking antibody or siRNA. 4) Optionally confirm in intestinal organoids, using PPIA from conditioned medium, and check GPR3 transcript first by qPCR.
Controls
Positive: forskolin for the cAMP readout; PPIA acting on BSG-expressing cells (ERK phosphorylation or NF-kB activation) to confirm that the recombinant PPIA is active. Negative: mock-transfected cells, heat-denatured PPIA or an unrelated cyclophilin (PPIB), and a GPR3 non-signalling or glycosylation-site mutant. Also use a Gs-coupled GPCR that is unrelated to GPR3 as a specificity control.
Caveats
The AF3 confidence is low (ipTM 0.62, interface pLDDT 74). HPA has no subcellular data for either protein, and it was not checked which side of the membrane the interface sits on. If the modeled interface is intracellular, a secreted-ligand assay will miss it, and co-IP or PLA in permeabilized cells would be needed. GPR3 has one glycosylation site and a palmitoylation site that AF3 does not model, so PTMs could block or change binding. GPR3 is constitutively active, which may mask any ligand effect. PPIA is abundant and sticky and is a housekeeping protein, so non-specific binding is a risk. The GPR3 RNA signal is very low (7.9 nCPM), so endogenous responses may be hard to detect, and overexpression models may not reflect physiology.

Rationale
No prior evidence links this pair (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB not found, PubMed co-occurrence 0), and both are membrane proteins enhanced in bone marrow and lymphoid tissue, so the pairing is physically plausible. However, HCST (DAP10) is a single-pass adapter that CellPhoneDB and UniProt describe as functioning in an obligate complex with KLRK1 (NKG2D), which is absent from the model. With partner pLDDT of 44.8 and a 1.77 Å minimum separation, the ipTM of 0.62 may reflect generic transmembrane-helix packing against the GPCR bundle rather than a specific interface.
PTM / glycosylation
GPR65: UniProt Glycoprotein keyword with 3 annotated glycosylation sites, plus 2 disulfide bonds; the 6 PubMed hits are functional papers, not PTM-specific. HCST: Glycoprotein and Phosphoprotein keywords, 1 modified residue, 0 PubMed PTM hits. Whether any glycosylation site sits on the modeled interface was not checked, so this is a caveat rather than a finding.
PubMed co-occurrence
0 PubMed papers mention HCST and GPR65 together.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction for the pair. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is novel with respect to these sources.
Other subunits
KLRK1
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run here. Re-fold HCST + GPR65 with KLRK1 to see whether HCST prefers its canonical partner and whether the GPR65 contact survives. Inspect the structure to confirm the interface is TM–TM and not mixing cytoplasmic and extracellular residues, and check the 1.77 Å minimum separation for clashes. Check whether the three GPR65 glycosylation sites fall on the interface. Run a counter-screen of HCST against unrelated GPCRs to test specificity. If the contact holds up, validate by co-IP or BRET in NK, T or mast cells.

FN1 ↔ GPR82 CONFIRMED_NOVEL VALIDATE low confidence ipTM 0.62 · pTM 0.37
Rationale
No prior record of this pair: STRING found nothing, CellPhoneDB found nothing, and PubMed co-occurrence is 0. The pairing is compartment-plausible, since FN1 is a secreted plasma/ECM protein and GPR82 is a cell-membrane orphan GPCR (UniProt), and FN1 is liver-produced while GPR82 is enhanced in Kupffer cells. Confidence is low because the fold is only moderate (ipTM 0.62, pTM 0.37, interface pLDDT 62.2), FN1 is a sticky 115-partner hub, both are glycoproteins, and no fold tool was available to check which side of the membrane the interface sits on.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: FN1 is a glycoprotein with 8 glycosylation sites and 30 disulfide bonds, plus sulfation and phosphorylation. GPR82 is a glycoprotein with 2 glycosylation sites, which on a GPCR are typically on the small extracellular N-terminus or loops, the same surface a secreted ligand would contact. PubMed PTM search: 157 hits for FN1 (top hits not PTM-specific), 0 for GPR82. Whether any glycosite sits on the modeled interface is unknown; this is an unresolved caveat, not a demonstrated artifact.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence count is 0 for FN1 and GPR82.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction (GPR82 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. UniProt lists GPR82 as an orphan receptor. The pair is novel.
Other subunits
ITGA5;ITGB1
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Inspect the AF3 model to confirm the interface is on GPR82's extracellular N-terminus or loops, not its cytoplasmic loops or tail (AF3 models no bilayer), and identify which FN1 domain is involved. 2) Check whether GPR82's 2 N-glycosites or FN1's 8 glycosites fall on the interface; if so, re-fold with glycans attached. 3) Re-fold with only the contacting FN1 domain(s) to see whether ipTM holds outside the 2813-token complex (pTM is 0.37). 4) Counter-screen the same FN1 fragment against unrelated GPCRs to rule out nonspecific stickiness. 5) Wet-lab: test FN1 fragment binding to GPR82-expressing cells and a GPCR signalling readout. The canonical FN1 receptor is integrin ITGA5:ITGB1 (from UniProt function text), which would be a useful positive-control comparison.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Include integrin-blocking arm (anti-α5β1 / RGD or ATN-161) and a plasma-FN vs. cellular-FN comparison; optional PNGase F / deglycosylated FN arm)
Why this method
FN1 is a secreted plasma/ECM protein and GPR82 is an orphan cell-surface GPCR, so the pair is a ligand–receptor (paracrine/endocrine) hypothesis, best tested functionally. The assay checks whether FN1 produces a GPR82-dependent signal, which co-localization could not show for an orphan GPCR. Integrins ITGA5/ITGB1 are listed as other subunits, so the integrin contribution must be separated from GPR82's.
Target tissue(s)
liver, lymphoid tissue, intestine
Why these tissues (HPA)
FN1 is made mainly in liver (nTPM about 1614) and secreted to blood, and blood vessel and placenta are also very high (about 2700 nTPM each). GPR82 is low-level and enriched in lymphoid tissue (6.5 nTPM) and intestine (2.5 nTPM). Within liver, Kupffer cells express GPR82 (65.1 nCPM) and sit next to FN1-secreting hepatocytes and sinusoidal endothelium, so liver is the one tissue where both proteins are plausibly present. Lymphoid tissue and intestine are the GPR82-bearing immune settings.
Cell type(s)
Kupffer cells, Hepatocytes, Liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, Lymphoid/myeloid immune cells
Protocol notes
1) Build the cell system: HEK293 or CHO cells stably expressing tagged GPR82 (HA-GPR82), with empty-vector and a related Gi-coupled GPCR as controls. Also use a macrophage line or primary Kupffer cells / monocyte-derived macrophages with GPR82 CRISPR knockout or siRNA knockdown. Check that the cells lack or have low endogenous α5β1, or block it. 2) Stimulate with recombinant human plasma FN (and an RGD-containing FN fragment vs. a fragment lacking RGD), in dose response (1–100 µg/mL) and over time. Read out Gi coupling by forskolin-induced cAMP (GloSensor/HTRF), β-arrestin recruitment (NanoBiT/PathHunter), pERK1/2 and Ca2+ flux with Gα16/Gqi5 co-expression. 3) Test direct binding with a cell-surface binding assay: biotin/Fc-tagged FN on GPR82-expressing vs. parental cells by flow cytometry. Then follow up with co-IP of GPR82 with FN, ± ITGA5/ITGB1, to see whether the integrin is a bridge or co-receptor. 4) Run a co-culture, with FN1-secreting hepatocytes (HepG2/primary) overlaid on GPR82+ Kupffer-like cells, ± FN1 siRNA.
Controls
Positive: a known GPR82 or Gi-coupled agonist/receptor pair in the same readout (e.g. forskolin/cAMP assay validation), and FN-induced integrin signalling (pFAK/pERK) in α5β1+ cells. Negative: parental/empty-vector cells, GPR82 KO/knockdown cells, a heat-denatured or BSA/other-ECM protein control (e.g. laminin), an RGD-mutant FN or integrin-blocking antibody to isolate the GPR82 contribution, and a non-related GPCR-expressing line.
Caveats
Confidence is low: ipTM 0.62, pTM 0.37, interface pLDDT 62.2. No tool was available to check which side of the membrane the interface sits on, so the interface may not be extracellular. FN1 is a sticky hub with 115 partners and may bind nonspecifically, and both proteins are glycoproteins, so the bare-sequence AF3 interface may differ from the glycosylated native one. FN1 also acts through ITGA5/ITGB1, so any signal must be shown to persist when integrins are blocked or absent. GPR82 is an orphan with poor signalling annotation and low RNA expression (≤6.5 nTPM in tissue, no protein data), so antibodies and endogenous signals may be weak. The HPA tags FN1 as both "predicted intracellular" and "secreted", and its protein intensity is only reported in blood vessel. Recombinant FN may differ from plasma FN in conformation and glycosylation.

GRIK1 ↔ GPR12 LIKELY_SUBCOMPLEX low confidence ipTM 0.61 · pTM 0.47
Rationale
I am keeping the verdict, and I could not re-read UniProt here to check the flagged text. (1) Glycan-binding flag: as I recall the annotation, GPR12 is an orphan class A GPCR that signals constitutively through Gs and cAMP. Its reported ligands (S1P, sphingosylphosphorylcholine) are lipids, and I know of no beta-galactoside or sialic-acid binding annotation. The flag looks like a keyword match, for example on glycosylation sites, and not on a real lectin mechanism. So I don't treat the interaction as glycan-mediated, and I don't move to LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM. Because the flag came from a code check I can't inspect, I'm not raising confidence above low. The ordinary caveat still applies: AF3 does not model glycans, GRIK1 has 9 glycosylation sites and GPR12 has 2, and the fold was not run, so interface overlap with those sites is unchecked. (2) The other facts do not support a stronger call. There is no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed support (known_interaction_strength=none), so the pair is novel. HPA plausibility is unknown, which gives no evidence for or against co-localization. Both proteins are membrane proteins in brain and retina. GRIK1 normally assembles as a tetramer (with GRIK4 or GRIK5) and was modeled alone, so a real contact could involve a different subunit arrangement.
PTM / glycosylation
GRIK1 has 9 glycosylation sites, mostly extracellular. GPR12 has 2 glycosylation sites and 1 palmitoylation site. The glycan-binding flag on GPR12 conflicts with my knowledge of it as a lipid-responsive orphan GPCR, so I read it as a probable mis-flag. AF3 does not model glycans, and site-level overlap with the interface is unchecked because the fold was not run.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence returned 0 hits for GRIK1 and GPR12.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association. CellPhoneDB: no interaction (GPR12 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 papers. The pair is novel (known_interaction_strength=none).
Other subunits
GRIK4;GRIK5
Follow-up (not yet executed): Re-read the GPR12 UniProt FUNCTION text to confirm the glycan-binding flag. Re-run AF3 with a GRIK1 tetramer (plus GRIK4 or GRIK5) and GPR12. Check whether any glycosylation sites sit at the predicted interface.
