ITGAD ↔ P2RY10 LIKELY_SUBCOMPLEX low confidence ipTM 0.61 · pTM 0.47
Rationale
ITGAD is an obligate alpha subunit of the integrin aD/b2 heterodimer (CellPhoneDB: integrin_aDb2_complex with ITGB2), and ITGB2 is absent from the model, so the large modeled surface (BSA 3982 A2) may include the face ITGB2 normally occupies. Both are plasma-membrane proteins co-enriched in lymphoid tissue and T/NK/innate lymphoid cells, so a cis interaction is physically possible, and there is no prior report (STRING none, CellPhoneDB none, PubMed 0). The fold itself is weak support: ipTM 0.61 with interface pLDDT only 58.5, a 1.55 A minimum separation suggesting clashes, and both proteins glycosylated (9 and 3 UniProt sites) with no check of whether those sites sit on the interface.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists ITGAD as a glycoprotein with 9 glycosylation sites and P2RY10 as a glycoprotein with 3. The PubMed PTM search returned nothing relevant (1 unrelated hit for ITGAD, 0 for P2RY10). If the interface involves the ITGAD ectodomain or the P2RY10 N-terminus/extracellular loops, unmodeled glycans could occlude it; site positions relative to the interface were not checked.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence count is 0 for ITGAD and P2RY10.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no curated interaction (P2RY10 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is unreported.
Other subunits
ITGB2
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run here. Re-fold ITGAD + ITGB2 + P2RY10 and see whether the P2RY10 interface survives with the beta-2 subunit present or sits on the alpha/beta face. Inspect the interface topology for any contact mixing extracellular and cytoplasmic residues, and check whether the N-glycosylation sites of either protein land on the interface. Resolve the 1.55 A clash signal by relaxing the model. If the interface survives, test by co-IP or proximity ligation in T/NK cells.

ITGB7 ↔ P2RY8 LIKELY_SUBCOMPLEX low confidence ipTM 0.61 · pTM 0.6
Rationale
ITGB7 is an obligate integrin heterodimer subunit (CellPhoneDB: a4b7 with ITGA4, aEb7 with ITGAE) and was modelled without its alpha chain, so the large modelled interface (BSA 2138 Å2, ipTM 0.61, interface pLDDT 69) may sit on the surface normally occupied by the alpha subunit or involve a pairing of the lone beta TM helix with the GPCR bundle. The pair is novel (no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed hit) and biologically plausible: both are plasma-membrane proteins enriched in lymphoid tissue. Both are glycoproteins (ITGB7 8 sites, P2RY8 2 sites), which is an untested additional caveat; no fold was run to check either concern.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists ITGB7 as a glycoprotein with 8 glycosylation sites (ectodomain) and 27 disulfide bonds, and P2RY8 as a glycoprotein with 2 glycosylation sites (likely N-terminus or extracellular loops). The PubMed PTM searches returned nothing specific to glycosylation of either protein. If the modelled interface is extracellular, glycans could occlude it; whether any site lies on the interface was not checked.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence count is 0 for ITGB7 and P2RY8.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no curated interaction (P2RY8 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is novel in the literature.
Other subunits
ITGA4;ITGAE
Follow-up (not yet executed): Re-fold ITGB7 + P2RY8 with one alpha subunit (ITGA4 as the representative; ITGA4 and ITGAE are mutually exclusive) and see whether the P2RY8 interface survives or is displaced by the alpha chain. Inspect the interface topology (TM–TM vs ectodomain vs cytoplasmic tail) and whether any of the ITGB7 or P2RY8 N-glycosylation sites lie on it. If it survives, test by co-IP or proximity ligation in B or T cells, and check whether GGG–P2RY8 signalling modulates a4b7 adhesion to MADCAM1.

SEMA4C ↔ GPR37 IMPLAUSIBLE low confidence ipTM 0.6 · pTM 0.61
Rationale
The flagged contradiction holds up. HPA shows no shared protein-level tissue for SEMA4C and GPR37, and neither protein is secreted, so a direct contact would need both to sit in the same place. My original argument for a cis or trans ectodomain contact rested on a general brain-relevance claim and on UniProt membrane annotations. Neither is concrete co-localization data. SEMA4C's low tissue specificity does not show it is present where GPR37 is, in oligodendrocytes. The pair has no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed support, and each protein already has its own known partners (PLXNB2 for SEMA4C; prosaposin, osteocalcin and neuroprotectin D1 for GPR37). No real fold was analysed (fold_evidence_status=not_run). The moderate ipTM of about 0.6 therefore can't offset the lack of co-expression, and both ectodomains are N-glycosylated, which AF3 does not model. I'm lowering the verdict from CONFIRMED_NOVEL to IMPLAUSIBLE with low confidence. Brain RNA-level overlap or a cell-type-specific contact could still exist, but the data I have don't show one.
PTM / glycosylation
SEMA4C has 6 and GPR37 has 3 UniProt N-glycosylation sites on the extracellular side. AF3 does not model these glycans, and no site-to-interface check was done. This is a secondary caveat that adds to the doubt about the modeled contact.
PubMed co-occurrence
pubmed_cooccurrence returned 0 papers mentioning SEMA4C and GPR37 together.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. known_interaction_strength=none, so the pair is not already known, but the absence of prior evidence also gives no support for a real interaction.
Other subunits
PLXNB2
Follow-up (not yet executed): Look for single-cell or RNA-level evidence that SEMA4C and GPR37 are co-expressed in the same brain cell type, such as oligodendrocyte lineage cells. Only if co-expression is shown, run a real AF3 fold, check glycan sites against the interface, and consider PLXNB2 as an additional subunit.

TREM2 ↔ GPR82 LIKELY_SUBCOMPLEX low confidence ipTM 0.59 · pTM 0.6
Rationale
No prior record of this pair (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB not found, PubMed 0 hits), and both are cell-membrane proteins of tissue-resident macrophages, so the pairing is physically plausible and novel. But CellPhoneDB and UniProt show TREM2 works as an obligate signalling complex with TYROBP (DAP12), which is absent from the model, and the AF3 support is only moderate (ipTM 0.59, interface pLDDT 66, partner pLDDT 59). Both proteins are also glycoproteins with 2 annotated glycosylation sites each, and I could not check whether those sites fall on the modeled interface.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: TREM2 is a glycoprotein with 2 glycosylation sites in its extracellular Ig domain, and it binds lipids and lipoproteins. GPR82 is a glycoprotein with 2 glycosylation sites, presumably extracellular. The TREM2 PubMed search returned 223 hits, including N-glycosylation literature in Alzheimer's disease; the GPR82 search returned 0. Whether any glycosylation site lies on the modeled interface is unknown, so this is a caveat rather than grounds for an artifact call.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-mention count is 0 for TREM2 and GPR82.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no curated interaction, and GPR82 is not in its gene table. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 papers. The pair is novel as far as these sources show.
Other subunits
TYROBP
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run for this triage. Next steps: (1) re-fold TREM2 + TYROBP + GPR82 and see whether the TREM2-GPR82 interface confidence holds once TYROBP occupies the TREM2 transmembrane helix; (2) inspect the interface topology to confirm it does not mix cytoplasmic and extracellular residues, since the large buried area (3476 Å2) on a 566-token complex suggests transmembrane-helix packing, which AF3 can over-predict without a bilayer; (3) check whether the TREM2 and GPR82 N-glycosylation sites sit on the interface, and re-fold with glycans if they do; (4) confirm co-expression in the same macrophage population from single-cell data. CORUM was not available, so a wider complex check is still needed.

  "function": "Forms a receptor signaling complex with TYROBP which mediates signaling and cell activation following ligand binding (PubMed:10799849). Acts as a receptor for amyloid-beta protein 42, a cleavage product of the amyloid-beta precursor protein APP, and mediates its uptake and degradation by microglia (PubMed:27477018, PubMed:29518356). Binding to amyloid-beta 42 mediates microglial activation, proliferation, migration, apoptosis and expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL6R and CCL3, and the anti-inflammatory cytokine ARG1 (By similarity). Acts as a receptor for lipoprotein particles such as LDL, VLDL, and HDL and for apolipoproteins such as APOA1, APOA2, APOB, APOE, APOE2, APOE3, APOE4, and CLU and enhances their uptake in microglia (PubMed:27477018). Binds phospholipids (preferably anionic lipids) such as phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylglycerol and sphingomyelin (PubMed:29794134). Regulates microglial proliferation by acting as an upstream regulator of the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling cascade (By similarity). Required for microglial phagocytosis of apoptotic neurons (PubMed:24990881). Also required for microglial activation and phagocytosis of myelin debris after neuronal injury and of neuronal synapses during synapse elimination in the developing brain (By similarity). Regulates microglial chemotaxis and process outgrowth, and also the microglial response to oxidative stress and lipopolysaccharide (By similarity). It suppresses PI3K and NF-kappa-B signaling in response to lipopolysaccharide; thus promoting phagocytosis, suppressing pro-inflammatory cytokine and nitric oxide production, inhibiting apoptosis and increasing expression of IL10 and TGFB (By similarity). Regulates age-related changes in microglial numbers (PubMed:29752066). Triggers activation of the immune responses in macrophages and dendritic cells (PubMed:10799849). Mediates cytokine-induced formation of multinucleated giant cells which are formed by the fusion of macrophages (By similarity). In dendritic cells, receptor of SEMA6D with PLEXNA1 as coreceptor and mediates up-regulation of chemokine receptor CCR7 and dendritic cell maturation and survival (PubMed:11602640). CEACAM1 ↔ MRGPRX3 LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM low confidence ipTM 0.59 · pTM 0.56
Rationale
No prior evidence links this pair (STRING and CellPhoneDB not found, 0 PubMed co-mentions), so it is novel, and both are plasma-membrane proteins per UniProt. However, CEACAM1's ectodomain carries 20 annotated N-glycosylation sites that AF3's bare-sequence model omits, and the modeled interface is very large (BSA 3024 Å2, 524 contacts) for a small orphan GPCR, at only moderate confidence (ipTM 0.59, interface pLDDT 69.4). Whether glycans actually sit on the modeled interface was not checked, and expression overlap is weak, so this is a caveat-driven call rather than a demonstrated artifact.
PTM / glycosylation
CEACAM1: UniProt keyword Glycoprotein with 20 Glycosylation features, plus Phosphoprotein; PubMed returns 112 PTM/glycosylation hits, including a paper on N-glycan conformations at the surface of the CEACAM1 Ig1 domain. This is plausibly relevant because any contact with a GPCR's extracellular face would use the glycosylated Ig ectodomain. MRGPRX3: no Glycosylation or Lipidation features in UniProt and 0 PubMed PTM hits. Whether specific glycan sites lie on the modeled interface was not determined.
PubMed co-occurrence
pubmed_cooccurrence returned 0 papers mentioning CEACAM1 and MRGPRX3 together.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: not found (MRGPRX3 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. Nothing indicates this pair is already known.
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run for this triage (the fold tool was not available in this session). Next steps: (1) map the modeled interface residues against CEACAM1's 20 N-glycosylation sites and against UniProt topology for both proteins, to rule out an interface that mixes cytoplasmic and extracellular residues or sits on the lipid-facing TM surface of MRGPRX3; (2) re-fold with core N-glycans attached at the CEACAM1 sites to see whether the interface survives; (3) check co-expression in the relevant cell types (e.g. DRG sensory neurons for MRGPRX3 versus epithelial or neutrophil CEACAM1) before any wet-lab binding assay. CellPhoneDB does not cover MRGPRX3 and CORUM was not available, so the absence of complex partners is not conclusive.

  "function": "Cell adhesion protein that mediates homophilic cell adhesion in a calcium-independent manner (By similarity). Plays a role as coinhibitory receptor in immune response, insulin action and also functions as an activator during angiogenesis (PubMed:18424730, PubMed:23696226, PubMed:25363763). Its coinhibitory receptor function is phosphorylation- and PTPN6 -dependent, which in turn, suppress signal transduction of associated receptors by dephosphorylation of their downstream effectors. Plays a role in immune response, of T cells, natural killer (NK) and neutrophils (PubMed:18424730, PubMed:23696226). Upon TCR/CD3 complex stimulation, inhibits TCR-mediated cytotoxicity by blocking granule exocytosis by mediating homophilic binding to adjacent cells, allowing interaction with and phosphorylation by LCK and interaction with the TCR/CD3 complex which recruits PTPN6 resulting in dephosphorylation of CD247 and ZAP70 (PubMed:18424730). Also inhibits T cell proliferation and cytokine production through inhibition of JNK cascade and plays a crucial role in regulating autoimmunity and anti-tumor immunity by inhibiting T cell through its interaction with HAVCR2 (PubMed:25363763). Upon natural killer (NK) cells activation, inhibit KLRK1-mediated cytolysis of CEACAM1-bearing tumor cells by trans-homophilic interactions with CEACAM1 on the target cell and lead to cis-interaction between CEACAM1 and KLRK1, allowing PTPN6 recruitment and then VAV1 dephosphorylation (PubMed:23696226). Upon neutrophils activation negatively regulates IL1B production by recruiting PTPN6 to a SYK-TLR4-CEACAM1 complex, that dephosphorylates SYK, reducing the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and lysosome disruption, which in turn, reduces the activity of the inflammasome. Down-regulates neutrophil production by acting as a coinhibitory receptor for CSF3R by down-regulating the CSF3R-STAT3 pathway through recruitment of PTPN6 that dephosphorylates CSF3R (By similarity). Also regulates insulin action by promoting INS clearance and regulating lipogenesis in liver through regulating insulin signaling (By similarity). Upon INS stimulation, undergoes phosphorylation by INSR leading to INS clearance by increasing receptor-mediated insulin endocytosis. This inernalization promotes interaction with FASN leading to receptor-mediated insulin degradation and to reduction of FASN activity leading to negative regulation of fatty acid synthesis. INSR-mediated phosphorylation also provokes a down-regulation of cell proliferation through SHC1 interaction resulting in decrease coupling of SHC1 to the MAPK3/ERK1-MAPK1/ERK2 and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase pathways (By similarity). Functions as activator in angiogenesis by promoting blood vessel remodeling through endothelial cell differentiation and migration and in arteriogenesis by increasing the number of collateral arteries and collateral vessel calibers after ischemia. Also regulates vascular permeability through the VEGFR2 signaling pathway resulting in control of nitric oxide production (By similarity). Down-regulates cell growth in response to EGF through its interaction with SHC1 that mediates interaction with EGFR resulting in decrease coupling of SHC1 to the MAPK3/ERK1-MAPK1/ERK2 pathway (By similarity). Negatively regulates platelet aggregation by decreasing platelet adhesion on type I collagen through the GPVI-FcRgamma complex (By similarity). Inhibits cell migration and cell scattering through interaction with FLNA; interferes with the interaction of FLNA with RALA (PubMed:16291724). Mediates bile acid transport activity in a phosphorylation dependent manner (By similarity). Negatively regulates osteoclastogenesis (By similarity) Cell adhesion protein that mediates homophilic cell adhesion in a calcium-independent manner (By similarity). Promotes populations of T cells regulating IgA production and secretion associated with control of the commensal microbiota and resistance to enteropathogens (By similarity)",

IL2 ↔ GPR171 CONFIRMED_NOVEL VALIDATE low confidence ipTM 0.58 · pTM 0.7
Rationale
IL2 is a secreted cytokine and GPR171 is a plasma-membrane GPCR enriched in T cells, so the pair is topologically plausible as an extracellular ligand-receptor contact, and STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed (0 hits) all show no prior report. Confidence is low because the AF3 ipTM is only modest (0.58), IL2 has a well-defined canonical receptor (IL2RA/IL2RB/IL2RG), GPR171's documented ligand is the 16-aa peptide BigLEN rather than a folded cytokine, and each protein carries one glycosylation site whose position relative to the interface I could not check.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt marks both as glycoproteins with one annotated glycosylation site each. From general knowledge rather than tool output, IL2's site is an N-terminal O-glycan not known to be needed for receptor binding, and GPR171's is probably in an extracellular region and could lie near a modeled ligand contact; neither position was checked against the interface. The PubMed PTM search for IL2 returned 2489 non-specific hits and for GPR171 returned 0. This is a caveat, not enough for LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM.
PubMed co-occurrence
pubmed_cooccurrence returned 0 papers mentioning IL2 and GPR171 together.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no curated interaction (GPR171 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. No evidence anywhere that this pair is already known.
Other subunits
IL2RA;IL2RB;IL2RG
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run for this triage. Next steps: (1) inspect the AF3 model to confirm the interface lies only on GPR171's extracellular face/TM-bundle opening and not on cytoplasmic loops; (2) check whether the GPR171 N-glycosylation site and IL2's O-glycosylated N-terminus sit on the interface, and re-fold with the glycan if so; (3) check whether the IL2 surface used overlaps the IL2RA/IL2RB/IL2RG epitopes (the listed other_subunits are IL2's canonical receptor, a competing complex rather than missing subunits); (4) counter-screen by folding IL2 against unrelated class A GPCRs, and BigLEN against GPR171, to test specificity; (5) wet-lab: IL2 binding and Gi signalling (cAMP) in GPR171-expressing cells lacking IL2R.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay
Why this method
IL2 is a secreted cytokine and GPR171 is a Gi/o-coupled plasma-membrane GPCR, so a paracrine ligand-receptor test with a functional readout fits better than co-localization. Because T cells co-express the canonical IL2R, the assay must separate IL2R-driven signalling from any GPR171-specific effect.
Target tissue(s)
lymphoid tissue, lymph node, tonsil, spleen
Why these tissues (HPA)
GPR171 RNA is enriched in lymphoid tissue (20.1 nTPM). At the single-cell level it is highest in T-cells (143.7 nCPM), NK-cells (43.7) and innate lymphoid cells (33.6). IL2 is made by T-cells (17.4 nCPM) and ILCs (12.1), so ligand-producing and receptor-bearing cells overlap in lymphoid tissue. Only lymphoid tissue appears in the HPA data given. Lymph node, tonsil and spleen are my own suggestions of other lymphoid organs and are not supported by the numbers provided.
Cell type(s)
T-cells, NK-cells, Innate lymphoid cells
Protocol notes
1) Build a clean receptor system. Use HEK293 or CHO cells stably expressing GPR171, with empty-vector cells as the negative control. Read out Gi/o signalling by cAMP (forskolin-stimulated cAMP decrease, GloSensor or HTRF), by β-arrestin recruitment (PathHunter or NanoBiT), or by pERK. Dose IL2 from 0.1 nM to 1 µM. Include BigLEN (the known GPR171 agonist) as the positive control. Also test whether IL2 competes with BigLEN binding or signalling. 2) Test primary human T cells and NK cells. Use GPR171 knockdown or CRISPR knockout and an IL2R-blocking antibody (anti-CD25, or anti-CD122 plus anti-CD132). Measure cAMP and pERK, and also pSTAT5 as the canonical IL2R readout. A GPR171-dependent response that persists with IL2R blocked would support a real interaction. 3) Add a direct binding check. Use SPR or BLI with recombinant IL2 and the purified GPR171 extracellular region, or flow cytometry for biotin-IL2 binding on GPR171-overexpressing cells that lack IL2R.
Controls
Positive: BigLEN peptide on GPR171 cells, and IL2 on IL2R-positive T cells (pSTAT5). Negative: parental or empty-vector cells, GPR171 knockout cells, heat-denatured IL2, an irrelevant cytokine (IL15 or IL4), and a GPR171 antagonist or pertussis toxin to confirm Gi/o dependence. Add an IL2R-blocking condition to isolate GPR171-specific signalling.
Caveats
Confidence is low: AF3 ipTM is only 0.58. IL2 has a well-defined canonical receptor (IL2RA/IL2RB/IL2RG), so any T-cell signal can be confounded by IL2R, and IL2R-negative systems are needed. GPR171's known ligand is the 16-aa peptide BigLEN, and a folded cytokine may not engage the orthosteric pocket. Each protein has one glycosylation site, and I could not check where it sits relative to the interface. A glycan could block or alter the contact, so this is partly a PTM-artifact concern. Recombinant IL2 made in E. coli lacks the O-glycan, so compare it with a glycosylated, mammalian-expressed IL2. GPR171 is annotated in HPA with vesicular as well as plasma-membrane localization, so surface expression should be confirmed. RNA levels in lymphoid tissue are modest, and no protein-level tissue data are available.

VCAM1 ↔ GPR171 CONFIRMED_NOVEL VALIDATE low confidence ipTM 0.58 · pTM 0.48
Rationale
No prior record of this pair (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB not found, 0 PubMed co-mentions), and the biology is compatible: both are lymphoid-tissue elevated, VCAM1 is a surface/shed adhesion glycoprotein and GPR171 is a plasma-membrane GPCR on T/NK cells, so a trans or soluble-VCAM1 extracellular contact is physically possible. Support is weak, though: ipTM 0.58 is only just above threshold, interface pLDDT is 69, min separation of 1.15 Å suggests clashes in the pose, VCAM1 carries 6 N-glycosylation sites that were not checked against the interface, and GPR171's documented ligand is a short neuropeptide (Big LEN) rather than an Ig-domain protein. No fold was run and the modeled interface side (extracellular vs cytoplasmic) is unverified.
PTM / glycosylation
VCAM1: UniProt Glycoprotein keyword with 6 annotated glycosylation sites on the extracellular Ig domains; the PubMed PTM search returned 947 hits but the top titles are generic VCAM1-as-inflammation-marker papers, not PTM studies. GPR171: UniProt Glycoprotein with 1 glycosylation site; 0 PubMed PTM hits. VCAM1's documented binding mechanism (integrins) is protein-protein, not glycan-mediated, so this is not a mechanism-level artifact, but a glycan on the modeled interface (BSA ~2090 Å2) cannot be excluded without per-residue data.
PubMed co-occurrence
0 PubMed papers mention VCAM1 and GPR171 together.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no match (GPR171 is not in the CellPhoneDB gene table, so this miss is uninformative for that side). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. No prior evidence anywhere for this pair.
Other subunits
ITGA4;ITGB1
Follow-up (not yet executed): Not done here: (1) inspect the structure to confirm the interface is between VCAM1's extracellular Ig domains and GPR171's extracellular loops/N-terminus, not a cytoplasmic/extracellular mix; (2) check whether any of VCAM1's 6 N-glycosylation sites or GPR171's single site sit on the interface, and re-fold with glycans if so; (3) check the 1.15 Å minimum separation for clashes; (4) counter-fold VCAM1 against a few unrelated class A GPCRs to test specificity. The other_subunits entry (ITGA4/ITGB1) is VCAM1's canonical integrin counter-receptor from its UniProt function text and general knowledge, not from CellPhoneDB, which returned no complexes; it is useful as a competition/positive control. Wet-lab: soluble VCAM1-Fc binding to GPR171-expressing T cells or transfectants.
Validation strategy: PLA (co-localization) (Run +/- PNGase F/neuraminidase pre-treatment, and +/- natalizumab or an anti-VCAM1 domain 1 blocking antibody, to test glycan dependence and whether the signal comes from the integrin-binding face.)
Why this method
Both proteins are surface-exposed on lymphoid-lineage cells. The question is physical proximity (trans, cell-cell, or cis), and no ligand-receptor signalling relationship is established. A GPCR with a non-Ig-domain ligand makes a stimulation readout hard to choose before binding is shown. PLA gives in situ evidence of proximity at about 40 nm on intact cells.
Target tissue(s)
Lymph node, Spleen, Tonsil, Bone marrow
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA lists both proteins as lymphoid-tissue elevated (VCAM1 RNA 366.8 nTPM; GPR171 20.1 nTPM). VCAM1 protein intensity is highest in bone marrow. GPR171 is expressed in T cells (143.7 nCPM) and NK cells (43.7 nCPM), which are close to VCAM1-high stromal cells in lymphoid organs and marrow.
Cell type(s)
T-cells, NK-cells, Bone marrow MSCs, Kupffer cells
Protocol notes
1) Test in two settings: (a) FFPE or frozen lymph node, tonsil and bone marrow sections; (b) co-culture of VCAM1-high stromal cells (TNFα-activated HUVEC, or MSCs) with GPR171+ T cells (primary CD3+ or Jurkat) and NK cells. Use mouse anti-VCAM1 (extracellular domain) with rabbit anti-GPR171 (extracellular N-terminus or ECL epitope), in non-permeabilised, lightly PFA-fixed cells so that only surface pairs are scored. 2) Check GPR171 antibody specificity by GPR171 siRNA/CRISPR knockout, since GPCR antibodies are often unreliable. Also test a soluble VCAM1 (sVCAM1) pull-down on GPR171-expressing cells. 3) Quantify PLA dots per cell by confocal microscopy. Compare cells with and without TNFα activation, and with and without anti-VCAM1 domain 1 blocking antibody. 4) If PLA is positive, confirm by co-IP from GPR171-HA/VCAM1-Fc transfected HEK293 cells, or by surface plasmon resonance or bio-layer interferometry between recombinant VCAM1 ectodomain and purified GPR171.
Controls
Positive: VCAM1-ITGA4/ITGB1 (VLA-4) PLA on the same T cells, which is a known interaction. Negative: single-antibody PLA, isotype-matched IgG, GPR171-knockout or VCAM1-knockdown cells, and an unrelated abundant T-cell surface protein such as CD3 or CD45 paired with VCAM1 to measure random proximity. Also include a GPR171 and Big LEN peptide competition arm to see whether the orthosteric site is involved.
Caveats
Confidence is low: ipTM is 0.58, interface pLDDT is 69, and the 1.15 Å minimum separation suggests clashes. The modeled interface side (extracellular vs cytoplasmic) is unverified. VCAM1 has 6 N-glycosylation sites that were not checked against the interface, so glycans could block the contact; the glycosidase arm addresses this. GPR171's known ligand is the Big LEN neuropeptide, not an Ig-domain protein. VCAM1 is expressed mainly on stroma, endothelium and macrophages and GPR171 on lymphocytes, so any interaction would be trans (cell-cell) or via soluble VCAM1, and PLA distance is about 40 nm, so it may pick up crowded VLA-4/VCAM1 clusters rather than a direct interaction. The HPA subcellular annotation for VCAM1 is cell junctions, and GPR171 is partly vesicular, which could reduce surface overlap. The ITGA4/ITGB1 partners may compete with or mediate the signal.

IL12RB1 ↔ GPR174 CONFIRMED_NOVEL VALIDATE low confidence ipTM 0.58 · pTM 0.5
Rationale
Both proteins are plasma-membrane receptors enriched in lymphoid tissue (GPR174 in T and NK cells), so a cis interaction on the same cell is physically plausible. STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed all return nothing for the pair, so it is novel. Confidence is low because the ipTM of 0.58 is only moderate, both are glycoproteins whose sites I could not place relative to the interface, and IL12RB1 normally works with IL12RB2 or IL23R, which were not in the model.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists both as glycoproteins: IL12RB1 has 6 annotated glycosylation sites and GPR174 has 2. Whether any of these sites falls on the modeled interface is unknown. The PubMed PTM searches (18 hits for IL12RB1, 2 for GPR174) returned nothing specific to glycosylation of an interface. Neither protein's function text describes a glycan-mediated binding mechanism, so this is an unresolved caveat and not grounds for an artifact call.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence returned 0 hits for IL12RB1 and GPR174.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no curated interaction, and GPR174 is not in its gene table. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 papers. No prior report of this pair anywhere.
Other subunits
IL12RB2;IL23R
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Inspect the AF3 model to see whether the interface is transmembrane-helix packing, ectodomain contact, or mixes cytoplasmic and extracellular residues (the last would be a physical impossibility). 2) Map the 6 IL12RB1 and 2 GPR174 N-glycosylation sites onto the interface, and re-fold with glycans if any land on it. 3) Re-fold with one of IL12RB2 or IL23R (they are alternative partners, so not both) to see whether the GPR174 interface survives in the native receptor complex. 4) Test experimentally by co-immunoprecipitation or proximity assay (BRET or PLA) in primary T or NK cells.
Validation strategy: PLA (co-localization)
Why this method
Both proteins are plasma-membrane receptors that HPA places in lymphoid tissue, and GPR174 is enriched in T and NK cells. The prediction is a cis interaction on the same cell, so in situ proximity detection (<40 nm) fits better than a stimulation assay, because neither protein is a secreted ligand. PLA also avoids detergent solubilisation of a GPCR and a cytokine receptor, which co-IP would require.
Target tissue(s)
Lymphoid tissue (lymph node), Tonsil, Spleen, Thymus
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA lists lymphoid tissue as the tissue-specific RNA site for both proteins (IL12RB1 22.7 nTPM, GPR174 15.7 nTPM), so this is the one tissue where both are clearly expressed. HPA single-cell data show GPR174 highest in T-cells (105 nCPM) and NK-cells (76 nCPM), with thymocytes at 38. These are also the cells where IL12RB1 is expected to be functionally relevant. I chose lymph node, tonsil, spleen and thymus as lymphoid tissue sources; this is my inference, since the HPA data provided give only the "lymphoid tissue" grouping.
Cell type(s)
T-cells (CD4+ and CD8+), NK-cells, Thymocytes, Innate lymphoid cells
Protocol notes
1) Use primary human T and NK cells, ideally after IL-2 or anti-CD3/CD28 activation to induce IL12RB1. Add a Jurkat or NK-92 line as a secondary system. Fix gently with 2–4% PFA without permeabilisation, so that only surface epitopes are detected. Also test FFPE tonsil or lymph node sections. 2) Run Duolink PLA with a mouse anti-IL12RB1 and a rabbit anti-GPR174 that target extracellular regions. Validate each antibody first by IF/flow on overexpressing versus knockout or knockdown cells. Co-stain CD3 or CD56 and a membrane marker to assign the PLA puncta to cell type and to the plasma membrane. Quantify puncta per cell by confocal imaging. 3) Run a parallel PLA with IL12RB1 against IL12RB2 or IL23R. Also test whether IL-12 or IL-23 stimulation (15–30 min) changes the IL12RB1–GPR174 PLA signal, to see whether the interaction depends on the receptor complex. Add a GPR174 ligand (lysophosphatidylserine) condition to test whether ligand engagement modulates proximity. 4) Confirm orthogonally with HEK293 co-transfection and co-IP, then a functional readout such as pSTAT4 by flow with and without GPR174 knockout.
Controls
Positive: IL12RB1–IL12RB2 or IL12RB1–IL23R PLA, or a known abundant same-cell surface pair such as CD3–TCR. Negative: single-antibody and no-primary-antibody PLA controls. Also use GPR174 CRISPR-knockout or siRNA-knockdown T cells, IL12RB1-knockout cells, and an irrelevant membrane receptor not expected to interact with IL12RB1 (for example CD45 or a different GPCR). Include an isotype-matched IgG PLA pair. For the expression-dependence control, use a cell line lacking both proteins, then transfect each protein alone and together.
Caveats
AF3 ipTM is only 0.58, so the model is low confidence. Both proteins are glycoproteins and I could not place the glycosylation sites relative to the predicted interface, so a glycan may block or gate the contact in cells. This pair is not flagged LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM, but a glycosidase arm (PNGase F) is a reasonable follow-up if the first PLA is negative. IL12RB1 normally acts with IL12RB2 or IL23R, which were not in the model, so the real interaction may need those subunits or be competed by them. PLA shows proximity only (<40 nm), not direct binding, and crowded T-cell membranes can give false positives. HPA provides no protein-level data for either gene here, only RNA, so antibody availability and protein expression must be checked. Surface expression of IL12RB1 on resting T cells is low.

CFC1 ↔ GPR33 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE medium confidence ipTM 0.58 · pTM 0.62
Rationale
No database or literature trace of this pair (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB no match, PubMed 0), and the topology is plausible in principle (secreted/GPI-anchored CFC1 with a plasma-membrane GPCR). But HPA reports GPR33 RNA as "Not detected" in every tissue and cell type and has no subcellular data for either protein, so there is no expression context to support the interaction. The fold is also borderline (ipTM 0.58, partner pLDDT 42.1), and both proteins carry glycosylation that AF3 did not model.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: CFC1 is a glycoprotein with 1 glycosylation site and 1 lipidation (GPI anchor) site; GPR33 is a glycoprotein with 4 glycosylation sites. The PubMed PTM search returned nothing specific (CFC1: 4 hits, none about glycosylation of CFC1 itself; GPR33: 0). Whether any of these sites sits on the modeled interface was not checked, so a glycan clash on GPR33's extracellular face is an open caveat.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-mention count is 0.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no curated interaction; GPR33 is not in its gene table. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is novel as far as these sources go.
Other subunits
NODAL;ACVR1B;ACVR2B
Follow-up (not yet executed): First confirm that GPR33 is expressed as an intact receptor in a relevant human cell type; my recollection (not from the tools) is that it is a pseudogene in most humans, which would fit the "Not detected" result. If it is expressed, fold the pair and check whether the interface is on GPR33's extracellular side and whether any of its 4 glycosylation sites fall on it. CFC1's curated partners are NODAL receptor complexes (ACVR1B/ACVR1C with ACVR2A/ACVR2B), so folding CFC1 against those would be a useful specificity control. No fold was run for this triage.

The pair is novel (no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed hit) and both are plasma-membrane receptors per UniProt, so a cis interaction is topologically possible. But HPA returned no subcellular location for either protein and no informative expression (both low tissue specificity; GPR4 single-cell 'Not detected'), so co-expression cannot be supported from the data pulled. The AF3 signal is only moderate (ipTM 0.58, interface pLDDT 62.7, min separation 1.79 Å suggesting clashes), and PLXND1 carries 18 glycosylation sites and GPR4 2, none of which were modelled.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: PLXND1 is a glycoprotein with 18 annotated glycosylation sites (on a large ectodomain); GPR4 is a glycoprotein with 2 sites. The PubMed PTM hits for both were non-specific and did not address glycosylation of the relevant domains. With a large buried surface (3459 Å2), an interface on PLXND1's ectodomain could plausibly overlap glycan sites, but no per-residue interface data was available to check.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence returned 0 papers mentioning PLXND1 and GPR4 together.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction (GPR4 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is novel as far as these sources show.
Other subunits
SEMA3E;NRP1
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Inspect the AF3 model for interface topology: an interface touching both extracellular and cytoplasmic residues would be an artifact. 2) Map PLXND1's 18 and GPR4's 2 N-glycosylation sites against the interface residues, and re-fold with glycans if any overlap. 3) Check endothelial single-cell datasets for co-expression. 4) Consider re-folding with the known PLXND1 ligand SEMA3E; SEMA3E and NRP1 are suggested from UniProt function text and general knowledge, not from a complex database (CellPhoneDB returned no complexes for either protein). 5) The 1.79 Å minimum separation suggests clashes, so relax the model before interpreting contacts.

SORL1 ↔ GPR52 LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM low confidence ipTM 0.58 · pTM 0.45
Rationale
The pair is novel (no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed hit), brain co-expression is plausible, and both proteins are membrane proteins that could meet at the cell surface or in endosomes. However, UniProt lists 27 glycosylation sites on SORL1 and 3 on GPR52, so a very large modeled interface (BSA ~4389 Å2, 810 contacts) at only borderline confidence (ipTM 0.58, interface pLDDT 61) could plausibly be occluded by glycans AF3 did not model. Whether any glycan site actually sits on the interface was not checked, so this is a caveat-driven call, not a demonstrated artifact.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: SORL1 is a Glycoprotein with 27 annotated glycosylation sites and 39 disulfide bonds, on its large ectodomain; GPR52 is a Glycoprotein with 3 glycosylation sites. PubMed returned a 2025 Nat Chem Biol paper titled "Post-translational modifications orchestrate the intrinsic signaling bias of GPR52"; the SORL1 PTM search hits were mostly not about glycosylation. The glycan density makes interference with a large ectodomain interface plausible, but per-residue overlap with the modeled interface was not verified.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-mention count is 0.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction (GPR52 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 papers. The pair is novel with respect to these sources.
Follow-up (not yet executed): Map the 27 SORL1 and 3 GPR52 UniProt glycosylation sites onto the modeled interface residues, and check the interface topology (extracellular vs TM vs cytoplasmic) to rule out a mixed-side or bare TM-helix packing artifact. If glycan sites are on the interface, re-fold with glycans attached; folding only the SORL1 domain(s) in contact with GPR52 would also be more informative than the 2575-token full complex. If the interface survives, test by co-IP or proximity labelling in striatal neurons, and check whether SORL1 alters GPR52 surface levels or trafficking, consistent with its sorting-receptor role.

  "function": "Sorting receptor that directs several proteins to their correct location within the cell (Probable). Along with AP-1 complex, involved Golgi apparatus - endosome sorting (PubMed:17646382). Sorting receptor for APP, regulating its intracellular trafficking and processing into amyloidogenic-beta peptides. Retains APP in the trans-Golgi network, hence preventing its transit through late endosomes where amyloid beta peptides Abeta40 and Abeta42 are generated (PubMed:16174740, PubMed:16407538, PubMed:17855360, PubMed:24523320). May also sort newly produced amyloid-beta peptides to lysosomes for catabolism (PubMed:24523320). Does not affect APP trafficking from the endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi compartments (PubMed:17855360). Sorting receptor for the BDNF receptor NTRK2/TRKB that facilitates NTRK2 trafficking between synaptic plasma membranes, postsynaptic densities and cell soma, hence positively regulates BDNF signaling by controlling the intracellular location of its receptor (PubMed:23977241). Sorting receptor for GDNF that promotes GDNF regulated, but not constitutive secretion (PubMed:21994944). Sorting receptor for the GDNF-GFRA1 complex, directing it from the cell surface to endosomes. GDNF is then targeted to lysosomes and degraded, while its receptor GFRA1 recycles back to the cell membrane, resulting in a GDNF clearance pathway. The SORL1-GFRA1 complex further targets RET for endocytosis, but not for degradation, affecting GDNF-induced neurotrophic activities (PubMed:23333276). Sorting receptor for ERBB2/HER2. Regulates ERBB2 subcellular distribution by promoting its recycling after internalization from endosomes back to the plasma membrane, hence stimulating phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)-dependent ERBB2 signaling. In ERBB2-dependent cancer cells, promotes cell proliferation (PubMed:31138794). Sorting receptor for lipoprotein lipase LPL. Promotes LPL localization to endosomes and later to the lysosomes, leading to degradation of newly synthesized LPL (PubMed:21385844). Potential sorting receptor for APOA5, inducing APOA5 internalization to early endosomes, then to late endosomes, wherefrom a portion is sent to lysosomes and degradation, another portion is sorted to the trans-Golgi network (PubMed:18603531). Sorting receptor for the insulin receptor INSR. Promotes recycling of internalized INSR via the Golgi apparatus back to the cell surface, thereby preventing lysosomal INSR catabolism, increasing INSR cell surface expression and strengthening insulin signal reception in adipose tissue. Does not affect INSR internalization (PubMed:27322061). Plays a role in renal ion homeostasis, controlling the phospho-regulation of SLC12A1/NKCC2 by STK39/SPAK kinase and PPP3CB/calcineurin A beta phosphatase, possibly through intracellular sorting of STK39 and PPP3CB (By similarity). Stimulates, via the N-terminal ectodomain, the proliferation and migration of smooth muscle cells, possibly by increasing cell surface expression of the urokinase receptor uPAR/PLAUR. This may promote extracellular matrix proteolysis and hence facilitate cell migration (PubMed:14764453). By acting on the migration of intimal smooth muscle cells, may accelerate intimal thickening following vascular injury (PubMed:14764453). Promotes adhesion of monocytes (PubMed:23486467). Stimulates proliferation and migration of monocytes/macrophages (By similarity). Through its action on intimal smooth muscle cells and macrophages, may accelerate intimal thickening and macrophage foam cell formation in the process of atherosclerosis (By similarity). Regulates hypoxia-enhanced adhesion of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells to the bone marrow stromal cells via a PLAUR-mediated pathway. This function is mediated by the N-terminal ectodomain (PubMed:23486467). Metabolic regulator, which functions to maintain the adequate balance between lipid storage and oxidation in response to changing environmental conditions, such as temperature and diet. The N-terminal ectodomain negatively regulates adipose tissue energy expenditure, acting through the inhibition the BMP/Smad pathway (By similarity). Sorting receptor that may regulate signaling by the heterodimeric neurotrophic cytokine CLCF1-CRLF1 bound to the CNTFR receptor by promoting the endocytosis of the tripartite complex CLCF1-CRLF1-CNTFR and lysosomal degradation (PubMed:26858303). May regulate IL6 signaling, decreasing cis signaling, possibly by interfering with IL6-binding to membrane-bound IL6R, while up-regulating trans signaling via soluble IL6R (PubMed:28265003)",

LAIR1 ↔ GPR65 CONFIRMED_NOVEL VALIDATE low confidence ipTM 0.58 · pTM 0.55
Rationale
No prior record of this pair (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB not found, PubMed co-occurrence 0), and both are membrane receptors with overlapping lymphoid/immune expression, so a cis interaction in the same membrane is physically possible. Support is weak: ipTM 0.58 is only just above threshold, partner pLDDT is 53.5, and the very large interface (BSA 4476 Å2, 995 contacts) may be non-specific packing of LAIR1's single TM helix against the GPCR bundle, which AF3 produces without a bilayer. Both are glycoproteins (LAIR1 1 site, GPR65 3 sites) and I could not check whether those sites sit on the modeled interface, so this is a novel but unverified hypothesis.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: LAIR1 has Glycoprotein and Phosphoprotein keywords, 1 glycosylation site and 2 modified residues (ITIM tyrosine phosphorylation recruits PTPN6/PTPN11). GPR65 has the Glycoprotein keyword and 3 glycosylation sites (extracellular N-terminus/loops expected). The PubMed PTM searches (32 and 6 hits) returned mostly unrelated functional papers. Neither protein's function text describes a glycan-mediated binding mechanism (LAIR1's known ligand is collagen; GPR65 senses protons). Whether any glycosylation site lies on the modeled interface is unknown because no per-residue or fold check was run, so this is a caveat rather than grounds for an artifact call.
PubMed co-occurrence
pubmed_cooccurrence returned 0 hits for LAIR1 + GPR65.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no match (GPR65 is not in the CellPhoneDB gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 papers. No hit anywhere, so the pair is novel.
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Inspect the AF3 model to see whether the interface is TM-helix packing (LAIR1 TM against the GPR65 bundle) or ectodomain–extracellular loop contact, and confirm it does not mix cytoplasmic and extracellular residues. 2) Map LAIR1's single N-glycosylation site and GPR65's three sites onto the interface; if any lie on it, re-fold with glycans attached. 3) Run a specificity control by folding LAIR1 against two or three unrelated class-A GPCRs; similar ipTM would indicate generic TM packing. 4) Validate experimentally by co-IP or proximity ligation/BRET in a cell type expressing both (e.g. monocytes/macrophages or mast cells). No CORUM check was available, and CellPhoneDB complex lookup found nothing for either protein.
Validation strategy: PLA (co-localization)
Why this method
Both are membrane proteins expected in the same immune cell, and the hypothesis is a cis interaction in one membrane. PLA tests in-situ proximity (<40 nm) in native membranes without detergent solubilisation. Detergent could break or create GPCR/TM-helix associations, so co-IP is less suitable. Neither protein is a secreted ligand, so a stimulation assay doesn't fit.
Target tissue(s)
bone marrow, lymphoid tissue, lung
Why these tissues (HPA)
Both show RNA in bone marrow and lymphoid tissue (LAIR1 lymphoid 44.5 nTPM; GPR65 bone marrow 11.9 and lymphoid 9.1 nTPM). LAIR1 protein is high in bone marrow, lymphoid tissue and lung. Lung is included as a LAIR1 protein-positive tissue that also contains mast cells (GPR65 single-cell peak, 495 nCPM), but GPR65 expression there is not shown in the data given.
Cell type(s)
Mast cells, Microglia, Lymphoid/myeloid immune cells (T cells, monocytes/macrophages)
Protocol notes
1) Use a cell system that expresses both proteins, such as human mast cell lines (LAD2, HMC-1), primary monocytes/T cells, or tonsil/lymph node sections. Add a HEK293 model with tagged LAIR1 and GPR65 for antibody validation and clean positive/negative arms. 2) Use mild fixation (4% PFA, no permeabilisation or only light permeabilisation) with a mouse anti-LAIR1 extracellular-domain antibody and a rabbit anti-GPR65 antibody. Use species-matched PLA probes, and add anti-tag antibodies in the HEK293 model if the endogenous antibodies are poor. 3) GPR65 is annotated as vesicular in HPA, so co-stain for the plasma membrane (e.g. WGA or CD45) and an endosome marker (EEA1 or LAMP1). Quantify PLA dots per cell at the surface versus in vesicles. 4) Run a pH series (7.4 vs 6.5), since GPR65 is a proton-sensing receptor, and check whether LAIR1 crosslinking with collagen or an agonist antibody changes the signal.
Controls
Positive: a known LAIR1-proximal pair (LAIR1 with SHP-1 or with itself, via two LAIR1 antibodies) and a known GPR65 partner or a GPR65 homodimer pair. Negative: single-antibody PLA, PLA in LAIR1 or GPR65 CRISPR-KO or siRNA cells, and LAIR1 with an unrelated abundant membrane protein (e.g. CD45 or an unrelated GPCR) to check for crowding artifacts. Extra specificity control: HEK293 cells expressing only one partner, or each partner co-expressed with an unrelated single-TM protein and an unrelated GPCR.
Caveats
Confidence is low: ipTM 0.58, GPR65 pLDDT 53.5, and a very large interface (4476 Å2) that is probably non-specific packing of LAIR1's single TM helix against the GPCR bundle, which AF3 produces without a bilayer. A positive PLA only shows proximity, and abundant membrane proteins can give false positives. LAIR1 (1 N-glycan site) and GPR65 (3 sites) are glycoproteins, and I did not check whether those sites lie on the modelled interface. Glycans could block the interface, so the AF3 pose is not guaranteed in vivo. If PLA is positive, test for a glycan role with PNGase F/Endo H treatment or glycan-site mutants. GPR65 is mainly vesicular in HPA, so it may not meet LAIR1 at the plasma membrane. HPA gives no GPR65 protein-level data, and mast cells are not among LAIR1's listed cell types (microglia), so the cell-level overlap is uncertain. Antibody quality is also a risk.

Rationale
No prior evidence for this pair (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB not found, PubMed 0 hits), so it is novel, but the model is unlikely to be trustworthy. UniProt describes CD22 as a siglec whose binding to surface partners is through alpha2,6-sialic acid glycans, and its ectodomain carries 11 annotated glycosylation sites, none of which AF3's bare-sequence fold represents. The fold itself is marginal (ipTM 0.57, interface pLDDT 60, minimum separation 1.64 Å with 1242 contacts and 4273 Å2 buried), which looks more like an over-packed or clashing interface than a clean one.
PTM / glycosylation
CD22 (UniProt P20273): keywords Glycoprotein and Lectin, 11 glycosylation sites, and a function text stating it binds alpha2,6-linked sialic acid on surface molecules in cis and trans. The 171 PubMed hits include work on CD22 cis-ligands. GPR25 (O00155): no annotated glycosylation sites and 0 PubMed PTM hits, so a genuine sialoglycan-mediated CD22–GPR25 contact is not supported either. Whether CD22 glycan sites sit on the modeled interface was not tested per residue.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence count is 0.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction; GPR25 is not in its gene table. PubMed co-occurrence: 0. The pair is novel; GPR25's only documented ligand is CXCL17.
Other subunits

Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run for this triage. Inspect the AF3 model for (a) clashes, given the 1.64 Å minimum separation, (b) whether the interface mixes extracellular and cytoplasmic residues, and (c) whether CD22 N-glycosylation sites lie on the interface. If the interface is ectodomain-to-ectodomain, re-fold with CD22 glycans attached. If it is the CD22 cytoplasmic ITIM tail against GPR25 intracellular loops, treat it as likely low-specificity. Before any wet-lab work, confirm that GPR25 and CD22 are expressed in the same or adjacent lymphocyte populations.

CD244 ↔ GPR34 LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM low confidence ipTM 0.57 · pTM 0.48
Rationale
The pair is novel (no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed hit) and both are cell-surface immune proteins, so contact is physically possible. But the fold is marginal (ipTM 0.57, partner pLDDT 58.1), and UniProt lists 8 N-glycosylation sites on CD244 and 5 on GPR34 that AF3 did not model. GPR34's documented ligand is a lipid (lysophosphatidylserine) and CD244's is CD48, so nothing supports a specific protein-protein interface here. No fold was run in this session, so whether any glycan site actually sits on the modeled interface is unverified; the verdict rests on the density of glycosylation, not on a confirmed site.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: CD244 carries the Glycoprotein keyword with 8 glycosylation sites (plus Phosphoprotein, relevant only to its cytoplasmic tail motifs); GPR34 carries Glycoprotein with 5 glycosylation sites. The PubMed PTM searches (28 hits for CD244, 8 for GPR34) returned mostly general signalling papers and nothing site-specific. This many unmodeled glycans on two ectodomains is plausibly relevant to any extracellular interface, but whether a site sits on the modeled interface was not determined.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence count is 0.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction, and GPR34 is not in its gene table. PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is genuinely unreported.
Other subunits
CD48;SH2D1A;SH2D1B
Follow-up (not yet executed): Run the fold with structural analysis to check (1) the interface topology labels, to see whether the contact is ectodomain-to-ectodomain, transmembrane helix packing, or an impossible mix of cytoplasmic and extracellular residues; and (2) whether any of the 8 CD244 or 5 GPR34 N-glycosylation sites lie on the interface. If one does, re-fold with the glycan attached. The very large buried surface (4179 Å2, 866 contacts) may reflect CD244's single helix packing against the GPR34 transmembrane bundle rather than a specific interface; AF3 models no lipid bilayer, so this needs direct inspection. Compare against a CD244–CD48 fold as a positive control. If the interface survives, test by co-immunoprecipitation or a cell-surface binding assay with glycosylated proteins.

  "function": "Heterophilic receptor of the signaling lymphocytic activation molecule (SLAM) family; its ligand is CD48. SLAM receptors triggered by homo- or heterotypic cell-cell interactions are modulating the activation and differentiation of a wide variety of immune cells and thus are involved in the regulation and interconnection of both innate and adaptive immune response. Activities are controlled by presence or absence of small cytoplasmic adapter proteins, SH2D1A/SAP and/or SH2D1B/EAT-2. Acts as activating natural killer (NK) cell receptor (PubMed:10359122, PubMed:11714776, PubMed:8376943). Activating function implicates association with SH2D1A and FYN (PubMed:15713798). Downstreaming signaling involves predominantly VAV1, and, to a lesser degree, INPP5D/SHIP1 and CBL. Signal attenuation in the absence of SH2D1A is proposed to be dependent on INPP5D and to a lesser extent PTPN6/SHP-1 and PTPN11/SHP-2 (PubMed:10934222, PubMed:15713798). Stimulates NK cell cytotoxicity, production of IFN-gamma and granule exocytosis (PubMed:11714776, PubMed:8376943). Optimal expansion and activation of NK cells seems to be dependent on the engagement of CD244 with CD48 expressed on neighboring NK cells (By similarity). Acts as costimulator in NK activation by enhancing signals by other NK receptors such as NCR3 and NCR1 (PubMed:10741393). At early stages of NK cell differentiation may function as an inhibitory receptor possibly ensuring the self-tolerance of developing NK cells (PubMed:11917118). Involved in the regulation of CD8(+) T-cell proliferation; expression on activated T-cells and binding to CD48 provides costimulatory-like function for neighboring T-cells (By similarity). Rationale
The pair is novel (no STRING, CellPhoneDB or PubMed hit) and biologically compatible: both are brain-expressed plasma-membrane proteins per HPA and UniProt. However, UniProt annotates 9 glycosylation sites on LRRC4B (an LRR/Ig synaptic adhesion protein) and 3 on GPR6, and AF3 modelled neither; the fold is also borderline (ipTM 0.57, partner pLDDT 62.6) with a very large interface (BSA 4891 Å2, 810 contacts) for a GPCR with little exposed extracellular surface. Whether any glycan site actually lies on the modelled interface was not checked, so the artifact call is a suspicion, not a demonstrated result.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: LRRC4B is a Glycoprotein with 9 annotated glycosylation sites, which for an LRR/Ig adhesion protein would be on the ectodomain (the only region that could contact GPR6's extracellular face). GPR6 is a Glycoprotein with 3 glycosylation sites and a Lipoprotein with 1 palmitoylation site. The PubMed PTM search gave 0 hits for LRRC4B and 8 non-specific hits for GPR6 (general GPCR signalling and transcriptomics papers, not PTM studies). No per-residue check was done, so it is unknown whether any glycan site is at the modelled interface.
PubMed co-occurrence
pubmed_cooccurrence returned 0 hits for LRRC4B + GPR6.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction (GPR6 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 papers. The pair is genuinely unreported.
Other subunits
PTPRF
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Map the 9 LRRC4B and 3 GPR6 N-glycosylation sites onto the modelled interface residues; if any are there, re-fold with the glycans attached. 2) Check the interface topology in the 3D model: a 4891 Å2 interface on a GPCR may involve transmembrane or cytoplasmic residues contacting the LRRC4B ectodomain, which would be physically impossible. 3) LRRC4B's known trans-synaptic partner is PTPRF (UniProt function text, by similarity); consider whether GPR6 would compete with it for the LRR surface. 4) If the interface survives these checks, test by co-immunoprecipitation or a cell-surface binding assay in neurons or HEK cells.

CCL11 ↔ GPR132 CONFIRMED_NOVEL VALIDATE low confidence ipTM 0.56 · pTM 0.66
Rationale
CCL11 is a secreted chemokine (HPA: secreted to blood; UniProt: Secreted) and GPR132 is a 7-TM cell-membrane GPCR (UniProt), so a ligand-receptor pairing is compartment-plausible, and STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence all returned nothing for the pair. Confidence is low because the fold is only marginally above threshold (ipTM 0.56, p_twoway 0.0499), CCL11's documented receptor is CCR3, GPR132 is annotated as a receptor for oxidized fatty acids and protons rather than chemokines, and both proteins carry one glycosylation site whose position relative to the modeled interface was not checked.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists the Glycoprotein keyword and 1 glycosylation site for each protein. The PubMed PTM searches were uninformative: 74 hits for CCL11 whose top titles are allergy/inflammation papers, and 1 hit for GPR132 on lactate signalling. Whether either glycan sits on the modeled interface is unknown, so this is a caveat rather than grounds for an artifact call. Neither protein's function text describes a glycan-mediated protein-binding mechanism.
PubMed co-occurrence
pubmed_cooccurrence returned 0 hits for CCL11 + GPR132.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no curated interaction (GPR132 is not in the CellPhoneDB gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 papers. Nothing indicates this pair is already known.
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run here. (1) Inspect the AF3 model to confirm CCL11 contacts the extracellular face or TM-bundle opening of GPR132 and not cytoplasmic loops. (2) Check whether the CCL11 glycosylation site or the GPR132 glycosylation site lies in the interface, and re-fold with the glycan attached if so. (3) Counter-screen by folding CCL11 against CCR3 as a positive control and against unrelated class-A GPCRs, to see whether ipTM ~0.56 is specific or generic chemokine-GPCR docking. (4) Test experimentally with a GPR132 beta-arrestin or Gq/IP1 assay with recombinant CCL11, or a binding competition assay.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Recombinant CCL11 on GPR132-expressing vs. parental cells, with CCR3 as a positive control for CCL11 and a glycosidase/glycosylation-site mutant arm)
Why this method
CCL11 is a secreted chemokine and GPR132 is a 7-TM GPCR, so this is a paracrine ligand-receptor pair. A functional readout (G-protein/β-arrestin signalling) tests whether CCL11 activates GPR132 and is more informative than co-localization. HPA gives no tissue-level GPR132 data, so a PLA in tissue isn't feasible.
Target tissue(s)
Fibroblasts (CCL11 source; HPA single-cell nCPM 44.2), Blood (CCL11 secretome location: secreted to blood), Immune cells such as macrophages and eosinophils (GPR132 candidate side; to be confirmed experimentally)
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA gives no tissue-level RNA or protein specificity for either gene. The only expression data is CCL11 RNA in fibroblasts (44.2 nCPM), and CCL11 is annotated as secreted to blood. There is no real overlap, so the assay uses a recombinant ligand or fibroblast co-culture on a receptor-expressing cell. GPR132 expression in the responder cells must be verified by qPCR first.
Cell type(s)
Fibroblasts (CCL11 secreting), GPR132-transfected HEK293 or CHO cells, Macrophages or other immune cells endogenously expressing GPR132
Protocol notes
1) Generate HEK293 (or CHO) cells stably expressing tagged GPR132 and parental or empty-vector controls. Confirm surface expression by FLAG/HA staining. Add a CCR3-expressing line as a CCL11 positive control. 2) Stimulate with recombinant human CCL11 (dose range 1 nM–1 µM, 5–60 min). Read out Gi/Gq/Gs signalling (cAMP, Ca2+ flux, or IP1), β-arrestin recruitment (e.g. PathHunter/BRET), and ERK phosphorylation. Optionally measure transwell chemotaxis. 3) Test fibroblast-conditioned medium or co-culture, with a CCL11-neutralizing antibody or CCL11 knockdown as a specificity control. 4) Run a binding check (e.g. fluorescent CCL11 binding or a BRET ligand-binding assay) to separate direct binding from indirect effects. Include the glycosidase arm described in the variant.
Controls
Positive: CCL11 on CCR3-expressing cells (calcium flux, chemotaxis). Positive for GPR132 function: its known agonist 9-HODE, or acidic pH/proton stimulation. Negative: parental or empty-vector cells, heat-denatured CCL11, an unrelated chemokine (e.g. CCL2), a CCR3 antagonist to rule out endogenous CCR3 signalling, and a GPR132-knockout or siRNA arm in endogenous cells.
Caveats
Confidence is low: ipTM 0.56 and p_twoway 0.0499 are only marginally above threshold. CCL11's established receptor is CCR3, and GPR132 is known as a receptor for oxidized fatty acids and protons. Any signal could therefore come from endogenous CCR3/ACKR receptors or from pH effects of the buffer, so control the buffer pH. Both proteins have one glycosylation site, and its position relative to the modeled interface was not checked. AF3 may have modeled a bare-sequence interface that a glycan blocks in reality, so a negative result in glycosylated protein, or a positive result only without glycan, would be informative. HPA lists GPR132 as 'predicted intracellular', and it has no tissue or cell-type RNA data, so confirm surface localization and endogenous expression.

SELPLG ↔ GPR171 LIKELY_ARTIFACT_PTM low confidence ipTM 0.56 · pTM 0.48
Rationale
No prior evidence for the pair (STRING and CellPhoneDB miss; the single PubMed hit is a GVHD transcriptomic gene list), and both are lymphoid-enhanced membrane proteins, so the pair is novel and broadly compatible. But UniProt describes SELPLG (PSGL-1) as a SLe(x)-type proteoglycan with Glycoprotein, Sialic acid and Sulfation keywords, whose known binding is glycan- and sulfotyrosine-dependent; AF3's bare-sequence model cannot represent that. The fold is also marginal (ipTM 0.56, partner pLDDT 32.5, interface pLDDT 64.4), consistent with a large low-confidence contact (BSA 3300 Å2) on a disordered mucin-like chain.
PTM / glycosylation
SELPLG (UniProt): function text "SLe(x)-type proteoglycan"; keywords Glycoprotein, Sialic acid, Sulfation, Phosphoprotein; 4 annotated glycosylation sites and 6 modified residues. PSGL-1 is, from general knowledge, a heavily O-glycosylated mucin, so its extracellular domain is unlikely to present a bare peptide surface. GPR171 (UniProt): Glycoprotein, 1 glycosylation site. The PubMed PTM searches returned nothing relevant (SELPLG 1 unrelated hit, GPR171 0). Whether any of these sites sits on the modeled interface was not determined.
PubMed co-occurrence
One PubMed hit (PMID 41855695), a GVHD transcriptomic/machine-learning gene signature paper; it co-mentions the genes and gives no evidence of a direct interaction.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no curated interaction. PubMed co-occurrence: 1 hit (PMID 41855695), a machine-learning transcriptomic study of GVHD immune genes, not a binding report. The pair is effectively novel.
Follow-up (not yet executed): Inspect the model to see whether the interface uses the SELPLG extracellular mucin domain (glycan-occluded, likely artifact), the TM helix (possible nonspecific helix packing), or an impossible mix of cytoplasmic and extracellular residues. If the interface is TM- or cytoplasmic-only, re-evaluate. Otherwise re-fold with the glycans and sulfotyrosines represented, or test directly by co-IP or proximity ligation in T cells.

FPR2 ↔ GPR183 IMPLAUSIBLE low confidence ipTM 0.56 · pTM 0.66
Rationale
I'm changing the verdict. The flagged contradiction is valid: both FPR2 and GPR183 are plasma-membrane receptors and neither is secreted, so a direct contact would need both on the same cell. HPA shows no shared protein-level tissue and no overlapping enriched cell types, so the data give no route for them to meet. My earlier support was an inference from receptor class. Both are immune Gi-coupled GPCRs, and each heteromerises with other partners (FPR1 for FPR2, CXCR5 for GPR183). That does not show these two are co-expressed. Nothing else supports the pair. STRING and CellPhoneDB have no entry, and the one PubMed hit is a CD nomenclature catalogue, not an interaction report. The fold_evidence_status is not_run, so there is no structural evidence in the flagged data to offset the expression gap. The AF3 ipTM of 0.56 is modest, and 7TM bundles pack together non-specifically. I could not rule out co-expression in some monocyte or macrophage subset, so confidence is low. The FPR2 glycosylation site position was never checked, but it does not change the conclusion.
PTM / glycosylation
FPR2 is a glycoprotein with 1 annotated site, and its position was not checked. GPR183 has no annotated glycosylation. Neither receptor is a lectin, and neither has a glycan-mediated ligand mechanism. The glycosylation point is not decisive.
PubMed co-occurrence
One PubMed hit, a nomenclature / antibody-validation survey of immune GPCRs; unrelated to any direct FPR2-GPR183 interaction.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: not found (GPR183 is not in its gene table). PubMed: 1 co-mention (PMID 41420480, CD nomenclature catalogue), which is not an interaction report. known_interaction_strength=none.
Other subunits
FPR1;CXCR5
Follow-up (not yet executed): If there is reason to think they are co-expressed, check single-cell data for monocyte or macrophage subsets that express both. Test heteromerisation experimentally, for example by BRET or proximity ligation in a cell type that expresses both.

  "protein_name": "N-formyl peptide receptor 2",
  "function": "Pattern recognition G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that recognizes peptides with N-terminal formyl methionine, which are derived from invading pathogens or host mitochondria as pathogen or damage-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs and DAMPs) (PubMed:1374236, PubMed:25605714, PubMed:35217703). Preferentially recognizes longer peptides or peptides with specific sequences such as the phenol-soluble modulin (PSM) family of formylated peptide toxins produced by Staphylococcus aureus (PubMed:30098280). Ligand binding causes a conformation change that triggers signaling via G(i)/GNAI1 inhibiting adenylate cyclase activity, leading to decreased intracellular cAMP levels (PubMed:40080544). In addition, can recognize a variety of chemically distinct endogenous ligands including proteins and lipids besides formylpeptides and thereby plays multiple roles in inflammation. Acts as a receptor for the chemokine-like protein FAM19A5, mediating FAM19A5-stimulated macrophage chemotaxis and the inhibitory effect on TNFSF11/RANKL-induced osteoclast differentiation (By similarity). Acts also as a ceramide membrane receptor, and long-chain ceramides (C14 to C20) binding induces conformational changes that inhibits diet-induced adipose thermogenesis (PubMed:40080544). Participates in neuroprotection via interaction with humanin/MT-RNR2 and Amyloid-beta protein 42, product of APP (PubMed:11689470, PubMed:35365641). Differential signaling is also defined by receptor oligomerization state. Binding of ANXA1 to FPR2 homodimer elicits activation of p38 MAPKinase pathway leading to HSPB1/HSP27 phosphorylation and IL10 production in monocytes.   "function": "G protein-coupled receptor expressed in lymphocytes that acts as a chemotactic receptor for B-cells, T-cells, splenic dendritic cells, monocytes/macrophages and astrocytes (By similarity). Receptor for oxysterol 7-alpha,25-dihydroxycholesterol (7-alpha,25-OHC) and other related oxysterols (PubMed:21796212, PubMed:22875855, PubMed:22930711). Mediates cell positioning and movement of a number of cells by binding the 7-alpha,25-OHC ligand that forms a chemotactic gradient (By similarity). Binding of 7-alpha,25-OHC mediates the correct localization of B-cells during humoral immune responses (By similarity). Guides B-cell movement along the B-cell zone-T-cell zone boundary and later to interfollicular and outer follicular regions (By similarity). Its specific expression during B-cell maturation helps position B-cells appropriately for mounting T-dependent antibody responses (By similarity). Collaborates with CXCR5 to mediate B-cell migration; probably by forming a heterodimer with CXCR5 that affects the interaction between of CXCL13 and CXCR5 (PubMed:22913878). Also acts as a chemotactic receptor for some T-cells upon binding to 7-alpha,25-OHC ligand (By similarity). Promotes follicular helper T (Tfh) cells differentiation by positioning activated T-cells at the follicle-T-zone interface, promoting contact of newly activated CD4 T-cells with activated dendritic cells and exposing them to Tfh-cell-promoting inducible costimulator (ICOS) ligand (By similarity). Expression in splenic dendritic cells is required for their homeostasis, localization and ability to induce B- and T-cell responses: GPR183 acts as a chemotactic receptor in dendritic cells that mediates the accumulation of CD4(+) dendritic cells in bridging channels (By similarity). Regulates migration of astrocytes and is involved in communication between astrocytes and macrophages (PubMed:25297897). Promotes osteoclast precursor migration to bone surfaces (By similarity). Signals constitutively through G(i)-alpha, but not G(s)-alpha or G(q)-alpha (PubMed:21673108, PubMed:25297897). Signals constitutively also via MAPK1/3 (ERK1/2) (By similarity)",

MET ↔ GPR21 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE medium confidence ipTM 0.56 · pTM 0.51
Rationale
No prior evidence for this pair (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB not found, 0 PubMed co-mentions), so it is novel, but the support is too thin to call it confirmed. HPA has no subcellular data for GPR21 and its RNA is "Not detected" in single-cell types (only blood vessel 5.1 nTPM), so coexpression with MET cannot be established. The AF3 signal is marginal (ipTM 0.56, interface pLDDT 49.4), and both proteins are glycoproteins (MET 14 annotated sites, GPR21 2) whose position relative to the modelled interface was not checked.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: MET is a Glycoprotein with 14 glycosylation sites (on its extracellular region, from background knowledge rather than tool output) and a Phosphoprotein; GPR21 is a Glycoprotein with 2 sites. The PubMed PTM search for MET (4,072 hits) was noise from the ambiguous symbol; the single GPR21 hit concerns plasmalogen signalling, not PTMs. Glycans could occlude an extracellular-side interface, but site positions relative to the modelled interface were not checked.
PubMed co-occurrence
pubmed_cooccurrence returned 0 hits for MET + GPR21.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no interaction (GPR21 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. Nothing known about this pair.
Other subunits
HGF
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run here. Inspect the AF3 model to see whether the interface is TM-helix/cytoplasmic or involves the MET ectodomain (heavily glycosylated), and check for an interface that touches both cytoplasmic and extracellular residues at once (a physically impossible artifact). HGF (listed under other_subunits) is MET's cognate ligand from its UniProt function text, suggested as an optional re-fold partner rather than a known member of a MET–GPR21 complex; MET has 147 HPA-listed interactors and no CellPhoneDB complex. If the interface looks topologically sensible, test GPR21 expression in MET-positive cells (hepatocytes, intestinal epithelium, endothelium) and try co-IP or BRET in a co-expressing system.

PPIA ↔ GPR75 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE low confidence ipTM 0.56 · pTM 0.51
Rationale
The panel-breadth flag is valid. PPIA cleared the confidence gate against 4 of 11 receptors (36%), so the PPIA<->GPR75 fold says more about PPIA than about GPR75. PPIA is an abundant, sticky hub with 195 known interactions, and that fits the non-specific explanation. The breadth is not obviously biological. PPIA's one well-documented receptor is BSG/CD147, and nothing suggests it is a shared ligand for many GPCRs. The fold itself is modest (ipTM 0.56, interface pLDDT 68.2), so it cannot make up for the missing specificity. Nothing else supports the pair: STRING and CellPhoneDB have no record, and PubMed co-occurrence is 0. HPA only says the pair is compartment-compatible (plausible), which is weak. The glycosylation question is also still open, because GPR75 has 3 glycosylation sites and none was mapped against the interface. I am withdrawing CONFIRMED_NOVEL, since the fold does not show specificity for this pair, but I am not calling it IMPLAUSIBLE, because the compartments are compatible. The evidence is insufficient to decide either way.
PTM / glycosylation
GPR75 has 3 glycosylation sites, and their positions relative to the modeled interface were not checked. This is a caveat only.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence count is 0 for PPIA and GPR75.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING not found, CellPhoneDB not found, PubMed co-occurrence 0. No prior record of the pair (known_interaction_strength=none).
Other subunits
BSG;CCL5
Follow-up (not yet executed): Check the PPIA fold against a negative-control receptor set to see whether its 4/11 hit rate is generic. Also test whether the GPR75 interface lies on extracellular loops near the glycosylation sites. Only treat the pair as novel if it is selective compared with the other receptors.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Recombinant PPIA (+/- CsA/PPIA catalytic-dead R55A, +/- CCL5 and BSG co-stimulation) on GPR75-expressing vs GPR75-knockout cells, with a PNGase F/glycosylation-site mutant arm as a secondary check)
Why this method
PPIA is secreted to blood and GPR75 is a plasma-membrane GPCR, so this is an extracellular ligand-receptor hypothesis. A functional GPCR readout is more informative than co-localization for this pair. GPR75 is known to couple to Gq/11 (CCL5 and 20-HETE signalling), so calcium and IP1 readouts are plausible.
Target tissue(s)
brain, retina
Why these tissues (HPA)
GPR75 RNA is tissue-enriched only in brain (9.8 nTPM) and retina (7.1 nTPM). PPIA is a housekeeping protein with very high, near-ubiquitous expression (e.g. 3194 nCPM in gastric progenitor cells) and is secreted to blood, so PPIA is available wherever GPR75 is. There is no tissue-specific PPIA restriction, so the receptor side determines the tissue choice. For the assay, use GPR75-expressing cells such as HEK293 transfectants, plus a brain/retina-derived line or primary cells, with recombinant PPIA supplied exogenously.
Cell type(s)
Neurons, Astrocytes, Retinal pigment epithelial cells, Photoreceptor/retinal neurons
Protocol notes
1) Use HEK293 cells stably expressing tagged GPR75 (HA- or FLAP-tagged, to confirm surface expression) and parental or GPR75-KO cells as the control. Optionally add a neuronal or RPE line with endogenous GPR75 (confirm by qPCR). Add a Gq-proximal readout: Fluo-4 calcium flux, IP-One HTRF, or NFAT-luciferase, plus ERK1/2 phosphorylation by western blot at 2-30 min. 2) Dose-response of endotoxin-free recombinant human PPIA (1 nM-10 µM), with heat-denatured PPIA as a protein control. Test CCL5 as a positive control for GPR75 activation. Test whether BSG/CD147 is required, by BSG knockdown or anti-CD147 blocking antibody, since PPIA signals via BSG and may produce a GPR75-independent response. 3) Confirm physical binding orthogonally: surface binding of biotin- or fluorophore-labelled PPIA to GPR75+ vs GPR75-KO cells by flow cytometry, or SPR/BLI with purified GPR75 or membrane preparations. Use cyclosporin A and PPIA R55A to test whether the isomerase active site is involved.
Controls
Positive: CCL5 (reported GPR75 ligand) and a Gq agonist such as carbachol or ATP for the assay window. Negative: parental/GPR75-KO cells, heat-denatured PPIA, an unrelated cyclophilin (PPIB), a GPCR-unrelated receptor-expressing line, and vehicle. For specificity, include an anti-CD147 blocking arm and a CsA arm.
Caveats
AF3 support is modest (ipTM 0.56, interface pLDDT 68.2), so the predicted interface may not be real. PPIA is an abundant hub with 195 known interactions, so non-specific binding is likely, and recombinant PPIA at high concentration can act through BSG/CD147 or other routes. GPR75 has 3 glycosylation sites, and their position relative to the predicted interface was not checked. Glycans could occlude or alter the interface, so run a glycosylation-site mutant (N-to-Q) or PNGase F arm for interpretation. The HPA data give no protein-level tissue data for either protein. GPR75 is a poorly characterised, low-expressed receptor, and antibodies and surface expression may be difficult. The proposed CCL5 and BSG partners are candidate co-factors, not confirmed members of a complex.
