input: {"gene": "CTSG"}
{
  "gene": "CTSG",
  "accession": "P08311",
  "protein_name": "Cathepsin G",
  "function": "Serine protease with trypsin- and chymotrypsin-like specificity (PubMed:29652924, PubMed:8194606). Also displays antibacterial activity against Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria independent of its protease activity (PubMed:2116408, PubMed:2117044). Prefers Phe and Tyr residues in the P1 position of substrates but also cleaves efficiently after Trp and Leu (PubMed:29652924). Shows a preference for negatively charged amino acids in the P2' position and for aliphatic amino acids both upstream and downstream of the cleavage site (PubMed:29652924). Required for recruitment and activation of platelets which is mediated by the F2RL3/PAR4 platelet receptor (PubMed:10702240, PubMed:3390156). Binds reversibly to and stimulates B cells and CD4(+) and CD8(+) T cells (PubMed:7842483, PubMed:9000539). Also binds reversibly to natural killer (NK) cells and enhances NK cell cytotoxicity through its protease activity (PubMed:9000539, PubMed:9536127). Cleaves complement C3 (PubMed:1861080). Cleaves vimentin (By similarity). Cleaves thrombin receptor F2R/PAR1 and acts as either an agonist or an inhibitor, depending on the F2R cleavage site (PubMed:10702240, PubMed:7744748). Cleavage of F2R at '41-Arg-|-Ser-42' results in receptor activation while cleavage at '55-Phe-|-Trp-56' results in inhibition of receptor activation (PubMed:7744748). Cleaves the synovial mucin-type protein PRG4/lubricin (PubMed:32144329). Cleaves and activates IL36G which promotes expression of chemokines CXCL1 and CXLC8 in keratinocytes (PubMed:30804664). Cleaves IL33 into mature forms which have greater activity than the unprocessed form (PubMed:22307629). Cleaves coagulation factor F8 to produce a partially activated form (PubMed:18217133). Also cleaves and activates coagulation factor F10 (PubMed:8920993). Cleaves leukocyte cell surface protein SPN/CD43 to release its extracellular domain and trigger its intramembrane proteolysis by gamma-secretase, releasing the CD43 cytoplasmic tail chain (CD43-ct) which translocates to the nucleus (PubMed:18586676). Cleaves CCL5/RANTES to produce RANTES(4-68) lacking the N-terminal three amino acids which exhibits reduced chemotactic and antiviral activities (PubMed:16963625). During apoptosis, cleaves SMARCA2/BRM to produce a 160 kDa cleavage product which localizes to the cytosol (PubMed:11259672). Cleaves myelin basic protein MBP in B cell lysosomes at '224-Phe-|-Lys-225' and '248-Phe-|-Ser-249', degrading the major immunogenic MBP epitope and preventing the activation of MBP-specific autoreactive T cells (PubMed:15100291). Cleaves annexin ANXA1 and antimicrobial peptide CAMP to produce peptides which act on neutrophil N-formyl peptide receptors to enhance the release of CXCL2 (PubMed:22879591). Acts as a ligand for the N-formyl peptide receptor FPR1, enhancing phagocyte chemotaxis (PubMed:15210802). Has antibacterial activity against the Gram-negative bacteria N.gonorrhoeae and P.aeruginosa (PubMed:1937776, PubMed:2116408). Likely to act against N.gonorrhoeae by interacting with N.gonorrhoeae penA/PBP2 (PubMed:2126324). Exhibits potent antimicrobial activity against the Gram-positive bacterium L.monocytogenes (PubMed:2117044). Has antibacterial activity against the Gram-positive bacterium S.aureus and degrades S.aureus biofilms, allowing polymorphonuclear leukocytes to penetrate the biofilm and phagocytose bacteria (PubMed:2117044, PubMed:32995850). PTPRD ↔ GPR52 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE medium confidence ipTM 0.5 · pTM 0.39
Rationale
No prior evidence links the pair (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB no match, PubMed 0 co-mentions), and both are brain-expressed membrane proteins, so the pair is novel and not ruled out. But the support is too weak to call CONFIRMED_NOVEL: the supplied AF3 metrics are borderline (ipTM 0.5, pTM 0.39, min interface PAE 9.34 Å, interface pLDDT 64.7), HPA has no subcellular or single-cell data for GPR52, and both proteins are N-glycosylated (UniProt: PTPRD 4 sites, GPR52 3 sites). The very large modelled interface (BSA 4304 Å2, 900 contacts, min separation 1.86 Å) on a small GPCR may span membrane-incompatible surfaces; I could not check which side of the membrane it falls on, and no fold was run.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists both as glycoproteins: PTPRD has 4 glycosylation sites on its extracellular Ig/FN3 domains, GPR52 has 3 on its extracellular N-terminus/loops. A PubMed hit (PMID 40087539) reports that post-translational modifications drive GPR52's intrinsic signalling bias. If the modelled interface is extracellular, glycans AF3 did not model could occlude it; whether any site sits on the interface is unknown because no per-residue interface data were available.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence count is 0.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: no association found. CellPhoneDB: no match (GPR52 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is unreported.
Other subunits
IL1RAP;IL1RAPL1;SLITRK2
Follow-up (not yet executed): 1) Inspect the AF3 model to see which PTPRD region (extracellular Ig/FN3 vs cytoplasmic phosphatase domains) contacts which GPR52 surface; an interface touching both extracellular and cytoplasmic residues would mark it as an artifact. 2) Re-fold trimmed constructs (PTPRD ectodomain or cytoplasmic D1/D2 domains against GPR52) to see whether ipTM rises clearly above 0.5; the full 2273-token complex dilutes confidence. 3) If the interface is extracellular, check whether the N-glycosylation sites of either protein lie on it and re-fold with glycans. 4) Confirm same-cell co-expression (e.g. striatal medium spiny neurons) in brain single-cell or spatial data. PTPRD's known trans-synaptic partners (IL1RAP, IL1RAPL1, SLITRK2, from UniProt) bind its Ig domains, so compare the modelled site with those to judge competition.

ADORA1 ↔ GPR62 CONFIRMED_NOVEL VALIDATE low confidence ipTM 0.5 · pTM 0.61
Rationale
No prior record of this pair (STRING not found, CellPhoneDB no match, PubMed 0 hits). Both are 7TM GPCRs with brain-elevated RNA and UniProt cell-membrane annotation, so a lateral GPCR heteromer in the same membrane is compartmentally plausible; UniProt also notes GPR62 likely heteromerizes with MTNR1B. Confidence is low because ipTM 0.5 sits exactly on the threshold, HPA shows no shared enriched cell type, GPR62 has no HPA localization data, and AF3 packing of two 7TM bundles without a bilayer is prone to non-specific interfaces.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt: ADORA1 is a glycoprotein and palmitoylated lipoprotein (1 glycosylation site, 1 lipidation site); GPR62 is a glycoprotein (2 glycosylation sites). The PubMed PTM search returned 6 hits for ADORA1, none clearly about its glycosylation in the titles shown, and 0 for GPR62. Whether any of these sites lies on the modeled interface was not checked; neither function text describes a glycan-mediated binding mechanism, so this is a minor caveat rather than grounds for an artifact call.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence count 0.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: no match (GPR62 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. Nothing indicates the pair is already known.
Other subunits
MTNR1B
Follow-up (not yet executed): No fold was run here. Inspect the AF3 model to confirm the interface is TM-helix to TM-helix in parallel orientation (not mixing cytoplasmic and extracellular residues) and that the glycosylation and palmitoylation sites are off the interface. Verify co-expression of ADORA1 and GPR62 in oligodendrocytes from full single-cell data. Test heteromerization by BRET/co-IP in co-transfected cells, with MTNR1B–GPR62 as a positive control and an unrelated GPCR as a specificity control; other_subunits lists MTNR1B as that reported GPR62 partner for comparison, not as a missing obligate subunit.
Validation strategy: PLA (co-localization)
Why this method
Both are plasma-membrane 7TM GPCRs expected in the same membrane, so a lateral heteromer is best tested by in situ proximity (<40 nm) in intact cells. PLA avoids detergent solubilisation, which often creates or destroys GPCR aggregates in co-IP. There is no known ligand pairing, so a stimulation assay has no obvious readout.
Target tissue(s)
brain (cerebral cortex), brain (white matter / corpus callosum), brain (hippocampus)
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA lists brain as the only tissue-enriched site for both: ADORA1 at 42.6 nTPM and GPR62 at 22.8 nTPM. Single-cell data do not overlap (ADORA1 in podocytes at 142 nCPM, GPR62 in oligodendrocytes at 29.5 nCPM), so brain regions where oligodendrocyte-lineage cells and ADORA1-positive neurons/glia sit close together are the best tissue targets. Cell-level co-expression must be confirmed first.
Cell type(s)
Oligodendrocytes, Oligodendrocyte precursor cells, Neurons (ADORA1-expressing)
Protocol notes
1) First run RT-qPCR or RNAscope for ADORA1 and GPR62 in human or mouse brain sections and in primary oligodendrocyte/OPC cultures, to find cells that express both. 2) Use a heterologous system as the main test: HEK293 cells transfected with tagged ADORA1 and GPR62 (HA/FLAG), with PLA on non-permeabilised cells using anti-tag antibodies, so only surface pairs are detected. Then do endogenous PLA on PFA-fixed brain sections or primary oligodendrocytes with validated antibodies from different host species. 3) Quantify PLA puncta per cell by confocal imaging. Optionally add MTNR1B co-expression, because UniProt reports GPR62 heteromerising with MTNR1B, to see whether the signal changes in a three-way complex. 4) Optionally follow up with an ADORA1 agonist (CPA) or antagonist (DPCPX) and a cAMP readout, to see whether GPR62 modulates ADORA1 Gi signalling.
Controls
Positive: a known GPCR heteromer pair, such as ADORA1–P2Y1 or ADORA1–A2A, or GPR62–MTNR1B if antibodies are available. Negative: a single-antibody PLA, cells expressing only one receptor, a non-interacting membrane protein of similar abundance (e.g. ADORA1 + an unrelated 7TM receptor or CD8-tagged construct), and, where possible, GPR62 knockout or siRNA knockdown to confirm the endogenous signal.
Caveats
Confidence is low: ipTM is about 0.5, and AF3 packing of two 7TM bundles without a lipid bilayer often produces non-specific interfaces. HPA shows no shared cell type (ADORA1 podocytes vs GPR62 oligodendrocytes), so the two may never meet in the same cell in vivo. GPR62 has no HPA localisation data and no validated antibodies, so epitope-tagged constructs may be needed, and overexpression can cause artefactual proximity. PLA shows proximity, not a direct interaction. Because GPCRs are densely packed in membranes, PLA positives need the negative-control receptors above.

PPIA ↔ GPR63 INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE medium confidence ipTM 0.5 · pTM 0.5
Rationale
The flagged contradiction holds. PPIA passed the confidence gate against 4 of the 11 receptors in this screen (36%), so the fold says more about PPIA than about GPR63. I see no biological reason for that breadth. PPIA is a small, abundant peptidyl-prolyl isomerase with about 195 known interactors, and its one established receptor is BSG/CD147, not a GPCR. The breadth looks like partner-driven stickiness, and the ipTM of 0.5 sits only at threshold, so CONFIRMED_NOVEL overstated the evidence. Nothing else contradicts the pair. STRING, CellPhoneDB and PubMed co-occurrence all show no prior record, and HPA compartments are plausible, with PPIA secreted and GPR63 at the plasma membrane. That is why I'm not calling it IMPLAUSIBLE, but compartment plausibility alone doesn't establish specificity. GPR63's 3 glycosylation sites were never checked against the interface, which is a further unresolved caveat. The pair is unsupported rather than confirmed.
PTM / glycosylation
UniProt lists 3 glycosylation sites on GPR63 and 1 on PPIA. Their position relative to the interface was not checked. PPIA also binds heparan sulfate. This is a caveat, not evidence of an artifact.
PubMed co-occurrence
PubMed co-occurrence for PPIA and GPR63 returned 0 papers.
STRING / CellPhoneDB
STRING: not found. CellPhoneDB: not found (GPR63 is not in its gene table). PubMed co-occurrence: 0 hits. The pair is not previously known, but a novel fold from a partner that is confident against 4 of 11 receptors is not evidence of a specific interaction.
Other subunits
BSG
Follow-up (not yet executed): Check whether the PPIA contacts differ between the 4 receptors where it was confident. If they land on the same PPIA surface, such as the active-site pocket, treat the signal as nonspecific. Compare ipTM for GPR63 against the other receptors in the panel. Map GPR63's glycosylation sites onto the modeled interface. Orthogonal validation would be needed before any novelty claim.
Validation strategy: Stimulation assay (Recombinant PPIA +/- BSG co-expression and +/- PNGase F / glycosylation-site mutant GPR63 arm)
Why this method
PPIA is a secreted protein and GPR63 is an orphan plasma-membrane GPCR, so this is a ligand-receptor hypothesis. A functional signalling readout (rather than proximity) tests whether PPIA actually engages and activates GPR63. Because PPIA is so abundant and sticky, binding alone would be hard to interpret.
Target tissue(s)
Choroid plexus (GPR63 side), Stomach (gastric mucosa, PPIA side), Blood/plasma (PPIA source), Brain
Why these tissues (HPA)
HPA gives no tissue-level overlap for the pair. PPIA is highest in gastric progenitor cells (nCPM ~3194) and is annotated as secreted to blood. GPR63 is enriched only in choroid plexus epithelial cells (nCPM ~115.8), so the pair is paracrine/endocrine, and the assay is run in engineered cells plus a choroid plexus-derived model. Any in vivo overlap would be through circulating or CSF PPIA.
Cell type(s)
Choroid plexus epithelial cells, Gastric progenitor cells
Protocol notes
1) Express GPR63 (tagged, e.g. N-terminal HA/FLAG, with surface expression confirmed by flow or ELISA) in HEK293 cells, with and without BSG/CD147 co-expression. Use mock-transfected cells and a parallel BSG-only line as controls. Also test a choroid plexus epithelial line (e.g. HIBCPP or Z310) for endogenous GPR63. 2) Stimulate with endotoxin-free recombinant human PPIA (dose range 1 nM to 1 µM, 5 to 60 min). Read out GPCR signalling in G-protein-agnostic ways: cAMP (GloSensor/HTRF, because GPR63 is reported to couple Gi/Gs/G12-type pathways), β-arrestin recruitment (PathHunter/NanoBiT), and SRE/NFAT/CRE reporters, plus pERK as the CD147 pathway readout. 3) Confirm direct binding with a orthogonal check: biotin-PPIA or His-PPIA pulldown from GPR63-expressing membranes, or a NanoBiT/BRET binding assay. Test cyclosporin A (a PPIA active-site inhibitor) and enzyme-dead PPIA R55A to see whether activity depends on the PPIase site. 4) Run the glycosylation arm in parallel: PNGase F or tunicamycin pretreatment, and N-to-Q mutants of the 3 predicted GPR63 N-glycosylation sites.
Controls
Positive: a known GPCR agonist for assay validity (e.g. forskolin for cAMP, or a reference receptor/ligand pair in the same cells) and PPIA-induced pERK in BSG-expressing cells (established CD147 axis). Negative: mock-transfected or empty-vector cells, heat-denatured PPIA, an unrelated cyclophilin (PPIB) or irrelevant protein at the same concentration, an unrelated GPCR expressed at similar levels, and GPR63 knockout or knockdown in the choroid plexus line.
Caveats
Confidence is low: ipTM is 0.5, only at threshold, and PPIA is a hub with 195 known interactors, so nonspecific stickiness is plausible. GPR63 has 3 unmodeled N-glycosylation sites, and their position relative to the predicted interface was not checked. A glycan could block or alter the interface, so the glycosidase and N-to-Q mutant arm is needed to interpret negative results. Any PPIA effect may be mediated by endogenous BSG/CD147 rather than GPR63, so BSG controls and GPR63 knockout are essential. GPR63 is an orphan receptor with no validated agonist or coupling assay, so the readout is uncertain. HPA also lists GPR63 in the nucleoplasm and cytosol as well as at the plasma membrane, so surface expression must be verified. HPA provides no tissue overlap, so physiological relevance is untested. Recombinant PPIA can carry endotoxin or tag artifacts.

  "function": "Catalyzes the cis-trans isomerization of proline imidic peptide bonds in oligopeptides (PubMed:2001362, PubMed:20676357, PubMed:21245143, PubMed:21593166, PubMed:25678563). Exerts a strong chemotactic effect on leukocytes partly through activation of one of its membrane receptors BSG/CD147, initiating a signaling cascade that culminates in MAPK/ERK activation (PubMed:11943775, PubMed:21245143). Activates endothelial cells (ECs) in a pro-inflammatory manner by stimulating activation of NF-kappa-B and ERK, JNK and p38 MAP-kinases and by inducing expression of adhesion molecules including SELE and VCAM1 (PubMed:15130913). Induces apoptosis in ECs by promoting the FOXO1-dependent expression of CCL2 and BCL2L11 which are involved in EC chemotaxis and apoptosis (PubMed:31063815). In response to oxidative stress, initiates pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic signaling in ECs via activation of NF-kappa-B and AKT1 and up-regulation of anti-apoptotic protein BCL2 (PubMed:23180369). Negatively regulates MAP3K5/ASK1 kinase activity, autophosphorylation and oxidative stress-induced apoptosis mediated by MAP3K5/ASK1 (PubMed:26095851). Necessary for the assembly of TARDBP in heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein (hnRNP) complexes and regulates TARDBP binding to RNA UG repeats and TARDBP-dependent expression of HDAC6, ATG7 and VCP which are involved in clearance of protein aggregates (PubMed:25678563). Plays an important role in platelet activation and aggregation (By similarity). Regulates calcium mobilization and integrin ITGA2B:ITGB3 bidirectional signaling via increased ROS production as well as by facilitating the interaction between integrin and the cell cytoskeleton (By similarity). Binds heparan sulfate glycosaminoglycans (PubMed:11943775). Inhibits replication of influenza A virus (IAV) (PubMed:19207730). Inhibits ITCH/AIP4-mediated ubiquitination of matrix protein 1 (M1) of IAV by impairing the interaction of ITCH/AIP4 with M1, followed by the suppression of the nuclear export of M1, and finally reduction of the replication of IAV (PubMed:22347431, PubMed:30328013) (Microbial infection) May act as a mediator between human SARS coronavirus nucleoprotein and BSG/CD147 in the process of invasion of host cells by the virus (PubMed:15688292) (Microbial infection) Stimulates RNA-binding ability of HCV NS5A in a peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase activity-dependent manner (Microbial infection) May act as a receptor for M.genitalium adhesin protein P140 (also called MgPa) (PubMed:29551599, PubMed:33013867)",
